Such faith is older than the activity of knowing, not only in us but among the gods themselves. By it all the gods are united, and about one centre gather all their powers and processions in a one-like way.

flags.taylor: neither gnostically
flags.why: Taylor's "gnostically" means by way of knowledge (gnōsis); Proclus means that the good is reached by a faith beyond knowing, not by an act of knowledge.

notes: "Faith, truth and love" is a triad of the Chaldean Oracles (frag. 46: "faith, truth and love", with hope), which Proclus finds in Plato as well.

paragraphs.modern: If we must define this faith more particularly, let no one suppose that it is the kind of belief concerned with what wanders among perceptible things. For this falls short of science, and much more of the truth of beings. But the faith of the gods goes beyond all knowledge, and joins second natures to first by the highest union. Nor, again, let anyone think it is a faith of the same kind as the famous belief in common notions; for we believe in common notions before all reasoning. But the knowledge of these is divided, and in no way equal to divine union; and the science of them comes not only after faith, but after intellectual simplicity too. For intellect is set above all science, both the first science and what comes after it. Nor, then, must we say that the activity of intellect is like this faith. For intellectual activity is of many forms, separated from what it thinks by difference; and, in short, it is intellectual motion about the intelligible. But divine faith must be one-like and still, wholly settled in the harbour of goodness. For neither the beautiful, nor wisdom, nor anything else among beings is so trustworthy and stable to all things, so free of all doubt, divided grasping and motion, as the good. Through it intellect too embraces another union older than intellectual activity, and before activity. And soul counts the variety of intellect and the splendour of Forms as nothing beside that transcendence of the good by which it is above the whole of things. It lets go of intellectual perception, running back to its own hyparxis; but it always pursues, seeks and longs for the good, hastens, as it were, to embrace it, and gives itself to this alone of all things without hesitation. But why speak of soul? These mortal living beings, as Diotima says somewhere, despise everything else, even life and being, through desire for the nature of the good; and all things have this one unmoving and inexpressible leaning to the good, while they pass over, put second and despise the order of everything else. This, then, is the one safe harbour of all beings.
notes: "Common notions" are the self-evident axioms all men grant before any proof. The Symposium 207a-208b: living things will fight, starve and die for their young, through love of the good and of immortality.

paragraphs.modern: This, too, is what all beings most of all believe in. And through this, joining and union with it is called faith by the theologians; and not by them alone, but also by Plato (if I may say what seems to me so), who proclaims in the Laws the kinship of this faith with truth and love. The many do not see that one who has an idea of these, speaking of their contraries, draws the same conclusion about the swervings from this triad. Plato clearly says in the Laws that the lover of falsehood is not to be trusted, and that he who is not to be trusted is without friends. So the lover of truth must be trustworthy, and he who is trustworthy must be well fitted for friendship. From these, then, we can see divine truth, faith and love, and grasp by reasoning their stable sharing with one another. If you are willing, let us first recall that Plato calls faithfulness the virtue that reconciles those who disagree and puts down the greatest of wars, I mean civil strife in cities. From this, faith appears to be the cause of union, sharing and stillness. And if there is such a power in us, it is far more, and first, in the gods themselves. For as Plato speaks of a divine temperance, justice and science, how could faith, which holds together the whole order of the virtues, not exist among the gods? In short, there are three things that fill divine natures and are the sources of fullness to all the higher kinds of beings: goodness, wisdom and beauty. And again there are three that gather together the natures that are filled, second to the former but running through all the divine orders: faith, truth and love. All things are saved through these and joined to their first causes: some through the frenzy of love, others through divine philosophy, others through theurgic power, which is better than all human wisdom, and holds within it the good of prophecy, the cleansing powers of perfecting good, and, in short, all that comes from being possessed by the gods. Of these things, perhaps, we will speak again at a better time.
notes: Laws V 730c: "the man who loves falsehood is not to be trusted, and he who is not to be trusted is without friends". Laws I 630a-c: faithfulness in dangers (pistotēs) is the virtue needed in civil war, which is the worst war. Divine temperance, justice and science: the Phaedrus 247d.

paragraphs.modern: Again, if you are willing, let us look into Plato's common teachings about divine natures from other dialogues. Where, then, shall we start, and what teachings shall we take, as we proceed in our search in a natural order? Shall we next recall what is written in the Phaedo? In his proofs of the soul's immortality drawn from its likeness to the divine, Socrates says that the being above the soul (to which the soul is by nature like, and being like it, shares in an immortal lot) is divine and immortal, intelligible and one-like, indissoluble, and always the same; but the being below the soul is wholly the contrary, and to it belong corruption and being acted on. For such a thing is perceptible and of many forms, and dissoluble, being compound; and he says of these all that belongs to a bodily existence. Let us then turn our attention to these common teachings, and examine how each of them belongs to the gods.
notes: The Phaedo 80a-b: the soul is most like "the divine, immortal, intelligible, one-like, indissoluble and always the same", the body like their contraries.

paragraphs.modern: First, then, what do we look to when we speak of what is said to be divine? From what has been said, it is clear that every god exists by the highest union of beings. For to us going up from bodies, the gods have appeared as henads beyond being, the generators, perfecters and measures of beings, who bind all first beings to themselves. But what is divine is not only the hyparxis and the one in each order of being, but at once what shares and what is shared: of these, what is shared is a god, and what shares is divine. Whether there is something separate and unshared before the shared henads will be clear in what follows. For now we will define the divine as this: being that shares in the one, or the one existing together with being, drawn together. For in the gods we take everything except the one, that is, being, life and intellect, as hanging from them and second. For the gods do not exist in these, but before them; they produce and hold these in themselves, but are not defined in them. We must not fail to see that these are really distinguished in this way. Yet in many places Plato grandly praises what shares in the gods by the same names, and calls them gods. Not only the Athenian Stranger in the Laws calls a divine soul a god, but so does Socrates in the Phaedrus. For he says that "the horses and charioteers of the gods are all good and of good stock"; and afterwards, still more clearly, "and this is the life of the gods". But this is not yet remarkable. Is it not admirable that he should call gods those beings who are always joined to the gods, and with them complete one series? For in many places he calls daemons gods, though they come after the gods in being and exist about them. In the Phaedrus, the Timaeus and other dialogues you will find him stretching the name of the gods as far as daemons. And, what is stranger still, he does not refuse to call certain men gods: in the Sophist he calls the Stranger from Elea so.

flags.taylor: but at the same time is that which participates and that which is participated; of which the latter is a God, but the former is divine
flags.why: Taylor's "latter" and "former" are the wrong way round for his own order of words: what is shared (the henad) is a god, and what shares in it (being) is divine. The modern English follows the sense.

flags.taylor: Whether however, prior to the participated unities, there is something which is separate and participated
flags.why: Taylor's "and participated" should be "and not participated", as the sense requires: the question is whether there is an unshared henad (the One) before the shared ones.

notes: The Phaedrus 246a-b, 248a; the Laws X 899b; the Sophist 216a-b, where Theodorus calls the Stranger "not a god, but divine", and Socrates answers that such philosophers do seem divine.

paragraphs.modern: From all that has been said, then, we must take this: one thing is a god simply; another by union; another by sharing; another by contact; and another by likeness. Of the natures beyond being, each is a god first; of the intellectual natures, each is a god by union; of divine souls, each is a god by sharing. Divine daemons are gods by contact with the gods; and the souls of men are given this name by likeness. Each of these, as we have said, is rather divine than a god. For the Athenian Stranger calls intellect itself divine. But what is divine comes after the first godhead, as the united comes after the One, the intellectual after intellect, and the ensouled after soul. And always the more one-like and simple natures go first, while the series of beings ends in the One itself. Let this, then, be the definition and distinction of the divine.

flags.taylor: the series of beings ends in the one itself
flags.why: "Ends" in the sense of having its summit there: going upward, the series of beings ends in the One.

paragraphs.modern: Next, let us look at the immortal. For in Plato there are many orders of immortality, running from on high as far as the last of things; and the last echo, as it were, of immortality is in those visible natures that are everlasting, which, the Stranger from Elea says in his account of the circuit of the universe, are given by the father a renewed immortality. For every body has its being and life hanging from another cause, but is not by nature fit to hold together, adorn or keep itself. The immortality of partial souls is, I think, clearer and more perfect than this, as Plato shows by many proofs in the Phaedo and in the tenth book of the Republic. By the immortality of partial souls I mean the one that is more ruling, as holding in itself the cause of everlasting remaining. We will not be wrong, however, if we set the immortality of daemons before both of these. For the kinds through which they exist are incorruptible: they neither lean towards mortality nor are filled with the nature of things that come to be and pass away. But I infer that the immortality of divine souls is still more worthy of reverence, and higher in being, than that of daemons. These souls we say are the first self-moving natures, the sources and principles of the life divided about bodies, through which bodies gain a renewed immortality. If, however, before these you think of the gods themselves and the immortality in them, and how in the Symposium Diotima does not give this kind of immortality even to daemons, but defines it as being in the gods alone, such an immortality will appear to you separate, and set apart from the whole of things. For there is eternity, the source of all immortality, and through it all things live and have life, some an everlasting life, others a life scattered into non-being. In short, the divine is immortal so far as it generates and holds in itself an everlasting life. For it is immortal not as sharing in life, but as the giver of a divine life, and as making life itself divine, whether you are willing to call such a life intelligible or by some other name.

flags.taylor: a renovated immortality
flags.why: The Statesman 270a: the universe receives from its maker "a renewed (or acquired) immortality"; its body does not hold itself together, but is renewed by its cause.

notes: The Symposium 202d-203a: love is not a god but a daemon, between mortal and immortal.

paragraphs.modern: Next, let us turn our attention to the intelligible. It is so called in contrast to what is perceptible, and grasped by opinion together with sense. For the intelligible first comes into light in the chief causes. Soul is intelligible, of this lot, set apart from perceptible things, and has a being separated from them. Before soul, intellect is intelligible; for we think it better to set soul in the middle than to count it among the first beings. That too is called intelligible which is older than intellect, which fills thinking and of itself brings it to perfection, and which Timaeus sets before the making intellect and intellectual activity, in the rank of a pattern. But above these is the divine intelligible, defined by union itself and a divine hyparxis. For this is intelligible as what intellect desires, as perfecting and holding intellect, and as the fullness of being. In one way, then, we must call the hyparxis of the gods intelligible; in another, true being and the first being; in another, intellect and all intellectual life; and in another, soul and the order of souls. And we must not shape the different natures of things to fit their names. Such, then, is the order of this triad: the divine is unmixed and ranks first; the immortal is second; and the intelligible is third. For the first of these is being made divine; the second is life existing by the immortality of the gods; and the third is intellect, called intelligible because it is filled with union.
notes: Timaeus 28a-29a, 39e: the Craftsman makes the world looking to the intelligible living being as his pattern.

paragraphs.modern: After this, we should next consider the one-like, the indissoluble, and what is always the same, from the same causes, as the forerunners of all the divine orders, running through them all. The one-like is highest. It is present with the divine monad, and seems most of all suited to what is first being, in which every kind of shared henad ends. For the One is before these, as will become clear as we proceed. The indissoluble is second. For it holds and binds the extremes by divine union; since the dissoluble is what it is through lack of connection and of a power that gathers multitude into one. And what is always the same is eternal, and full of the everlastingness of the gods; from it the sharing in immortality and everlasting sameness comes to other things. So the one-like belongs with the divine, the indissoluble with the immortal, and what is always the same we must refer to the intelligible.
notes: Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Do you not see how each of these is in a way fitted to the other? The first of them, through the first henad shared by being, is, as is fitting, one-like. For if a god exists by the One, the divine will surely be one-like. What is immortal through one cause of life is likewise indissoluble. For life is the bond of dissoluble natures; Timaeus too, pointing this out to us, sets the dissoluble against the immortal: "You are not immortal," says the Craftsman, "yet you shall never be dissolved, nor meet with the fate of death." Everything mortal, then, is dissoluble, but the immortal is indissoluble. What has a renewed immortality is, for the same reason, neither indissoluble nor mortal. For being in the middle of both, it is neither of the extremes in either opposition. The third of these, set by the fullness of whole intelligibles, is at once and always the same. For the intelligible is the cause of sameness and everlasting remaining, and intellect is wholly eternal through it. These triads, then, proceed from the first and chief causes, as we showed of the triads already mentioned. But these things we will consider later.
notes: Timaeus 41b: the Craftsman to the young gods, "you are not wholly immortal nor indissoluble, but you shall never be dissolved, nor meet with the fate of death, having my will as a greater bond". Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: With these discussed, let us turn our attention to the unbegotten in divine natures, and unfold what we say it is. We say that all true being is without generation, and Socrates proves in the Phaedrus that souls are unbegotten. Before these, the gods themselves are set above generations and existence in time. How, then, shall we define the unbegotten when said of a divine nature, and by what reason? Is it because the divine is set apart from all generation: not only from that in parts of time, such as we say the generation of material things is, nor only from that stretched through the whole of time, such as Timaeus shows the generation of the heavenly bodies to be, but also from the generation of soul? For Timaeus calls soul unbegotten in time, but the best of things generated. In short, a divine nature is set apart from all division and separation in being. For the procession of the gods is always by a union of second natures, set in a one-like way in the natures before them, the producers holding the produced in themselves. The undivided, the unseparated and the united, then, are really unbegotten. So if certain generations of the gods are spoken of by Plato in myths, as in Diotima's myth the birth of Aphrodite is celebrated, and of Love at the birth of Aphrodite, we must not fail to see how such things are said: they are composed to point to things by symbols, and myths, for the sake of concealment, call the inexpressible coming into light through causes "generation". In the Orphic writings, for this reason, the first cause is called Time; for there is another reason too, that existing as cause may be the same as existing in time. And the procession of the gods from the best of causes is fittingly called generation in time. So when Plato tells myths, it fits him to devise such things in keeping with the theologians; but when he speaks dialectically, searching out and unfolding divine natures by intellect and not by mystery, it fits him to praise the unbegotten being of the gods. For the gods first set in themselves the pattern of not being generated. An intellectual nature is unbegotten in a second degree, and after it the being of soul. And in bodies there is a last likeness of unbegotten power; seeing this, some after Plato have declared, without qualification, that the whole heaven is unbegotten. The gods, then, are unbegotten. But there is an order among them of first, middle and last processions, and a rising above and a being set below of powers. There are in them also one-like embraces of causes, and offspring of many forms of things caused. All things exist in one another, but in different ways. Some exist before second natures as filling them; others, as being filled, long for more perfect natures, and by sharing in their power generate what comes after them and perfect their hyparxis.

flags.taylor: in the Orphic writings, indeed, the first cause is on this account denominated Time
flags.why: In the Orphic theogony the first principle is Chronos, Time; Proclus takes the name as a symbol of order by cause, not of a beginning in time.

flags.taylor: some posterior to Plato perceiving, have indefinitely shown that the whole heaven is unbegotten
flags.why: Proclus seems to mean Aristotle (On the Heavens I.10-12), who holds that the heaven is unbegotten and imperishable. "Indefinitely" means without qualifying in what sense.

notes: The Phaedrus 245d: the source of motion is "unbegotten and indestructible". Timaeus 34b-37a, the soul as "the best of things generated" (37a). The Symposium 203b-c: Love was conceived at the feast for Aphrodite's birth.

paragraphs.modern: With this in view, we can unfold what is said in myths about father causes and the fertile powers of mothers. Everywhere, we may suppose, the cause of a higher, more one-like nature is a father; and we may say that the cause of a lower, more partial nature exists before it in the rank of a mother. For among the gods a father answers to the monad, the cause of limit; a mother to the dyad, and to the unlimited power that generates beings. With Plato, the father cause is one-like, set in a higher order than the natures that proceed from it, and comes before its offspring in the lot of the desirable. The mother cause, again, has the form of the dyad: at one time it appears in the myths as higher than its offspring, at another as below it in being; as in the Symposium Plato calls Poverty the mother of Love. And this is so not only in myths but in the philosophic study of beings, as is clear in the Timaeus. For there Plato calls being the father, and matter the mother and nurse of coming to be. So the powers that are fertile and perfect second natures, giving life and causing separation, are mothers, set above the natures they produce. But the powers that receive the natures coming into light, multiply their activities, and stretch out even the lower lot of the offspring, are also themselves called mothers. Again, the offspring of such causes at one time proceed by union from their own principles and are filled from both the father and the mother cause; at another they hold the bond of them, set in the middle, carrying the gifts of the fathers to the mothers' laps, and turning what receives them to the completion of the first causes. Of the natures that come from two principles existing before them, some are made like the father cause, and such kinds of gods produce, guard and hold together. For to produce, to hold and to guard belong to the cause of limit. Others are made like the mother cause, and generate, give life, and give motion, the multiplying of powers, variety and processions. For all these are offspring of the unlimited and the first multitude.
notes: Symposium 203b-c: Love is the son of Poros (Plenty) and Penia (Poverty). Timaeus 50d, 51a, 52d: the Forms are like a father, the receptacle like a mother and nurse. Limit and the unlimited: the Philebus 23c-27c. Taylor's footnote supplies "father" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: This, then, may be enough about the unbegotten hyparxis of the gods. It remains, I think, to speak of the divine names. For Socrates in the Cratylus sees fit to unfold with great care the rightness of names among divine natures. Parmenides, in the first hypothesis, just as he denies of the One everything else that is known, and all knowledge, so also denies it name and speech. But in the second hypothesis, besides everything else, he shows that this one can be spoken of and has a name. In short, we must grant that the first, chief and truly divine names are set in the gods themselves. We must say that the second names, imitations of the first, which exist in an intellectual way, are of the lot of daemons. And again we may say that the names third from the truth, devised by reason and receiving the last likeness of divine natures, are unfolded by men of science, acting at one time divinely and at another by intellect, and generating moving images of their inward visions. For as the making intellect sets up likenesses about matter of the first Forms in itself, and produces images in time of things eternal, divided images of undivided things, and, as it were, shadowy images of true beings, so too, I think, our science, imitating intellect's production, fashions likenesses of other things and of the gods themselves. It shows what is uncompounded in them by composition, what is simple by variety, and what is united by multitude; and so, shaping names, it shows at last images of divine natures. For it generates every name as if it were a statue of the gods. And as the theurgic art, through certain symbols, calls the overflowing and ungrudging goodness of the gods to light up statues made by art, so the intellectual science of divine things unfolds the hidden being of the gods by the compositions and divisions of sounds. Rightly, then, does Socrates in the Philebus say that out of reverence for the gods he feels the greatest fear about their names. For we must revere even the last echoes of the gods, and, revering these, become settled in their first patterns. So much, then, about divine names, which may be enough for now for understanding Plato's theology. For we will discuss them exactly when we speak of the partial powers.
notes: The Parmenides 142a (the One of the first hypothesis has no name), 155d (the One of the second can be named). The Cratylus 400d-401a: we do not know the gods' true names, "which they call themselves". The Philebus 12c: "my fear about the names of the gods is not human, but beyond the greatest fear". Taylor's footnote supplies a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: The most fitting beginning of the study we have set ourselves is the one from which we can discover the first cause of all beings. For if we set out from this as we should, with our ideas about it made pure, we will more easily distinguish everything else. About these things, then, we must speak from the beginning as follows. All beings, and all the natures of beings, must be either many only, with no one in them, neither in each nor in all of them; or one only, with no multitude, all things being forced into one and the same power of existence; or both one and many, being being one, so that neither does multitude alone by itself overcome beings, nor are we forced to bring all things and their contraries together into the same thing at once. These being three, which shall we choose? To which of these claims shall we give our vote? We must discuss one by one the absurdities that follow from these positions, and so see how the truth stands.
notes: Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated ("cause" for "being"). The method follows the Parmenides, which tests what follows if the One is, and if it is not; and the Sophist (244b-245e), against those who say that all is many or all is one.

paragraphs.modern: If beings are many, and many in the way we said at the start, so that the One is nowhere to be found, many absurdities follow; or rather, the whole nature of beings is destroyed at once from the first, since there will at once be nothing able to share in the One. For we must grant that every being is either some one thing, or nothing. What is some being is also one; what is not even one being does not exist at all. So if many things exist, each of the many is something, a certain one. But if each of them is nothing, not even one thing, the many cannot exist either, for the many are many so far as each member of the multitude exists. So if the many alone exist, and the One in no way is, the many will not exist either. For things that are in no way one do not exist at all. And if the One is not, far less do the many exist; for it follows of necessity that none of the things the many are made of will exist.
notes: Compare the Parmenides 165e-166c: if the One is not, nothing is, neither one nor many.

paragraphs.modern: Further, if the many alone exist, as we said, all things will be endlessly unlimited; and whichever of these unlimited things you take, this too will at once be unlimited. And of the things that make it up, which are unlimited, each too will be unlimited. For take some one of the many, which we say is not one. This will be a multitude by its own nature, since it belongs to beings and is not nothing. But if it is a multitude, it too will be made of many things, and will be many. And if you take something of these many, it will at once appear to you not one but many. The same reasoning will at once hold for these; and in the same way each (and we say "each" falsely) will be a multitude in act. Each, so to speak, will be unlimited, or rather endlessly unlimited. For there is nothing that will not be of this kind, since a part is many, and in the same way the part of a part, and so on without end. For multitude, as it proceeds, will never stop, nor will unlimitedness, being deprived of the nature of the One. But to make beings endlessly unlimited is impossible, both in truth and for our purpose. For if being is endlessly unlimited, being can be neither known nor discovered, since the unlimited cannot be grasped or known at all. If being is endlessly unlimited, there will also be something more unlimited than the unlimited. But if something is more unlimited, something else will be less unlimited. And what is less unlimited, since it is not perfectly unlimited, will clearly be limited, so far as it falls short of the nature of the unlimited. So if there is something more unlimited in multitude than what is unlimited in multitude, there will be something more than the unlimited, and the unlimited will be less, and that not in multitude. But this is impossible. So there is no endlessly unlimited.

flags.taylor: will be multitude in energy
flags.why: That is, many in act and not only in potential: each supposed part would actually be many, without end.

notes: The Parmenides 164c-165a: if the One is not, each mass of the others is endlessly many, and the smallest appears huge.

paragraphs.modern: Again, on this hypothesis the same things will be like and unlike in the same respect. For if all the many are not one, and each thing in all respects is not one, what is not one will clearly undergo the same thing through being deprived of the One. All things, then, being deprived of the One in the same way, will for this reason be in the same state with respect to each other. And things in the same state, so far as they are so, are clearly like each other. So the many will be like each other so far as they are deprived of the One. But by this same deprivation of the One they will be wholly unlike. For things that are like must undergo the same thing, so that things that undergo nothing the same will not be like. And things that undergo something the same undergo one thing. So things deprived of every one will not undergo anything the same. The many, then, will be like and unlike in the same respect. But this is impossible. So it is impossible for the many to exist that are in no way one.
notes: The Parmenides 165c-d: the others, if the One is not, appear both like and unlike.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, the many will be the same as and different from each other in the same respect. For if all things are equally deprived of the One, then, so far as all are equally deprived, they will be the same by this deprivation; since things that are in the same way by possession are the same, and so are things deprived in the same way by deprivation. But so far as each of them is deprived of every one, so far the many will be different from each other. For if the One in the many is the same, what is in no way one will in no way be the same. The many, then, will be the same and not the same as each other. And if they are the same and not the same, they are clearly different from each other. For what is the same and not the same, so far as it is not the same, is not the same by nothing else than the different. Further, these many will be moved and unmoved, if the One is not. For if each of them is not one, they will be unmoved by the deprivation of the One. For if what is not one were changed, each of them would come to have the One; since when deprivations are changed, they always lead what is changed into possessions. So what is not one must remain unmoved by the deprivation of the One; though this very thing is impossible, that the many should stand still. For everything that stands still is in something the same, either in the same form or in the same place. And everything in the same is in one thing that is the same, for the same in which it is is one thing. So everything that stands still is in one thing. But the many do not share in the One. And it is wholly impossible that things that do not share in the One should be in some one thing. And things not in one thing cannot stand still, since things that stand still are always in one and the same thing. So it is impossible that the many should stand still and remain unmoved. Yet it was shown that the many must stand unmoved. The same things, then, by the same condition (I mean the deprivation of the possession of the One) are moved and unmoved. For unmoved things, and things that stand still, so far as they are unstable, must so far appear to be moved.

flags.taylor: privations being changed, entirely lead into habits the things that are changed
flags.why: Taylor's "privation" and "habit" are Aristotle's pair, deprivation (sterēsis) and possession (hexis): a thing that changes out of lacking something comes to have it.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, there is no number of beings if the One in no way is; all things and each thing will be not one. For the monad, the smallest part of number, is one, and every number itself is one. If there are five units, there is the pentad; if three, the triad. But the triad itself is a certain unity, and so is the pentad. So if there is no one, there will be neither any part nor the whole of numbers. For how can there be any number if the One does not exist? The One is the principle of numbers. But if the principle does not exist, the things that proceed from it cannot exist either. So if the One does not exist, there will be no number.
notes: The Parmenides 165b-c: without the One, the others cannot be numbered.

paragraphs.modern: Again, there will be no knowledge of beings if the One is not. For it will not be possible to speak of or think of any being. For each thing itself, and everything we can speak of and on which we stamp the nature of the One, will not exist, because the One does not exist. So there will be no speech and no knowledge. For speech, if it is complete, is one thing made of many things. And knowledge exists when what knows becomes one with what is known. But if there is no union, there will be no knowledge of things, and it will be impossible to speak about things we know. To this we may add that what cannot be unfolded in each of the unlimited things will always escape the limit of knowledge. For each seeming unlimited thing that the knower wants to understand will at once slip away from the power of knowing as it hastens to touch it and hold to it, since it can be neither touched nor held. If, then, the many alone exist and the One does not exist at all, so many absurdities, and still more, must follow for those who take up this hypothesis.

But if the One, the One itself, alone exists, and there is nothing else (for if there were, there would be not one but many things, since one and another are more than one, and not one thing only), then among all things there will be neither a whole nor what has parts. For everything that has parts is many, and every whole has parts. But the One is in no way many. So there will be neither a whole nor what has parts. Further, there cannot be a beginning or end of anything. For what has a beginning, middle and end is divisible. But the One is not divisible, since it has no parts. So it has neither beginning, middle nor end. Again, if the One alone exists, no being will have a shape. For everything that has a shape is either straight, or round, or mixed from these. If it is straight, it will have as its parts the middle and the ends. If it is round, there will be one thing in it as a middle, and other things as the ends, to which the middle reaches. And if it is mixed from the straight and the round, it will be made of many things, and will not be one.
notes: The Parmenides 137c-138a: the One of the first hypothesis is neither a whole nor has parts, has no beginning, middle or end, and no shape.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, no being will be either in itself or in another. For what is in another is different from what it is in. But if the One alone exists and nothing else (for it will by no means be in another), there will be no being that is in another. And what is in itself will at once hold and be held; and in it to hold will not be the same as to be held, nor will the account of both be the same. So there will be two things, and no longer the One alone. Again, no being will be moved. For if it is moved, it must be changed. And if changed, it must be in another. But if the One alone exists, nothing can appear to be in something else. So no being can be changed. Yet everything that stands still must be in the same. And what is in the same is in some same thing. But the One is in no same thing. For what is in some thing is either in itself or in something else. And it has been shown that it is neither in itself nor in another. So it is not in some same thing either. Nor, then, does any being stand still.
notes: The Parmenides 138a-139b: the One is neither in itself nor in another, neither moved nor at rest. Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, it is impossible for anything to be the same as, or different from, anything. For if there is nothing besides the One itself, there is nothing that will be the same as or different from something else, since there will be no other being. And the One itself will not be different from itself, for then it would be many and not one. Nor will it be the same as itself. For the same is something other, and the same is not the One itself. The One is simply one, because it is not many; but what is the same is the same as something else. Again, nothing can be like or unlike anything. For everything like undergoes something the same, and everything unlike something different. But the One cannot undergo anything, nor can anything else besides the One, since nothing else exists at all if the One alone exists.
notes: The Parmenides 139b-140b: the One is neither the same nor different, neither like nor unlike, itself or another.

paragraphs.modern: Further, we say that nothing can be touched or be separate, if there is nothing besides the One. For how can things that do not exist be separate, or touch anything? And the One cannot be separate from itself or touch itself, for then it would undergo being touched and being separate. But the One undergoes nothing besides itself. Likewise, nothing can be equal or unequal to anything. For what is equal to another is said to be so in relation to another, and so too with the unequal. But nothing else exists, if the One alone exists. Nor can the One be equal or unequal to itself. If unequal, there will be one thing in it greater and another less, so that it will be two and not one. And if the One is equal to itself, the One will measure itself. But this is impossible. For the One will measure and be measured by itself, so that it will not be the One itself. So there will be no equality or inequality among beings. But if these things are impossible (that, if the One alone exists, free of multitude and without all these things, no being can touch another or be separate, be like or unlike, the same or different, stand still or be moved, be in anything at all, have a shape, be a whole or have parts), and if it is also impossible, as was shown before, for the many alone to exist, then every being must be both many and one.
notes: The Parmenides 140b-d, 148d-149d: touching and being separate, equal and unequal.

paragraphs.modern: If this is so, either the many must share in the One, or the One in the many, or both must share in each other, or neither in the other, the many being separate and the One separate too, so that the many and the One may exist, as reason shows. If, then, neither the One shares in the many nor the many in the One, the same absurdities will follow that we gathered on the hypothesis that the many alone exist. For again there will be the many separate from the One. For if the One exists by itself, and the many do not share in the One in any way, the many will be endlessly unlimited, like and unlike, same and different, moved and stable, and there will be neither number nor knowledge of the many. For the absence of the One forces all these consequences on the many. So it is impossible that neither the many share in the One nor the One in the many.

But if the One shares in the many and the many in the One, and both are in each other, there must be another nature besides these, which is neither one nor many. For since both are mixed in each other, there must be a cause of their mixture, which joins multitude to the One and the One to multitude. For everything mixed must have a cause of its mixture. In short, if the One and multitude share in each other, neither is the One the cause of being to multitude, nor multitude to the One, but some third thing, before them, is the cause of being to both. For what will make this to be multitude, and that to be one? And what is the cause of their sharing and keeping company with each other, when the One, so far as it is one, never shares with the many? For the many as many and the One as one are different from each other; and so far as neither comes from the other, they have no sympathy with each other. What, then, gathers them into one, when they flee each other and are unmixed? Being so at odds, they cannot desire each other; or if they did, their coming together would be by chance. For if this happened, there was a time when they were separate from each other, since now they exist together by a cause. But it is impossible for the many to exist separate from the One. So the mixture is not by chance. Nor does the mixture come from the many, if neither the One is the cause of the many, nor the many of the One. What, then, is this higher thing that causes the mixture? It is either one or not one. If it is the One itself, we must ask again of it whether it shares in multitude or in nothing. If it shares, clearly some other thing before it will for the same reason come into view, and so on without end. But if such a thing is wholly free of multitude, then what was said at first will not be true, that the many do not share in the One, nor the One in the many. I mean, though, what is most chiefly and first one. For there is a one in the many, and there is also the unshared One, which is simply one and nothing else. If, however, what is before both is not one, this not-one must be higher than the One. Yet all things are, and come to be what they are, through the One. Together with the One, every being is kept; separate from the One, it goes to its own destruction. And the mixture of the One and multitude, which the not-one would give to beings, is sharing and union. So the One and the not-one would be the cause of nothing else to beings than of their being one. But if the One is the cause of this, the not-one will not be the cause of anything higher than union. Yet everywhere what is higher must be the cause to beings of some other, higher thing, by its own power. For this is how it will be higher: as more good, and as the cause from its own nature of a greater and higher good to those things to which a lesser good is the cause of lesser goodness. From this, then, it follows that the many must share in the One, that the One must be unmixed with multitude, that nothing must be better than the One, and that it must also be the cause of being to the many. For everything deprived of the One at once flees into nothing and its own destruction. But what is not many is not at the same time not many and nothing. For to the One is opposed what is nothing, or not one; and to the many, what is not many. If, then, the One and the many are not the same, being not many will not be the same as being nothing. Considering the matter this way, then, it appears that the One is beyond multitude and is the cause of being to the many.

flags.taylor: since now also they subsist together causally. It is however impossible for the many to subsist separate from the one. The mixture therefore is not causal
flags.why: Taylor's "causally" here must mean "by chance" (the Greek is probably kata symbebēkos or apo tychēs): the argument is that the mixture is not a matter of chance, since the many cannot ever have existed apart from the One.

flags.taylor: The one therefore, and that which is not one, are the cause of nothing else to beings than of their being one
flags.why: That is, even a supposed not-one above the One would give beings nothing but union, which is what the One gives; so it would be no higher than the One. Taylor's footnotes correct and supply words of the Greek here.

paragraphs.modern: We must now treat the same subject in another way, and see again whether we can in some way follow what has been said and bring it to the same end. Let us begin from this. There must be either one principle or many. If there are many principles, they must either be in sympathy with each other or torn apart from each other, and they must be either finite or unlimited. If there is one principle, it must be either not being or being. If it is being, it must be either bodily or bodiless. If bodiless, either separate from bodies or inseparable from them. If separate, either moved or unmoved. And if it is not being, it must be either lower than all being, or shared by being, or unshared. If, then, there are many principles, with no sympathy with each other, no being will come from them jointly, nor will they be common to all things, but each will produce by itself. For what sharing can there be between things foreign by nature, or what working together between things wholly different in kind? Besides this, there will be the many that do not share in the One. For if there is some one common in all of them, they will not be wholly separated in being from each other. If, then, they are different, and there is nothing the same about them, they are many only and in no way one. But if there are many principles, in sympathy with each other, they will have something common that leads all of them to sympathy, and shows all of them alike. For we call those things sympathetic that are affected by the same thing. And like things are like by sharing in one form and one nature. If this is so, this whole that is everywhere and in all the principles must be more of a principle than the many. It gives them the power to be in sympathy with each other, and gives them sharing by nature.

flags.taylor: they must be divulsed from each other
flags.why: Taylor's "divulsed" means torn apart: principles with nothing in common.

paragraphs.modern: Again, if there are unlimited principles, either the things that come from them are unlimited, and there will be the unlimited twice over; or they are limited, and so not all the principles will be principles. For things limited in number will always come from limited principles. So the principles are unlimited in vain. Besides, unlimitedness makes both the principles and what comes from them unknown. For if the principles are unknown, what comes from them must be unknown, since we think we know anything when we know its causes and first principles. But if the principles are limited, there will clearly be some number of them; for we say that number is a defined multitude. And if there is a number of principles, there must be a cause of their whole number. For every number comes from one; and this, the One, is the principle of numbers. This, then, will be the principle of principles, and the cause of limited multitude, since number itself is one, the end in the many is one, and it bounds the many by what is one. But if the principle is one, and it is being, then, if this is granted, whether it is bodily or bodiless, it must be acknowledged as the principle of other things.
notes: Aristotle, Physics I.4 (187b): if the principles are unlimited, what comes from them cannot be known.

paragraphs.modern: If, then, body is the cause of the generation of beings, it must be divisible and have parts. For every body is divisible by its own nature, since every magnitude is a certain whole, and a whole is made of parts. These parts (I mean each of them) must either share in some one, or not. If they do not, they will be many only, and in no way one. So neither will what is made of them be a whole. For if there is no one, what is made of all of them will not be one. But if each of the parts shares in something of this kind, and there is something the same in all of them, it must be bodiless and undivided in its own nature. For if it too is bodily, it is either wholly in each of the parts, or not wholly. If wholly in each, it will be separated from itself, for the parts it is in are separate from each other. If not wholly in each of the parts, it too will be divisible, and will have parts as the parts already named do; and the same question will arise again about these, whether there is something common in them too, or nothing. For if there is nothing common, we will set the many apart from the One.

Let us consider the whole, though; for every body is a whole and has parts. What, then, will hold together the parts, since they are many? We must say either that the whole unifies the parts, or the parts the whole, or that some third thing before both, which neither is a whole nor has any part, holds together and unites the whole with its parts and the parts with the whole. If the whole holds the parts together, the whole will be bodiless and undivided. For if it is a body, it too will be divisible, and will need a nature able to hold the parts together; and so on without end. But if the parts hold the whole together, how can the many hold together the one, and divided things what is made of them? For, on the contrary, the one must have the power of uniting the many, and not the many of uniting the one. And if what holds both together neither is a whole nor has parts, it will be wholly undivided. But being undivided, it must also be without extension. For everything with extension has parts and is divisible. And being without extension, it is bodiless; for every body has extension.

Further, the principle must be everlasting; for every being is everlasting or perishable. So we must grant that the principle of beings is everlasting or perishable. But if we grant that it can perish, there will be no imperishable being. For if the principle is destroyed, it will not itself be generated from anything, nor will anything else be generated from it. For it cannot generate itself (since it is not, if it is not everlasting), nor can anything else generate it, if it is the principle of all things. But if it is imperishable, it will have the power of not perishing, and this power will be unlimited, so that it may exist without end through the whole of time. For every limited power of existence belongs by nature to what is perishable, while an unlimited power belongs to everlasting natures, whose existence goes on without end. This unlimited, then, I mean unlimited in power, is either undivided or divisible. If divisible, there will be the unlimited in a limited body. For the principle is limited; if it were unlimited, there would be nothing else besides it. But if it is undivided, the power of existing without end will be bodiless. And the principle of beings is bodiless, so far as it is this power by which what underlies it always is. From this, then, it is clear that the principle of beings cannot be bodily.
notes: Aristotle, Physics VIII.10 (266a-267b): no limited body can have an unlimited power, so the first mover is without magnitude. Taylor's footnote supplies the words "is bodiless" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: If it is bodiless, it must be either separate from bodies or inseparable from them. If inseparable, it will have all its activities in bodies and about them. For what is inseparable from body is what is by nature fit to act nowhere except in and with bodies. And if the principle is of this kind, it is clearly necessary that none of the things that exist by it should be more powerful or have more authority than the principle of all beings. But if nothing in bodies is higher than the power that exists in bodies and acts about them, and a bodily being, there will nowhere be intellect, or the power that acts by intellect. For every such motion (that is, activity) comes from a power that is, in its activities, wholly free of body. And it never was, nor is, lawful for what is generated to go beyond the power of its causes. For everything in what is begotten comes from first natures, and these are the masters of the being of what comes after them. So if the principle of beings can generate intellect and wisdom, how could it not generate it, on its own account and in itself? For one of two things is necessary: either intellectual perception belongs in no way to beings, or it is lower than them, and if it exists, acts in bodies only. But these things cannot be said. And if what is first of beings, and the principle of all things, is separate from bodies, we must certainly grant that it is either unmoved or moved. If it is moved, there will be something else before it, about which it is moved. For everything moved is by nature fit to be moved about something else that remains. And besides this, it is moved through desire for something else. For it must be moved because it desires something, since motion by itself is undefined; but its end is that for the sake of which it is. It desires either something else or itself. But everything that desires itself is unmoved. For why should anything present to itself want to be in something else? Of things that are moved, the motion is less in that to which the good is nearer, and greater in that from which the good is further. But what has the good in itself, and that for the sake of which it is, will be unmoved and stable, since, being always in itself, it is in the good. And what is in itself is in the same; for each thing is the same as itself. Of what is in itself we say that it stands still and is unmoved; while what is not unmoved is not in itself but in another, is moved towards another, and wholly lacks the good. If, then, the principle of beings is moved, and everything moved is moved through lack of good, towards something else it desires, there will be something else, besides itself, desired by the principle of beings, about which, as always the same, we must say it is moved. But this is impossible. For the principle is that for the sake of which all things are, which all things desire, and which lacks nothing. If it lacked something, it would be wholly below what it lacked, to which its activity was directed as to what it desired. But if the principle is unmoved (for this is what remains), it must be one bodiless being, eternally the same. But how does it have the One? And how is it one being? If being and the One are the same, we must grant that the principle of beings is being. But if being is different from the One, we must grant that to be one is not the same as to be being. And if being is better than the One, then by this it must be said to be with the principle. But if the One is better than being and beyond it, the One is also the principle of being. And if they rank together, the many will be before the One. But this is impossible, as we showed before. It is clear, indeed, that being is not the same as the One. For to say "one" and to say "being is one" are not one and the same; the first is not yet a sentence, and the second is. Besides, if being and the One are the same, multitude will be the same as what does not exist and is not being. But this is impossible. For the many are held in being, and the One is in what is not being. But if being and the One are not the same, they will not rank together; for if they did, there would be something else before them, if all things must come from one principle. And if one of them is better than the other, either the One is before being or being before the One. If the One is before being, this and not being is the principle of all things. For nothing must be better than the principle. And if being is before the One, the One will be an attribute of being, and not being of the One. But if the One is an attribute of being, the One and being must be everything, and all things that are one must be being, but not all things that are being must be one. There will, then, be some being deprived of the One. But if this is so, it will be nothing. For what is deprived of the One is nothing. So the One is before being.

flags.taylor: the one will be passive to essence
flags.why: Taylor's "passive to" means "an attribute of", something that being "undergoes" or has: if being were before the One, oneness would be only a property of being. Taylor's footnote: if being and the One ranked together, they would be two, and so share in the first many.

notes: "Many are in being, and the One is in what is not being": things that do not exist are not many, but even "nothing" is spoken of as one. Aristotle, Metaphysics XII.7 (1072a-b): the first mover moves as desired, being itself unmoved.

paragraphs.modern: But if what is first is something that is not being, it is absurd to say that it is below being. For the principle is what has the greatest power and the most absolute authority, and is most sufficient to itself; it is not the meanest thing, needing the many. In short, no second nature must be better than the principle, for beings must not be badly governed. But if the principle has an order lower than the things that proceed from it, and these are better than it, all things will be badly confused, and the principle will by nature be nothing else than something that is not the best of things, and the things that proceed from it will not have from it a power of ruling over their principle. The principle of beings, then, will be by chance, and so will the beings that are its offspring. But this is impossible. For things by chance (if to be by chance is not to exist by intellect, nor with a view to a defined end) are disordered, unlimited and undefined, and are all things that happen less often. But the principle is always principle, and other things proceed from it. If, then, what is not being is better than all being, it will be either shared by it, or wholly unshared. If being shares in the principle, of what will it be the principle? And how will it be the principle of all beings? For the principle of beings must be none of the beings; if it were one of them, it would certainly not be the principle of all beings. And everything shared by another is said to belong to what shares in it, and to be first in it. But the principle is separate, and belongs more to itself than to other things. Besides, everything shared proceeds from another, higher cause; for the unshared is better than the shared. And it is not possible to think of anything better than what is best, which we call the principle. For it is not lawful to say that things second to the principle, which proceed from it, are in any way better than their principle. So the cause of all beings is above all being, separate from every being, and is neither being, nor has being added to its nature. For such an addition is a lessening of its simplicity and of its being one.
notes: "Beyond being": Republic VI 509b, the Good is "not being, but beyond being in dignity and power".

paragraphs.modern: See, then, the third argument after these, leading us to the same conclusion as the earlier arguments. The cause of all beings must be that in which all beings share, to which they refer their existence, and which is separated from nothing that is said to exist in any way. For this alone is the object of desire to beings which, first or in some other way, is itself the cause of their existence. And everything produced in relation to it and because of it must have a certain relation to it, and through this a likeness to it. For every relation of one thing to another is spoken of in two ways: either both share in one thing that gives them sharing with each other; or one shares in the other, the higher giving something to what is below it, and the lower being made like the higher, so far as it shares in it. So if all perceptible natures have a relation to what is first, long for it and exist about it, either some third thing must be the cause of the relation, or the principle must give the natures after it a leaning towards itself, and the desire by which each thing is kept and exists. But nothing is higher than what is first. So the relation of beings, their existence, and their leaning towards the first come from there. And all things share in their own principle, if what is shared must appear from there in all beings, since it is the principle of all things and leaves no being. What, then, will this nature be, which is everywhere and in all beings? Is it life and motion? But many things lack these. Is rest everywhere, then, and in all things? But this is not true either. For motion, as motion, will not share in remaining at rest. Is intellect, so much honoured, as intellect, shared by all beings? This too is impossible. For then all beings would have intellectual perception, and no being would lack intellect.

flags.taylor: Is, therefore, permanency every where
flags.why: Taylor's "permanency" is rest, stillness (stasis), one of the Sophist's five great kinds.

paragraphs.modern: Shall we say, then, that being itself, and being in the sense of what is, is shared by all things that exist in any way? But how can this be? For what is in coming to be, or passing into existence, is said to be, yet lacks being. Nor should we wonder if this too, since it ranks among beings, should at last share in being. For so far as it is coming to be, it is not; but it ends in existence and being when it has actually come to be, and is no longer rising into existence. So not all things that exist in any way share in being. What, then, will be everywhere and shared by all things? Let us consider every being, and see what all beings undergo, and what is common in all of them, as in being, sameness, difference, rest (remaining as it is) and motion. Can we say that each of these is anything other than one thing? And not only each by itself, but the things that come from them; in short, in a certain way we cannot speak of all things otherwise than this, that all things and each thing are one. For if anything were deprived of the One, whether you speak of parts or of beings, what becomes deprived of the One will at once be nothing at all. For why do we say that what is not is wholly nothing, not even one thing, unless the One is the last thing to leave beings? This, then, is what it is to become what in no way is: to be wholly deprived of the One. For it is possible for what is not moved to be, and for what has no being to have a hyparxis; but what is not even one thing, and is deprived of the One itself, will be nothing at all. So the One is present to all beings; and even if you speak of multitude itself, this too must share in the One, for if it does not become one thing, it cannot exist. And if you divide the whole without end, at once nothing else than one turns up. For either what is divided does not exist, or, coming to be or being something else, it will at once be one. The one, then, that appears everywhere, is in all beings, and leaves no being, comes either from the One that is simply one, or from what is higher than the One. For it is not possible for the one to be an attribute of anything except from the first One, to which the one is no longer present as an attribute, but which is the One itself, nothing else than one.

flags.taylor: that which is in generation, or passing into existence, is said to be, and is destitute of essence
flags.why: Proclus means that what is coming to be (genesis) is spoken of as being, yet is not yet being in the full sense; Timaeus 27d-28a: what always comes to be "never really is".

notes: "Being, sameness, difference, rest and motion" are the five great kinds of the Sophist (254b-255e). Taylor's footnote corrects "being" to "one" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Again, from another starting point, we can reach the same conclusion, speaking as follows. Either the causes of beings and the things caused must go on without end, with nothing first or last among beings; or there is no first, but there is a last, the unlimited being on one side only; or, on the contrary, beings go on without end from a defined principle; or there is a first and a last, and a boundary of beings both ways. And if there are boundaries of beings, either things come from each other, and the generation of beings is in a circle; or, if they do not come from each other, either one of them comes from the other, or the first is one and the last not one, or the contrary, or both are one, or neither is one. If, then, first things and the causes of beings are unlimited, each thing will be made of unlimited things. For what proceeds from a principle must share in the principle it proceeds from. And what has its existence from many causes will be of many forms in its own nature, as sharing in many powers. And what is produced from unlimited things before it will have unlimited distinctive characters from the principles, suited to itself. So every being, being unlimited and made of unlimited things, will make all things endlessly unlimited, and there will be neither knowledge of any being nor any unfolding of powers. For the power of the unlimited is wholly unknown and beyond grasp by the natures to which it is unlimited.

But if things are unlimited in a downward procession, is each of them unlimited, always proceeding further down, in the same way as we say all things are? Or is each whole limited, while the beings produced from them are unlimited? For if every being is defined at its beginning but unlimited at its end, there will be, neither in parts nor in wholes, a return of beings to their own principle; nor will what is second in order ever be such as to be made like the last of the order before it; though, as we often say, the summits of the lower are joined to the boundaries of the higher. For where there is no last, by what means can such a likeness in procession, and such holding together of beings, remain, by which second things are always joined to the natures before them? But if all things alone have such an unlimitedness, each bounded by what comes after it, wholes will be lower than parts, and the parts of beings will by nature be more perfect than wholes. For wholes will have no return to the principle before them, while parts will return to it after their procession. Yet the more every being hastens to be joined to what is more perfect than itself, the more it must excel, as it seems to me. And if this whole, going on without end, is not rolled back to its own summit, and turned back in a circle and perfected by such a return, it will not desire its own good. If, however, we grant that there is unlimitedness both ways, these things must follow.

flags.taylor: the summits of inferiors are conjoined with the boundaries of superiors
flags.why: A rule of Proclus' system (Elements of Theology 147): the highest member of each lower order is joined to the lowest member of the order above.

paragraphs.modern: Besides this, there will be no common object of desire for all beings, nor any union or sympathy among them. For things wholly unlimited have nothing first in them; and having no first, we will not be able to say what the common end of beings is, nor why some things are higher while others have a lower nature. For we call one thing better and another worse by nearness to what is best, just as we define the more and less hot by sharing in what is hot in the first degree. In short, we judge the more and the less by reference to what is greatest. So the boundary among beings must be what is first and what is last.
notes: Aristotle, Metaphysics II.1 (993b): what is most of all a thing is the cause of it in others, as fire, the hottest, is the cause of heat.

paragraphs.modern: But if these come from each other, the same thing will be older and younger, cause and at the same time what is caused, and each thing will be first and last. For it makes no difference whether these come from each other, or the things between them do. For if the extremes are no different, how could a change in being come between them? But if one comes from the other, does the first come from the last, as some say, who generate higher things from lower, and more perfect from less perfect? But in that case, must not what has the power of generating and producing the perfect, far before that, perfect and adorn itself by the power present to it? And how could it leave itself in a lower lot and assign a higher order to another? For everything longs for its own perfection, and simply desires good, though not everything can share in it. If, then, it has the power of producing this most perfect thing, what is last will act on its own account before other things, and the whole of good, and all perfection, will be set first in itself.

flags.taylor: as some say, who generate things more excellent from things subordinate
flags.why: Proclus seems to mean the old physicists, and the Pythagoreans and Speusippus as Aristotle reports them (Metaphysics XII.7, 1072b; XIV.4-5), who held that the good and the beautiful come at the end, not the beginning.

paragraphs.modern: But if what is last is produced from what is first, and the most imperfect from the most perfect, is each of them one, or is this one and that not one? If what is first, or what is last, is not one, neither of them will be first or last. For since there will be multitude in each, each will have the better and the worse in it. Neither will what is best be unmixed with what is lower than it, nor will what is dimmest of all in being be so low as to be wholly deprived of a more perfect nature. There will be something further out than the last, and something more perfect than the first. For everywhere, if what is best receives some addition through what is lower, it will be less perfect than what remains in the best without that addition. If, then, we say these things rightly, the One is the principle of all things, and the last of beings is one. For the end of the procession of beings must, I think, be made like the principle, and the power of the first must reach as far as this.

flags.taylor: that which is best if it receives another addition through that which is inferior will be more perfect than that which does not abide in the best
flags.why: Taylor's English says the opposite of what the argument needs: what is best, if mixed with something lower, will be less perfect than what remains purely in the best. The modern English follows the argument.

paragraphs.modern: To sum up what we have said, then: either the first principle must be one, or there must be many first principles only, or one holding multitude in itself, or many sharing in one. But if there are many first principles only, nothing one will come from them. For what will make one thing, and a whole, if there are many principles and nothing that produces one? For the things after the principles must surely be made like them. Either, then, there will be no one in any being, or it will not come from these principles; so that each of the things that exist in any way will be divided multitude only. And again each of the parts of any being will be of this kind, and we will never stop dividing being and existence into tiny parts. For all things will be many, and the One will be nowhere in the whole of things, and neither wholes nor parts will appear.
notes: Taylor's footnote: "many first principles only" means multitude without any sharing in the One.

paragraphs.modern: But if there must be many principles, and they share in the One, the One will be ranked together with the many. Again, though, everywhere the unranked must be older than the ranked, and what is set apart than what is shared. For how is the One in each of the many, except from one principle that orders the multitude together and turns it to itself by sharing in the One? Again, if the first One were multiplied, the One would be acted on; for at the same time it would be one and not one, and would not be that which is one only. But in each kind of thing there must be what is unmixed with a lower nature, so that there may be what is mixed, as we say of the Forms. For from the Equal itself, things here that are equal appear equal, though they are filled with a contrary nature; and from what is first being comes what is mixed with non-being, and appears as being. In short, everywhere the simple, unmixed existence of each thing comes before the things that, by falling short, are mixed with their own deprivations. So the One by itself is set apart from all multitude; and what is one and at the same time not one is not the first One, but hangs from what is first one: sharing in the One through the principle, but, through the lessening that comes with multitude, now plainly showing in itself the cause of separation.
notes: The Equal itself and equal things here: the Phaedo 74a-75b. Taylor's footnote corrects "is set apart" to "hangs from" in the Greek he translated, and changes its punctuation.

paragraphs.modern: That the One, then, is the principle of all things and the first cause, and that all other things come after the One, is, I think, clear from what has been said. I am astonished, though, at all the other interpreters of Plato who grant the existence of the intellectual kingdom, but do not revere the inexpressible transcendence of the One, and its hyparxis above the whole of things. I wonder at it most in Origen, who shared the same schooling as Plotinus. For Origen ends in intellect and first being, and leaves out the One, which is beyond every intellect and every being. If he leaves it out as something better than all knowledge, speech and intellectual perception, we must say he disagrees neither with Plato nor with the nature of things. But if he leaves it out because the One has no hyparxis at all and no existence, because intellect is the best of things, and because what is first being is the same as what is first one, we cannot agree with him in saying these things, nor will Plato admit him and count him among his own. For I think such a teaching is far from Plato's philosophy, and full of Peripatetic novelty. If you are willing, we will bring some arguments against this teaching, and against all others who champion this opinion. We will fight hard for Plato's teaching, and show that by him the first cause is beyond intellect and set apart from all beings, as Plotinus and Porphyry, and all who have received their philosophy, take him to say.

flags.taylor: Origen, who was a partaker of the same erudition with Plotinus
flags.why: This is Origen the Platonist, a fellow pupil of Plotinus under Ammonius Saccas, not the Christian Origen. He wrote a treatise "That the King is the only Maker", which Proclus takes as making intellect the first principle.

flags.taylor: because the one is perfectly unhyparctic
flags.why: Taylor's "unhyparctic" means without hyparxis, without any existence of its own.

paragraphs.modern: We will begin, then, from the Republic. For here Socrates clearly shows that the Good is set above being and the whole intellectual order, following the analogy of the first goodness to the sun. As the ruling sun is to coming to be, to everything visible and to all that sees, by its power of generating light, so the Good must be to intellect and intelligibles, as the cause that produces truth. If this is so, we must say that the sun is set apart both from what sees and from what is seen, and must grant that the Good is above the natures that always think and those that are eternally intelligible. It is better, though, to hear Plato's own words: "You will say that the sun not only gives to visible things the power of being seen, but is also the cause of their coming to be, growth and nourishment, though it is not itself coming to be. Certainly. Say, then, that the things known not only have from the Good their being known, but their being and their very being are added to them by it, though the Good is not being, but beyond being, above it in dignity and power." Through all this, then, it is clear how the Good and the first principle are defined by Plato as spread out above not only the intellectual but the intelligible extent, and being itself, by union, just as it follows that the sun goes beyond all visible things, and perfects and generates all things by its light. How, then, following Plato, can we grant that intellect is the best of things and the cause of all things? How can we say that being itself and the very being of things are the same as the principle that leads all the divine processions? For being and intellect are said to exist first from the Good, to have their hyparxis about the Good, to be filled with the light of truth that comes from there, and to receive the share suited to them from the union of this light, which is more divine than intellect itself and being, as hanging first from the Good, and giving beings a likeness to what is first. For the light sent out from the sun makes everything visible sun-like; and sharing in the light of truth makes the intelligible good-like and divine. So intellect is a god through a light older than intellectual light and intellect itself; and what is at once intelligible and intellectual shares in a divine hyparxis through the fullness of this light given to it as fits it. In short, every divine nature is what it is said to be because of this light, and through it is united to the cause of all beings. By no means, then, is the first Good to be thought the same as intellect, nor must we grant that the intelligible is older than all the hyparxis of the whole of things, since it is even below the light that comes from the Good, and, perfected by this light, is joined in its own order to the Good itself. For we must not say that the intelligible is united to the first in the same way as the light of truth. The light, through being continuous with the Good, is set in it with nothing between; the intelligible, through this light, shares in nearness to the Good. So too among perceptible things the light of the sun is born first together with the sun's circuit, rises as far as the centre of the whole sphere, and is everywhere about it; and all perceptible things through it gain a likeness to the sun, each, by its own nature, filled with sun-like light. These things will be enough to remind those who love the contemplation of truth of Plato's ideas on this subject, and to show that the order of intellect comes after the set-apart transcendence of the One.
notes: Republic VI 508a-509b; the words quoted are 509b. Taylor's footnotes: the Greek he translated has "the One itself" for "being itself", and one sentence of it is badly corrupt.

paragraphs.modern: If we must show the same thing through many witnesses, let us look at what the Stranger from Elea in the Sophist decides about these things.
