He says that the multitude of all beings, whether contraries or not, must hang from the one being (being marked by the one), and that the one being itself must hang from the One. For when we call the hot or the cold, rest or motion, being, we do not call each of these the same as being itself. If rest were being itself, motion would not be being; or if motion were such being, rest would not share in the name of being. But it is clear that being comes to rest, to motion, and to every multitude of beings from one thing that is first being. This very thing, then, which is the cause of being to all things and is shared by all other things, shares in this One; and for this reason, as it is being only, so it is first being. It is being itself, and does not have its being by sharing; but it is one by sharing, and so is acted on by the One. But it is being first. If, then, Plato gives the One an existence beyond being, as he supposes that what is first among wholes goes beyond beings, how could being not come after the One, since it shares in it and is for this reason called one?

flags.taylor: permanency or motion
flags.why: Taylor's "permanency" is rest (stasis): the Sophist's kinds, rest and motion, both are, but neither is being itself (250a-c). "Rest" here means remaining still.

notes: The Sophist 244b-245d: the whole of being, if it is one, is acted on by the One and is not the One itself, "for the truly One must be wholly without parts". Taylor's two footnotes correct "one" to "being" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, Socrates in the Philebus clearly shows the same thing to those who can know wholes from parts: that intellect does not have the same rank as the first cause of all. Searching for the good of the human soul and its end, sharing in which fully in every way it will reap the fruits of a happiness suited to its nature, he first removes pleasure from such an end, and after it intellect, because this too is not filled with all the marks of the good. If, then, the intellect in us is an image of the first intellect, and the good of our whole life is not to be defined by this alone, must not, among wholes too, the cause of good be set above intellectual perfection? For if what is first good existed as the whole intellect, then in us too, and in all other intellectual natures, self-sufficiency and their proper good would be present through sharing in intellect. Our intellect, indeed, is cut off from the good, and lacks it, and so needs pleasure for human perfection. But a divine intellect always shares in the good, and for this reason is divine. For it has the form of the good by sharing in good, but is divine as hanging from the first godhead. It is the same reasoning, then, that concludes that the Good is set apart from the first intellect, and that defines happiness as lying not in thinking alone, but in the all-perfect presence of the good. For the intellectual kind of activity is of itself lacking with respect to blessedness. And why go on at length? Parmenides teaches us most clearly the difference of the One from being and what is, and shows that the One is set apart from all other things and from being; for he shows this of the One at the end of the first hypothesis. And how could the cause of being, set apart from it by highest transcendence, not also be beyond the intellectual order? For intellect is being. And if in intellect there are rest and motion, and Parmenides shows that the One is above both, does he not at once bring us to the inexpressible cause of all things, which is before every intellect? And if every intellect turns back to itself and is in itself, but the One is shown to be neither in itself nor in another, how can we still think intellect the same as the first cause of all? And in what will the One before being differ from the one being, the subject of the second hypothesis, if intellect is the best of things and the first principle of all? For the one being shares in the One, and what shares is second to what is shared. That the One, by Plato, is older than intellect and being has been recalled to our memory by what has been said.
notes: The Philebus 20b-22e, 60a-61a: neither pleasure nor thought alone is the good, but a mixed life; intellect is only "akin" to the good. The Parmenides 141e-142a: the One "in no way is", and is not even one; 138a-139b: it is neither in itself nor in another, neither at rest nor moved.

paragraphs.modern: Next, if the One is neither intelligible nor intellectual, nor in short shares in the power of being, let us look at what ways will lead us to it, and through what intellectual ideas Plato, as far as he can, unfolds to his own the inexpressible and unknown transcendence of the first. I say, then, that at one time he unfolds it through analogy and the likeness of second natures to it, and at another shows its set-apart transcendence and its separation from the whole of things through negations. In the Republic he points to the inexpressible character and hyparxis of the Good through its analogy to the sun; in the Parmenides he shows the difference of the One from all that comes after it through negations. He seems to me to unfold, through one of these ways, the procession from the first cause of all other things, and before other things of the divine orders. For this is why the first cause is set apart from all the natures it produces: everywhere a cause is set above its effects. And this is why the first is none of all things: all things proceed from it. For it is the principle of all things, of beings and also of non-beings. But through the other of these ways he sketches the return to the first of the things that have proceeded from it. For in each order of beings, through likeness to it, there is a monad answering to the Good, which has the same relation to the whole series joined to it that the Good has to all the orders of the gods. And the cause of this likeness is surely the return of the whole of things to the Good. These things, then, proceed from there and return to it. The procession of all things shows us the ascent to the first through negations; the return of all things shows it through analogies. But let no one, thinking these negations are like privations, despise this way of discussion; nor, defining sameness in words analogously, and words in relations, try to slander this leading up to the first principle. For negations, it seems to me, show a threefold character in things. At one time, being of earlier birth than affirmations, they generate them and bring them to perfection. At another, they have a rank equal to affirmations, and negation is then in no way more worthy of reverence than affirmation. And again at another time they have a rank below affirmations, and are nothing else than their privations. For of non-being itself, with which there is also a denial of beings, at one time, thinking of it as beyond being, we say that it is the cause and giver of beings; at another we show that it is equal to being, as, I think, the Stranger from Elea shows in the Sophist that non-being is, if it is lawful to say so, in no way less than being; and at another we leave it as a privation of being and lacking being. For in this way we call all coming to be, and matter itself, non-being.

flags.taylor: nor defining the sameness in words analogously, and words in habitudes, endeavour to calumniate this anagogic progression
flags.why: The sense seems to be: let no one object that analogy only finds a sameness of words or of relations (habitudes), and so slander this way that leads up (anagogic) to the first.

notes: The Sophist 258b: "non-being is in no way less being than being". Matter as non-being: Plotinus II.4.16 and I.8.3.

paragraphs.modern: Analogies, though, are taken only to point to the likeness of second natures to the first principle. No proportion, no relation and no sharing of this principle with what comes after it appears from them. For its set-apart nature is not like what we see in the second and third orders of beings. The Good goes beyond the whole of things far more than intellect goes beyond the natures after it, whether the making intellect, or the intellect of the whole world, or any other of those called divine. Every intellect and every god has a transcendence over lower natures, and over what it causes, less than that which the first principle has over every being. For this principle goes beyond all things alike, not some more and others less, since so we would bring in a greater and lesser relation of it to second natures. We must keep it without relation to all things, and equally set apart from the whole of things. Of other natures, some are nearer to it and others further. For each thing proceeds from it, since it produces all things by one cause; and different things return to it in different ways, while this principle meanwhile receives no relation to or sharing with what comes after it.

The way of showing what concerns the One is, then, twofold, as we have said. And again Plato gives us two names for the inexpressible cause. In the Republic he calls it the Good, and shows it to be the source of the truth that unites intellect and intelligibles. In the Parmenides he calls such a principle the One, and shows that it gives existence to the divine henads. Again, of these names, one is the image of the procession of the whole of things, the other of their return. Because all things have their existence and proceed from the first principle, we give it the name of the One, and show that it is the cause of all multitude and every procession. For from where does multitude come into light except from the One? And because, again, what proceeds from it by nature returns to it, and desires its inexpressible hyparxis, which cannot be grasped, we call it the Good. For what else turns all things back, and is reached for by all beings as their object of desire, but the Good? All other things exist in a distributed way, and are prized by some beings but not by others; and everything said to exist in any way longs for some things and avoids others. But the Good is the common object of desire of all beings, and all things by their nature lean and reach towards it. And everywhere the leaning of desiring natures is towards the object of desire proper to them. So the Good turns back, and the One gives existence to, all second natures. But let no one suppose that the inexpressible can for this reason be named, or that the cause of all union is made double. For here we carry names over to it, looking to what comes after it, and to the processions from it, or the turnings back in a circle to it. Because multitude exists from it, we give it the name of the One; because all things, even those with the dimmest existence, turn back to it, we call it the Good.

We try, then, to know the unknown nature of the first principle through the things that proceed from it and return to it; and through the same things we also try to name what is inexpressible. This principle, however, is neither known by beings nor expressible by any of all things. Set apart from all knowledge and all speech, and beyond grasp, it produces from itself by one cause all knowledge, everything known, all words, and whatever can be grasped by speech. Its unified nature, above all division, shines out to view in a twofold way in the natures after it, or rather in a threefold way. For all things remain in the One, proceed from it, and return to it. At one and the same time they are united to it, are set below its union, which is set apart from the whole of things, and desire to share in it. Union gives to all second natures a stable transcendence, which exists in a joining with their cause that does not proceed. Being set below defines the procession of beings and their separation from the unshared, first unity. And desire perfects the return of the natures that exist, and their circling towards the inexpressible. First natures, then, being always wholly united to the inexpressible, some more distantly and others more nearly, and receiving through this union their hyparxis and their share of good, we try to show by names the procession and return of the whole of things. But their stable holding in the first, if it is lawful to say so, and their union with the inexpressible, since this cannot be grasped or reached by knowledge, those wise in divine things could not point to in words. For as the inexpressible is first hidden in places no one can reach, and set apart from all beings, so too the union of all things with it is hidden, inexpressible and unknown to all beings. For every being is united to it neither by intellectual reaching nor by the activity of being, since things without knowledge are united to the first, and things deprived of all activity share, in their order, in a joining with it. What is unknown in beings by their union with the first, then, we neither try to know nor to show by names. Better able to look at their procession and return, we give the first two names, which we draw as likenesses from second natures. We also define two ways up to the first, joining the way through analogy with the name of the Good, and the way through negations with the name of the One. Plato points to this: in the Republic he calls the first the Good, and at the same time makes a return to it through analogy; in the Parmenides, setting it up as the One itself, he unfolds its transcendence, set apart from beings, through negative conclusions. By both ways, then, the first principle goes beyond the powers of knowing and the parts of speech, while all other things give us the cause of knowledge and of naming. The first principle gives existence in a unified way to all the unions and hyparxes of second natures, while the things after this cause share in it in a divided way. These, as we said before, are made many by remaining, proceeding and returning; but the One is at once wholly set apart from all fertile processions, all powers of return, and all one-like realities in beings. What, then, are the ways of the teaching about the first, through what names Plato tries to point to it, and from where the names and ways of this pointing, which is unknown to all things, are drawn, is, I think, clear enough from what has been said.

flags.taylor: neither by intellectual injection, [or projection]
flags.why: Taylor's "injection" and "projection" render epibolē, the mind's reaching out to its object. Things are united to the One not by any act of knowing.

paragraphs.modern: If we must look at each of the teachings about the first principle scattered in Plato's writings, and bring them together into one science of theology, let us consider first, if you are willing, what Socrates shows in the sixth book of the Republic by the way already mentioned, and how through analogy he teaches us the wonderful transcendence of the Good over all beings and the summits of the whole of things. First, he distinguishes beings from each other: he sets some down as intelligible and others as perceptible, and defines science by knowledge of beings. He joins sense with perceptible things; and, dividing all things in two, he sets one set-apart monad over intelligible multitude, and a second over perceptible multitude, by likeness to the first. Of these monads, he shows that one generates intelligible light and the other perceptible light. And he shows that by intelligible light all intelligibles are god-like and good-like, by sharing in the first God; and by perceptible light, through the perfection that comes from the sun, all perceptible natures are sun-like, and like their one monad. Besides this, he hangs the second monad from the one that reigns in the intelligible. And so he stretches all things, the first and the last of beings, intelligibles and perceptibles, towards the Good. This way of leading back to the first seems to me the best, and most suited to theology: to gather all the gods in the world into one union and hang them from their nearest monad; to refer the gods above the world to the intellectual kingdom; to hang the intellectual gods from intelligible union; and to refer the intelligible gods themselves, and all beings through them, to what is first. For as the monad of the natures in the world is above the world, as the monad of the natures above the world is intellectual, and that of intellectual natures intelligible, so first intelligibles must hang from the monad above intelligibles, be perfected by it, and, filled with godhead, light up second natures with intelligible light. The intellectual natures, which enjoy their being from intelligibles, but their good and one-like hyparxis from the first cause, must hold together the natures above the world by intellectual light. And the kinds of gods before the world, receiving a pure intellect from the intellectual gods, intelligible light from the intelligible gods, and a unified light from the father of the whole of things, must send into this visible world the light they have. For this reason the sun, the summit of the natures in the world, proceeding from the depths of the aether, gives visible things a perfection beyond nature, and makes them as like as possible to the worlds above the heavens. These things, though, we will discuss more fully later.
notes: Republic VI 507b-509b: the many beautiful things and the Beautiful itself; sight, light and the sun, "the offspring of the Good, which the Good begot in proportion to itself" (508b-c).

paragraphs.modern: The present account, then, hangs all things from the Good, the first unity, in the way described. For if the sun holds together everything perceptible, and the Good produces and perfects everything intelligible, and of these the second monad (the sun) is called the offspring of the Good, and so makes the perceptible bright, adorns it and fills it with good because it imitates the first-born cause of itself, then all things will share in the Good in this way, and will reach towards this one principle: intelligibles, and the most divine of beings, with nothing between, and perceptible things through their monad, the sun.

flags.taylor: imitates the primogenial cause of itself
flags.why: Taylor's "primogenial" means first-born, original; Proclus means that the sun imitates the Good, its own cause.

paragraphs.modern: Again, and in another way, Plato tells us in this passage of the Republic the analysis that leads up to the first principle. He hangs all the multitudes in the world from the intelligible monads: all beautiful things, for instance, from the Beautiful itself, all good things from the Good, and all equal things from the Equal itself. Again, he takes some things as intelligible and others as perceptible, but their summits are set in a one-like way in the intelligibles. Again, from these intelligible Forms he sees fit to go up still higher; and, revering more the goodness beyond intelligibles, he takes it that all intelligibles, and the monads they hold, exist and are perfected through it. For as we refer perceptible multitude to a monad not ranked with perceptible things, and think that through this monad the multitude of perceptible things has its existence, so we must refer intelligible multitude to another cause, not counted among intelligibles, from which they have their being and their divine hyparxis.

But let no one imagine that Plato grants the Good the same rank in the intelligible Forms as before intelligibles. The good that is ranked with the beautiful must be taken as a good of being, one of the Forms among intelligibles. The first Good, which, by joining the article to the noun, we usually call "the Good", is taken to be beyond being, and better than all beings in dignity and power. For Socrates too, discussing the beautiful and the good, calls one the Beautiful itself and the other the Good itself, and so, he says, we name all the things we then rightly took as many. Again, taking each as being one, we name each thing what it is. So Socrates leads us from perceptible things that are beautiful and good, and in short from things that are shared, exist in other things, and are made many, to the henads of intelligibles, beyond being, and the first beings; and from these again he carries us over to the set-apart cause of everything beautiful and good. For in the Forms the Beautiful itself leads many beautiful things, and the Good itself many goods, and each Form gives existence only to things like itself. But the first Good is the cause not only of what is good, but of beautiful things as well, as Plato says elsewhere: "all things are for its sake, and it is the cause of everything beautiful".

flags.taylor: to the superessential unities of intelligibles and the first essences
flags.why: Proclus seems to mean the henads at the summit of the intelligible order, beyond being, and the first beings that hang from them.

notes: Republic VI 507b: "we speak of many beautiful things and many good things ... and again of the Beautiful itself and the Good itself". The Second Letter 312e, quoted here, is discussed in chapters 8-9.

paragraphs.modern: Further, the good that is in the Forms is intelligible and known, as Socrates himself teaches; but the Good before the Forms is beyond beings and set above all knowledge. The first is the source of the perfection of being; the second gives good to the gods as gods, and generates goods that come before beings. So we must not take it that, when Socrates calls the first principle the Good from the name of a Form, he means outright the intelligible goodness. Though the first principle is above all speech and naming, we allow Socrates to call it the cause of everything beautiful and good, carrying names over to it through the things it fills most nearly. For I think this is what Socrates points to in all he says about the Good: that it is beyond knowledge and things known, and beyond being and what is, by its analogy to the sun. And in a wonderful way he gives us a short form of the negations of the One in the Parmenides. For saying that the Good is neither truth, nor being, nor intellect, nor science, at once separates it from the henads beyond being and every kind of gods, from the intellectual and intelligible orders, and from every existence of soul. These are the first things, and through the first hypothesis of the Parmenides these are taken away from the principle of the whole of things.

flags.taylor: from the name of idea
flags.why: That is, from the name of a Form (idea): the Good is named after the Form of the good, though it is beyond the Forms.

notes: Republic VI 508e-509a: the Good is the cause of knowledge and truth, yet "more beautiful than these"; neither science nor truth is the Good.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, when he praises the Good, the leader of the divine orders, as the brightest of being, he does not call it brightest as sharing in light. For the first light proceeds from it to intelligibles and intellect. He gives it this name as the cause of the light spread everywhere, and as the source of every intelligible, intellectual or cosmic godhead. For this light is nothing else than sharing in a divine hyparxis. As all things become good-like by sharing in the Good, and are filled with the light that comes from there, so the natures that are first beings are god-like, and, as is said, intelligible and intellectual beings become divine by sharing in godhead. Looking, then, to all that has been said, we will keep the set-apart transcendence of the Good over all beings and the divine orders. But again, in each order of beings we must grant that there is a monad answering to it: not only among perceptible things, as Plato says the sun is, but among the natures above the world, and in the kinds of gods ranked from the Good before these. For clearly the natures nearer to the first cause, which share in it more, are more like it. And as it is the cause of all beings, so these set up monads that lead more partial orders. Plato ranks the multitudes under the monads, but stretches all the monads towards the set-apart principle of the whole of things, and sets them in a one-like way about it. So the science of theology must be unfolded in keeping with the divine orders, and our ideas about the first must be transcendent, unmixed and unconnected with other things. We should see all second natures as existing by it and perfected about it; but we should set it above all the monads in beings, by one excess of simplicity, and as ranked in a unified way before the whole orders of gods. For as the gods themselves enact the order among them, so the truth about them, the prior causes of beings, and the second and third offspring of these, must be clearly distinguished.

flags.taylor: as the most splendid of being
flags.why: Republic VI 518c: the Good is "the brightest of being" (to phanotaton tou ontos), which the soul must learn to bear to look at.

paragraphs.modern: This, then, is the one truth about the first principle, with one reasoning that fits Plato's hypothesis remarkably well: that this principle exists before the whole orders of gods, gives existence to the good-like being of the gods, is the source of goodness beyond being, and that all things after it, reaching towards it, are filled with good, are united to it in an inexpressible way, and exist in a one-like way about it. For its unified nature is not barren; it generates other things all the more as it sets up beforehand a union set apart from the things that exist. Nor does its fertility tend to multitude and division; it remains with undefiled purity, hidden in places no one can reach. For in the natures after it too, we see everywhere that what is perfect desires to generate, and what is full hastens to give its fullness to other things. Much more, then, must the nature that holds all perfections in one, and is not a certain good but the Good itself and more than full (if it is lawful to say so), generate the whole of things and give them existence: producing all things by being set apart from all things, and by being unshared, generating alike the first and the last of beings.

You must not suppose, however, that this generation and procession is sent out by the Good being moved, or multiplied, or having a power of generating, or acting; for all these come after the singleness of the first. For if the Good were moved, it would not be the Good, since the Good itself, which is nothing else, would leave goodness if it were moved. How, then, could what is the source of goodness to beings produce other things when deprived of good? Or if the Good is multiplied through weakness, there will be a procession of the whole of things through a lessening, not an overflowing, of goodness. For what, in generating, leaves its own transcendence hastens to adorn lower natures not through fertile perfection, but through a lessening and lack of its own power. And if the Good produces all things by using power, there will be a lessening of goodness about it. For it will be two things and not one: good and power. And if it lacks power, what is first good will be in need. But if to be the Good itself is enough for the perfection of the things produced and the fullness of all things, why do we take on power in addition? For additions, among the gods, are takings away from transcendent unions. So let the Good be alone, before power and before activity. For all activity is the offspring of power. The Good, then, neither gives existence to all things by acting through activity, nor fills all things with powers by lacking power, nor do all things share in good by its being multiplied, nor do all beings enjoy the first principle by its being moved. For the Good comes before all powers and all activities, every multitude and motion, since each of these is referred to the Good as to its end. The Good, then, is the final end of all ends, and the centre of all desirable natures. All desirable natures give an end to second beings; but what exists before all things, not bounded by any, is the first Good.
notes: Taylor's footnote corrects "all things present" to "all beings" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: After this, let us turn our attention to the ideas about the first principle in Plato's letter to Dionysius, and look at the way he considers its inexpressible and boundless transcendence. But perhaps someone will be angry with us for rashly drawing Plato's words to our own hypotheses, and will say that the three kings he speaks of are all intellectual gods, and that Plato does not see fit to rank or count the Good with second natures. For such counting together should not be thought fitting to the set-apart transcendence of the Good over other things; nor, in short, must we say that the Good joins, as first, with some second or third cause, to complete a triad together with other natures. Rather, it goes before every triad and every number far more than the intelligible gods go before the intellectual. How, then, can we count the Good, which is set apart at once from all the divine numbers, with the other kings, and rank one as first, another as second, and another as third? Someone may also bring many other things showing the transcendence of the first principle over everything divine. But such a person, in interpreting Plato's words this way, will agree remarkably well with us, who say that the Good is unshared, above all the intelligible and intellectual kinds, and set above all the divine monads.
notes: The Second Letter 312e: "All things are about the king of all, and all are for his sake, and he is the cause of all beautiful things; second things are about the second, and third things about the third." Proclus' commentators often doubted the letter; he takes it as Plato's.

paragraphs.modern: That Plato grants the first God to be the king of all things, and says that all things are for his sake and that he is the cause of all beautiful things, does not, I think, need much proof for those who consider his words by themselves, apart from their own guesses, by bringing in which they try by force to agree with Plato. But that we do not say these things counting the first God with second natures Plato himself makes plain. He does not call the first king the first, but only the king of all things; nor does he say that some things are about him, as he says that second things are about the second and third things about the third; he says, in short, that all things are about him. To the other kings he gives number and a divided kingdom; but to the king of all he gives neither a place in a number nor a share of rule set against that of the others. This way of speaking, then, neither counts the king of all with the other kings, nor ranks him as the leader of a triad with the second and third power. For in a threefold division the first monad leads the first orders, those ranked with it; the second the second, and the third the third. If, however, someone takes it that the first monad leads all things, so as to hold at once the second and third lots, still the cause that exists by holding things is different from the cause that reaches equally to all things. To the king of all, all things are subject by one reason and one order; but to the first of the triad, first things are subject by the same order, and second and third things must serve by their sharing with the remaining kings. Does not what Plato says here, then, remarkably praise the set-apart nature of the first cause, and his being unranked with the other kingdoms of the gods? For he says that this cause reigns equally over all things, that all things exist about him, and that being and activity are in all things for his sake.
notes: Taylor's footnote corrects "and" to "but" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: And if Socrates in the Republic clearly teaches that the sun reigns over the world by analogy with the Good, let no one dare to accuse this analogy of counting the Good together with the king of the natures in the world. For unless, together with the likeness of second causes to first principles, we see fit to keep that set-apart rule of the first cause, we will be unable to show that the kings above the world have their lot by analogy with the first cause, who exists before the whole of things by one transcendence. But why go on at length? Plato calls the first God king, but does not see fit to give the others the same name, not only at the beginning of what he says about the first, but shortly after, where he adds: "About the king, and the things I have spoken of, there is nothing of this kind." The first God alone, then, is called king. And he is called the king not only of first things, as the second is of second things and the third of third, but as the cause at once of all being and all beauty. So the first God goes before the other causes in a set-apart and one-like way, by a transcendence over the whole of things, and Plato neither praises him as ranked with them nor as the leader of a triad.
notes: The Second Letter 313a: "About the king and the things I spoke of, there is nothing of the kind" (nothing like the qualities the soul looks for). Taylor's two footnotes correct the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: That these things are said by Plato about the first God we will learn by going back a little to the words just before, which are these: "You say that I have not sufficiently shown you the things about the first nature. I must speak to you in riddles, so that if the letter comes to harm, on land or sea, whoever reads it may not understand. All things are about the king of all, and all are for his sake, and he is the cause of all beautiful things." In these words, then, Plato, setting out to purify our ideas about the first principle through riddles, praises the king of all things, and refers to him the cause of the whole of beautiful and good things. Who, then, is the king of all things, if not the unified God, set apart from all things, who produces all things from himself, and leads all orders by one cause? Who turns all ends back to himself and sets them about himself? For if you call him, for whose sake all things are, the end of all ends and the first-born cause, you will not stray from the truth about him. Who is the cause of all beautiful things, shining on them with divine light, and shutting up what is ugly and without measure, and the dimmest of all things, at the furthest edge of the universe?
notes: The Second Letter 312d-e.

paragraphs.modern: If you are willing, we will also show from the words of Plato that follow these that it is not fitting for the first principle to receive either speech or knowledge. For the words, "This question of yours about the cause of all beautiful things is a question about something with a certain quality", are to be referred to this principle. For it cannot be grasped by intellect, because it is unknown, nor unfolded, because it is unbounded; whatever you say of it, you will speak of it as of something; you will speak about it, but you will not speak it. For speaking of the things of which it is the cause, we cannot say, or grasp by thinking, what it is. Here, then, the adding of quality and the busy activity of the soul take it away from the goodness set apart from all things, by the overflow of the soul's ideas about it. This also draws the soul down to akin, inborn and many-formed intelligibles, and keeps it from receiving what is marked by unity and hidden in sharing in the Good. And it is not only fitting that the human soul should be cleansed of the things ranked with it, for union and sharing with what is first, and for this should leave all its own multitude behind, and, rousing its own hyparxis, come near with closed eyes, as is said, to the king of all things, and share in his light as far as is lawful for it. Intellect too, which is before us, and all divine natures, by their highest unions, their torches beyond being and their first hyparxes, are united to what is first, and always share in its overflowing fullness; and this not as they are what they are, but as they are set apart from what is akin to them and converge on the One, the principle of all. For the cause of all has sown in all things tokens of his own all-perfect transcendence, and through these sets all things about himself, and, set apart from the whole of things, is present to all things in an inexpressible way. So everything, going into the inexpressible of its own nature, finds there the symbol of the father of all. All things too by nature revere him and are united to him through a fitting mystic token, stripping off their own nature and hastening to become his token alone, and to share in him alone, through desire for his unknown nature and for the source of good. So when they have run up as far as this cause, they become still, and are freed from the birth pangs and the desire for goodness, unknown, inexpressible, unshared and more than full, that all things have by nature. That what is said here is about the first God, and that Plato in these ideas leaves him unranked with the other causes and set apart from them, has, I think, been shown well enough.

flags.taylor: but you will not speak it
flags.why: Proclus' distinction: we can speak about the first, from what comes after it, but never say what it is.

flags.taylor: superessential torches
flags.why: Taylor's "torches" are the lights or flames of the gods (a Chaldean image): their summits, beyond being, by which they touch the first.

notes: The Second Letter 313a: "the soul asks what kind of thing it is, looking at things akin to itself, none of which is adequate". "With closed eyes": compare Plotinus I.6.8, "close your eyes and wake another way of seeing".

paragraphs.modern: Let us next consider each of these teachings, and fit them to our ideas about cause, so that from them we may grasp by reasoning the aim of the whole of Plato's theology. Let one truth about the first principle, then, be most of all the one that praises his inexpressible, simple and all-transcending nature: which sets all things about him, but does not say that he generates or produces anything, or that he exists before as the end of what comes after him. For such a way of speaking neither adds anything to the unknown one, set apart from all things, nor makes many him who is set above all union, nor attributes the relation and sharing of second things to him who is wholly unshared. Nor, in short, does it claim to teach anything about him or his nature, but only about the second and third natures that exist after him.

This, then, being this way of pointing to the first God, and such the way it reveres the inexpressible, the second after it is the one that turns all the desires of things to him, and praises him as the object of desire and the common end of all things, by one cause that comes before all other causes. For the last of things exists only for the sake of something else, but the first is only that for the sake of which all other things exist; and all the middle natures share in both these characters. So they cling truly to the natures above them, as objects of desire, but give the perfection of desire to lower beings.

The third view of the principle of things is far below the ones before, taking him as giving existence to all beautiful things. To praise him as the giver of good, and as the end coming before the two orders of things, is not very far from the account that says that all causes come after him and have their existence from him, both those that are fathers and sources of good and those that give fertile powers. But to give him a producing and generating causality is still further from the all-perfect union of the first. For since it cannot be known or spoken of by second natures, we must not say that it is the cause, or that it generates beings, but should praise in silence this inexpressible nature, this wholly causeless cause before all causes. If, though, as we try to give it the name of the Good and the One, we likewise give it causality, and the character of end or of father, we must forgive the soul's labour about this inexpressible principle, as it longs to see him with the eye of intellect and to speak about him; but at the same time the set-apart, boundless transcendence of the One must be taken as going beyond this kind of pointing. From these, then, we can receive Plato's sacred ideas, and an order suited to the things themselves. We may say that the first part of this sentence points well enough to the simplicity, transcendence, and in short the unrankedness with all things, of the king of all. For saying that all things exist about him unfolds the hyparxis of second things, but leaves what is beyond all things without any connection to what comes after it. The second part praises the cause of all the gods as set beforehand in the rank of the end. For the highest of all causes is joined at once to what comes before cause; and of this kind is the final cause, that for the sake of which all things exist. This part, then, comes after the other, and is woven together with the order of things and the procession of Plato's teaching.
notes: Taylor's three footnotes correct the Greek he translated ("order" for "action", and "of the gods" for "of the god").

paragraphs.modern: Again, the third part says that he produces all beautiful things, and so adds to him a kind of cause lower than the final. This, I think, is why Plotinus does not hesitate to call the first God the source of the beautiful. We must give what is best to the best of all things, so that he may be the cause of all, and really before cause. And this is the Good. This too, which is remarkable, can be seen in Plato's words: the first of these three divine teachings neither dares to say anything about the Good, this inexpressible nature, nor lets us refer any kind of cause to it. The second leaves the Good inexpressible, as it should, but from the relation of what comes after it lets us gather the final cause: it does not refuse to call it that for the sake of which all things are. But when it says that all things are for the sake of the Good, it rouses in us the idea of sharing and ranking between the object of desire and the natures that desire it. And the third shows that the Good is the cause of all beautiful things. But this is to say something about it, to add to the simplicity of the first cause, and, not remaining in the idea of the end, to join to it the producing principle of second things. It seems to me that Plato here points to the natures that come into light next after the first. For it is not possible to say anything about it except as moved to this at one time from all things, and at another from the best of things; for it is the cause of hyparxis to all things, and unfolds its own separate union through their distinctive characters. We give it the name of the One and the Good, then, from the gift that reaches all things from it. For of what all things share in, we say there is no other cause than what is set before all of them. But the "about which", the "for the sake of which" and the "from which" belong first to the intelligible gods, and from them are given to the first God. For from where can we suppose the unified gods get their distinctive characters, if not from what is before them? So "about" fits this summit of intelligibles, because all the divine orders proceed in a hidden way about this summit, ranked before them. "For the sake of which" belongs to the middle order of intelligibles, for all things exist for the sake of eternity and a wholly entire hyparxis. And "from which" fits the furthest edge of intelligibles, for this first produces all things and adorns them in a one-like way. These things we will make better known in the teaching about the intelligible gods, which will follow shortly.

flags.taylor: the fountain of the beautiful
flags.why: Plotinus (VI.7.32-33, I.6.9) calls the Good "the source and principle of beauty", beyond beauty itself.

notes: The three intelligible orders (being, eternity or life, and the intelligible living being, Timaeus' "pattern") are the subject of Book III. Taylor's footnotes correct two words of the Greek he translated ("of cause"; "for the sake of which" for "through which", the final, not the instrumental, cause).

paragraphs.modern: Next, let us finish the discussion of the first God with Parmenides' study, and unfold the mystic ideas of the first hypothesis as far as our present purpose requires; for the most complete interpretation of them we refer the reader to our commentary on that dialogue. First, we must settle this about the first hypothesis: that it holds as many conclusions in denial as the hypothesis after it holds in affirmation. The second shows all the orders proceeding from the One; the first shows that the One is set apart from all the divine kinds. From both, it is plain to everyone that the cause of the whole of things must go beyond what it produces. For because the One is the cause of all the gods, it goes beyond all things. And because it is set apart from them by transcendence, it gives all things their realities. For through being spread out above all things, it makes all things exist. In the second and third orders of beings too, causes wholly set apart from their effects generate and hold together their offspring more perfectly than causes ranked with their effects. And the One, by producing all the divine orders in an inexpressible way, appears set above all in a unified way. For in the productions after it, the cause is everywhere different from what it causes. So nature, being bodiless, is a cause that goes beyond bodies; soul, being wholly everlasting, is the cause of things that come to be; and intellect, being unmoved, is the cause of everything moved. If, then, in each procession of beings the effects are denied of their causes, we must surely take all things away alike from the cause of all.
notes: Proclus' Commentary on the Parmenides, of which the books on the first hypothesis survive (Book VII in the Latin of William of Moerbeke).

paragraphs.modern: Second, I think the order of the negations must be defined by those who receive theology in keeping with Parmenides' aim. We must grant that they proceed from the monads that exist first in the divine kinds, and that Parmenides takes away from the One all second and third natures in the order fitting each. For what goes beyond more ruling causes must far more come before lower ones. But Parmenides does not begin his negations from the gods united to the first. For this kind is hard to distinguish from the One, since, ranked by nature right after it, it is most unified and hidden, and surpassingly like its producing cause. So Parmenides, beginning where division and multitude first appear, before all other things, and going in order through all the second orders as far as the last of things, comes back again to the beginning, and shows how the One differs from the gods most like it, which first share in it, by one inexpressible cause.

flags.taylor: does not begin his negations from the Gods that are united to the first
flags.why: That is, the first denial ("the One is not many", 137c) answers not to the highest gods (the intelligible gods, united to the One) but to the order where multitude first appears; the denials of being at the end (141e) return to the highest.

paragraphs.modern: Third, besides what has been said, I settle this about the manner of the negations: they do not deprive their subjects, but generate what are, as it were, their opposites. For because the first principle is not many, the many proceed from it; because it is not a whole, wholeness proceeds from it; and so with the rest. In settling this I speak in keeping with Plato, who sees fit to remain in negations and add nothing to the One. For whatever you add, you lessen the One, and then show that it is not the One, but what is acted on by the One, or shares in it. For it is then not one only, but besides this has something else by sharing. This way of negation, then, is set apart, unified and first, a going out from the whole of things into an unknown and inexpressible transcendence of simplicity. And having given such a way to the first God, we must again set him apart from the negations too. For no speech and no name belongs to the One, says Parmenides. But if no speech belongs to it, clearly no negation does either. For all things come after the One: things knowable, knowledge, and the instruments of knowledge; and in a way the impossible shows itself at the end of the hypothesis. For if nothing at all can be said of the One, this discussion itself does not fit the One either. Nor is it at all surprising that the speech of those who want to know the inexpressible by words should end in the impossible, since all knowledge joined to an object that does not belong to it loses its power. Sense, if we said it belonged to what science knows, would overturn itself; and so would science and every kind of knowledge if we said they belonged to the intelligible. So speech, when concerned with the inexpressible, overturned about itself, has no rest, and opposes itself.
notes: The Parmenides 142a: "there is no name of it, nor speech, nor any science, perception or opinion"; and Parmenides concludes, "Can these things be so about the One? I think not."

paragraphs.modern: Now, then, if ever, let us put away knowledge of many forms, root out of ourselves all the variety of life, and in perfect stillness come near to the cause of all things. For this, let not only opinion and imagination be at rest, nor only the passions that hinder our rising up to the first be at peace; but let the air be still, and the universe itself be still. Let all things carry us with a calm power to sharing with the inexpressible. And standing there, having gone beyond the intelligible (if we hold anything of this kind), with eyes almost closed, as if worshipping the rising sun, since it is not lawful for any being at all to look at him steadily, let us look at the sun from which the light of the intelligible gods proceeds, rising, as the poets say, from the bosom of the ocean. Then, coming down from this divine stillness into intellect, and from intellect using the reasonings of the soul, let us tell ourselves what the natures are from which, in this procession, we will see the first God set apart. Let us praise him, as it were, not as founding the earth and the heavens, nor as giving existence to souls and to the generations of all living things; for these he produced too, but among the last of things. Before these, let us praise him as bringing into light the whole intelligible and intellectual kind of gods, together with all the gods above the world and in the world: as the God of all gods, the henad of all henads, beyond the first inner sanctuaries, more inexpressible than all silence and more unknown than all being, holy among the holy, and hidden in the intelligible gods. And again after these things, coming down into reasoning from an intellectual hymn, and using the blameless science of dialectic, let us, following the contemplation of first causes, see how the first God is set apart from the whole of things. And let our descent go as far as this. For opinion, imagination and sense keep us from sharing in the presence of the gods, draw us down from Olympian goods to motions born of earth, divide the intellect in us in the manner of the Titans, and tear us away from being settled among wholes to the images of beings.

flags.taylor: beyond the first adyta
flags.why: The adyta are the innermost shrines of a temple, which only priests may enter; Proclus sets the One beyond even the first, the intelligible gods.

flags.taylor: Titannically divide the intellect that is in us
flags.why: In the Orphic myth the Titans tore the child Dionysus to pieces; the Neoplatonists read this as the dividing of the one intellect into many, and of the soul into the body.

notes: "Let the air be still, and the universe itself be still": an echo of Plotinus V.1.2, where the soul is to see the world-soul flowing in "while the earth is still, and the sea and the air, and the heaven itself". The sun "rising from the ocean": Iliad VII.421-422.

paragraphs.modern: What, then, will be the first idea of the science that proceeds from intellect and unfolds itself into light? What else can we say it is than the simplest and best known of all the ideas this science holds? What is this? "The One," says Parmenides, "if it is one, will not be many." For the many must share in the One; but the One does not share in the one, but is the One itself. Nor is what is first one shared. For it would not be purely one if mixed with the many, nor would it be what is one, if it took on the addition of something lower. So the One is set apart from the many. The many first exist in the summit of the first intellectual gods, and in the intelligible place of vision, as we are taught in the second hypothesis. So the One wholly goes beyond an order of this kind, and is its cause. For the not-many is not a privation, as we have said, but the cause of the many. Parmenides does not think he needs to prove this; as something most plain to everyone, he shows it first, through the opposition, as it were, of the many to the One. Using this, he takes away what follows; and he takes away what comes after this using the conclusions before it, and he always does this in the same way. At one time he takes the elements of his proofs from the nearest conclusions, at another from those further off. For after this intelligible order of gods, as we have said, he gives existence, from their set-apart cause, to the order that holds together and bounds their extent. This order he calls, in the second hypothesis, parts and a whole. These he denies of the One, using the many to distinguish the subjects from the One. For, as he says, what is a whole and has parts is many; but the One is beyond the many. If, then, the One goes beyond the intelligible simplicity, but the whole and what has parts proceed from it, to become the bond of the whole of this division, must not the One be neither a whole nor in need of parts? And I think it is through this transcendence that the One exists before as the cause of this order of gods, and produces this order, but in a set-apart way.

flags.taylor: in the summit of the first intellectual Gods, and in the intelligible place of survey
flags.why: Proclus' "intellectual gods" here are the intelligible and at the same time intellectual gods, the middle rank between the intelligible and the intellectual (Book IV); "the place of vision" is the Phaedrus' plain above the heavens, which he puts at their summit.

notes: The Parmenides 137c-d: "If the One is, it will not be many ... so it will neither be a whole nor have parts."

paragraphs.modern: Third after these, we can look at the order that has the boundary of the gods at once intelligible and intellectual, proceeding from the One, and see the One wholly spread out above it. This order exists from the second kinds, and from the intellectual wholeness of the kinds. But the One, as has been shown, is set apart from this wholeness as its cause. So the One has neither beginning, middle nor end, nor has it extremes, nor does it share in any shape. For through these gods the order of gods just mentioned comes to light. Whether, then, there is a perfecting summit in these gods, or what is praised as the middle centre, or an ending that turns the end of these gods back to their beginning, the One is equally beyond every threefold division. For the One would have parts, and would be many, if it shared in things of this kind. But it has been shown that the One exists in a unified way before the many, and before wholeness with its parts, as their cause. And you see how Parmenides shows us one negation of the highest order, two of the middle, and three of the last. Besides this, he shows that the One has no limit; but the unlimited is a thing of this kind. And separately from this he shows that the One does not receive any shape.
notes: The Parmenides 137d-138a: the One has no beginning, middle or end, is unlimited, and has no shape, neither straight nor round.

paragraphs.modern: Again, after these threefold orders, we must turn our attention to the intellectual gods that exist from them and receive a threefold division, and show that the One goes beyond these too. For such is the One, says Parmenides, since it is neither in itself nor in another. If it were in another, it would be held all round by what it is in, and would touch everywhere what holds it. But then it would have a shape, would be made of parts, and so would be many and not one. And if it were in itself, it would hold itself wholly in itself. But holding and at the same time being held, it will be two, and no longer first one. The argument, then, comes to the same conclusion, and shows that the One will not be one, through the summit of the intellectual order, if anyone tries to mix it with other things. So the One, wholly set apart from this summit too, gives it existence; this summit at one and the same time sharing in the third of the gods set above it, being produced from the second of these gods, and perfected from the first, and wholly set in it.
notes: The Parmenides 138a-b: the One is neither in another, for it would be held round and touched at many points, nor in itself, for it would be two.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, the One also generates the second intellectual order, unmixed with it. For the One neither stands still nor is moved. It shares in neither of these; but, equally set apart from both, it goes at the same time beyond the middle orders of the intellectual procession of the gods. If it were moved, it would be moved in one of two ways, by change of quality or by motion in place. But the One cannot be changed in quality, for, so changed, it would not be one, and would fall away from a unified hyparxis. Nor can it be moved in place. It cannot be moved in a circle, because it would have parts, a middle and extremes. And if it exchanged one place for another, it would be divisible. For it would have to be neither wholly in the place it is moved to, nor in the place it starts from. For if it were wholly in either, it would be unmoved, partly not yet moved, partly having already stopped. But if the One stands still, it must surely remain in the same thing. And it has been shown that the One is nowhere; so it is neither in itself nor in another. In no way, then, is the One moved, nor does it stand still: things (motion and rest) that belong most of all to the middle order of the intellectual gods, as will be clear from the second hypothesis. For the first God produces this order too, being set apart from it.
notes: The Parmenides 138b-139b: the One is neither altered nor carried round nor moved from place to place, nor does it stand still.

paragraphs.modern: Third, through what follows next, we can look at the last order of the intellectual gods, proceeding from the One and set below it. For in this order sameness and difference exist united. But at the same time the One exists before both. For the different is said to be different both from itself and from other things; and likewise the same is the same as itself and as other things. But the One is not different from itself, because what is different from the One will be not one. And it is not the same as other things, lest, becoming the same as them, it should pass unnoticed into their nature. Moreover, the One is not different from other things either. For it would at the same time be one and have, as an addition, the power of difference. For so far as it is different, it will not be one, since difference is not the One. So, being one and different, it will be many and not the One. Nor is the One the same as itself. For if the One and the same differed only in name, then the many, by sharing in sameness with each other, would not be many. For it is impossible that the many should become one by sharing in the many. But if the One and sameness are different in being, what is first one does not share in sameness, lest, taking on sameness in addition to the one, it should become a one that is acted on, and not what is first one. If, then, the furthest edge of the intellectual gods is marked by this tetrad, it is clear that the One, existing beyond this too, unfolds it into light from above, and sets over the wholes of the universe a fourfold monad, the source of adornment to all second natures. For from here other things first receive sharing with the One, being also produced and held together by the One.

flags.taylor: For if the one and the same differ only in name, the many will not be in consequence of participating of sameness with each other
flags.why: The argument (Parmenides 139d-e): if being the same were being one, then whatever is the same as something would be one with it, and the many, being the same as each other, would be one. The modern English follows the sense.

notes: The Parmenides 139b-e: the One is neither the same as nor different from itself or another.

paragraphs.modern: After the intellectual gods, the inexpressible transcendence of the One orders the extent of the gods above the world, while the One meanwhile is set apart, in a hidden way, from its offspring above the world. This extent exists next after the intellectual gods, but receives its hyparxis in a one-like way from the first God. Parmenides produces this through likeness and unlikeness, from the godhead that closes the boundary of the intellectual monads. For the like is what is acted on by sameness, as unlikeness is what is acted on by difference. So Parmenides shows that the One goes beyond such a character of the gods too, by one simplicity. For what is set above the power of the same and the different goes far more beyond the kinds whose existence is by likeness and unlikeness.
notes: The Parmenides 139e-140b: the One is neither like nor unlike, since it has nothing the same and nothing different.

paragraphs.modern: What, then, remains after this? Is it not clear that it is the multitude of the gods in the world? But this too is twofold: one heavenly, the other below the moon. Of these, the kind that circles in the heavens proceeds together with the equal, the greater and the less. In the kind below the moon, the equal has a difference in multitude from the heavenly equality, and the unequal is again divided by the power of the more and the less. By another kind of the divine orders, then, there will be a monad and a dyad; but above they are akin to the One and to sameness, and below to multitude and the intellectual cause of difference. So the One goes beyond all these. For the equal everywhere is made of the same parts. By what means, then, could the nature that is at once set apart from sameness, and from the difference that goes with it, share in equality and inequality?
notes: The Parmenides 140b-d: the One is neither equal nor unequal, to itself or to another, since it would have the same or different measures.

paragraphs.modern: Beyond all these divine orders, then, we must see with intellect the kinds of souls made divine and distributed about the gods. For in each of the divine processions, and in the processions of souls, the first kind appears born together with the gods, since both in the heavens and in the region below the moon divine souls receive the division of the gods into the world, as the Athenian Stranger shows somewhere. The extent of soul, then, is marked by time and a life in time. And the distinctive character of divine souls is shown by Parmenides to lie in their becoming at the same time younger and older than themselves and other things. For, circling always by the same time, and joining the beginning with the end, as at one and the same time they go on to the end of the whole period they become younger, and as they come round to its beginning they become older. Yet all their ages always keep the same measures of time. Again, there is sameness in them, and difference: the first keeps equality, the second inequality, in time. So the One exists before divine souls, and generates these too together with the gods. We now come to the end of the whole division of the higher natures; and the cause of all intelligibles at once brings into light the kinds that follow the gods, divided three ways by the three parts of time. But this cause is shown by Parmenides' intellectual reachings to be set apart from these too. For what is beyond all time, and the life in time, can by no means become subject to the more partial periods of time.

flags.taylor: younger and at the same time older both than themselves and other things
flags.why: The Parmenides 140e-141d: the One is neither older nor younger, nor the same age, nor in time at all. Proclus reads these as the marks of divine souls, which live in time but in circles, always returning to their beginning.

notes: The Laws X 898c-899b: the souls that drive the sun, moon and stars are gods, and divide the heaven among them.

paragraphs.modern: What is first of all things, then, brings into light all the gods, divine souls and the higher kinds, and is neither entangled with its offspring nor multiplied about them; wholly set apart from them in a wonderful simplicity and transcendence of union, it gives all things alike procession, and order in the procession. So Parmenides, beginning from the intelligible place of vision of the first intellectual gods, goes this far, by the measures of generation, giving existence to the kinds of gods and to the natures united to and following the gods, and always shows that the One is inexpressibly set apart from all things. But again from here he returns to the beginning, and, imitating the return of the whole of things, separates the One from the highest, the intelligible gods. For in this way most of all we can see the transcendence of the One, and the boundless difference of its union from all other things: if we show not only that it is set above the second or third processions in the divine orders, but that it exists before the intelligible henads themselves; and this in a way fitting the simplicity of their hidden nature, not through a variety of words but through the reaching of intellect alone. For intelligibles are by nature fit to be known by intellect. Parmenides shows this too in fact, leaving logical methods behind, and, acting by intellect, says that the One is above being and what is marked by the One. For this was not gathered from the conclusions before it. For the account of the first gods themselves would be without proof, if it drew its credit from lower things. At the same time, then, Parmenides contends that all knowledge, and all the instruments of knowledge, fall short of the transcendence of the One, and end beautifully in the inexpressible of that God who is beyond all things. For after acts of science and reachings of intellect, a union with the unknown follows. To this Parmenides refers his whole discussion, and so concludes the first hypothesis, hanging all the divine kinds from the One, but showing that the One is set apart from all things in a unified way, existing without sharing in intelligibles or perceptibles, and giving existence in an inexpressible way to the shared monads. So the One is also said to be beyond the one joined with being, and at the same time beyond every shared multitude of henads.

flags.taylor: asserting that the one is above essence, and being characterized by the one
flags.why: The Parmenides 141e-142a: the One does not share in being, and so "is not even one"; Proclus reads this as setting the One above the one being, the summit of the intelligible gods. Taylor's footnote corrects the Greek he translated ("to the gods").

paragraphs.modern: Such, then, as it seems to me, is Plato's theology concerning the first God, and so great is the transcendence it has over all other discussions of divine things. At one and the same time it reverently keeps the inexpressible union of this God, set apart from the whole of things, beyond the grasp of all acts of knowing, and apart from all beings; and it unfolds the paths that lead up to him, brings to fulfilment the desire, always in labour, that souls have for the father and forefather of all things, and kindles in them that torch by which they are most of all joined to the unknown transcendence of the One. After this unshared and inexpressible cause, truly beyond being, separated from all being, power and activity, the discussion of the gods follows at once. For what else before the henads is it lawful to join to the One, or what can be more united to the unified God than the multitude of gods? Concerning these, then, we will next unfold Plato's account, which is not a matter of art, calling on the gods themselves to kindle in us the light of truth. Before going into the details of this account, though, I want to convince the reader, and make it plain to him by proof, that there are necessarily as many orders of gods as the Parmenides of Plato unfolds to us in the second hypothesis.

flags.taylor: the inartificial theory of Plato
flags.why: Taylor's "inartificial" seems to mean unlaboured, natural (atechnos): Plato's account of the gods comes not from art or contrivance, but from the things themselves.

paragraphs.modern: This, I think, is plain before all else to those whose ideas are not perverted: that everywhere, and especially in the divine orders, second processions are completed through their likeness to their own principles. For nature, intellect and every generating cause are by nature fit to produce and join to themselves like things before unlike things. For if the procession of beings must be continuous, with no void coming between, whether in bodiless natures or in bodies, then everything that proceeds by nature must proceed through likeness. For it is by no means lawful for what is caused to be the same as its cause, since it is a slackening and falling short of the union of the producing cause that generates second natures. Again, if the second were the same as the first, each would be the same alike, and one would not be cause and the other caused. But if one, by its very being, has an overflowing of productive power, and the other falls short of the power that produced it, they are separated from each other by nature, the generating cause goes before what is generated in excellence, and there is no sameness between things that differ so greatly. But if the second is not the same as the first, and is only different, they will not be joined to each other, nor will one share in the other. For contact and sharing are a communion of things joined, and a sympathy of the sharers with the natures they share in. But if it is at once the same as and different from the first, and the sameness is in need and overcome by the contrary power, the One will no longer lead the procession of beings, nor will every generating cause exist before second things in the rank of the good. For the One is the cause not of division but of friendship. And the Good turns what is generated back to its causes. But the return and friendship of second things to first is through likeness, not through an unlike nature. If, then, the One is the cause of the whole of things, and the Good is desired by all things in a set-apart way, it will everywhere give existence to the offspring of prior causes through likeness, so that procession may be by the One, and the return of what has proceeded may be to the Good. For without likeness there will be neither the return of things to their own principles nor the generation of effects. Let this, then, be taken as granted here.
notes: Elements of Theology 28-29: every producing cause brings into existence things like itself before unlike things, and all procession is through likeness.

paragraphs.modern: The second point, after this, which is shown through it, is that every monad must produce a number ranked with itself: nature a natural number, soul a soul's number, and intellect an intellectual number. For if everything generating generates like things before unlike ones, as has been shown, every cause will surely hand on its own form and character to its own offspring, and before it gives existence to far-off processions, separated from its nature, it will produce things near it in being and joined to it through likeness. Every monad, then, gives existence to a multitude, as generating what is second to itself, which divides the powers that exist beforehand in it in a hidden way. For what is in the monad one-like and drawn together appears separately in the monad's offspring. The wholeness of nature shows this: it holds in one the forming principles of all things, in the heavens and below the moon, but distributes its powers to the natures divided from it about bodies. For the nature of earth, of fire and of the moon has its character and form from the wholeness of nature, acts together with this wholeness, and holds its own lot. The monad of the mathematical sciences and of numbers shows this too. For it is all things first, and produces in itself the forms of numbers like seeds, and distributes different powers to different numbers that proceed outward. For what is generated cannot receive all at once the whole abundance of what generates it; and the fertile power of everything that exists beforehand in the cause itself must come to light. The monad, then, gives existence to a multitude about itself, and to a number that distributes the characters that remain gathered in itself. But since, as was said before, the like is always more akin to the cause than the unlike, there will be one multitude like the monad, proceeding from the monad, and another of unlike things. And again, the multitude like the monad is, in a divided way, what the monad is undividedly. For if the monad has a distinctive power and hyparxis, there will be the same form of hyparxis in the multitude, with a slackening with respect to the whole.

flags.taylor: it contains in one the reasons, [i.e. productive principles] of all things
flags.why: Taylor's "reasons" and "productive principles" are logoi, the forming principles that nature holds and spreads into bodies.

notes: Elements of Theology 21: every order begins from a monad and proceeds into a multitude ranked with the monad. Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: After this, third, we must consider that among processions, those nearer their cause point to a greater multitude of things, and are in a way equal to the causes that hold them; while those further off have a less extended power of meaning, and, through the lessening of their power, change and lessen at the same time the breadth of their production. For if, of processions, the first in order is more like its principle, and what gives existence to the greatest number is more like, in being and power, to the principle that generates all things, then of second natures those nearer the monad, which receive rule after it, must give a greater extent to their productions; while those more separated from their first monad will neither reach through all things alike nor stretch their effective activities to far-off processions. And again, likewise, the nature that gives existence to the greatest number of effects must be ranked next to the monad, its principle; and the nature that generates a more numerous offspring, because it is more like the giver of all things than what generates few, must be ranked nearer the monad in hyparxis. For if it is further off, it will be more unlike the first principle; and if more unlike, it will have neither a power that holds the power of like natures nor a richly fertile activity. For an abundant cause is akin to the cause of all. And in general, what generates more is more akin by nature to its principle than what produces fewer offspring. For producing fewer effects is a lack of power; a lack of power is a lessening of being; and a lessening of being comes about through unlikeness to its cause and departure from the first principle.

flags.taylor: possess a less extended power of signification
flags.why: Taylor's "signification" seems to mean reach or scope: the further causes are from the first, the fewer things they extend to. Compare Elements of Theology 56-62.

paragraphs.modern: Again, besides what has been said, we will state this, which has the most certain truth: that before shared causes, unshared causes must everywhere exist first in the whole of things. For if a cause must have the same relation to its offspring as the One to all the nature of beings, and must by nature have this order towards second things; and if the One is unshared, equally set apart from all beings, as producing all things in a unified way; then every other cause that imitates the transcendence of the One over all things must be set apart from the natures in the second ranks and shared by them. And again, likewise, every unshared and first cause must set up monads of second natures like itself before unlike ones. I mean, for instance, that one soul must distribute many souls to different natures, and one intellect shared intellects to many souls. For so the first set-apart kind will everywhere have an order answering to the One. And second natures that share in akin causes will answer to these causes, and through their likeness will be joined to their unshared principle. So before the Forms that are in other things are set those that exist in themselves; set-apart causes before ranked ones; and unshared monads before shared ones. And so, as is shown together with this, set-apart causes generate the ranked ones, and unshared natures stretch out shared monads to their offspring; and natures that exist from themselves produce the powers that reside in other things. These things discussed, let us consider how each of the divine kinds exists by analogy, and, following Plato himself, see what the first and most universal orders of the gods are. For having found and shown this, we will perhaps be able to see the truth about each of these orders.
notes: Elements of Theology 23-24: every unshared term gives rise to shared ones, and the unshared comes before the shared. Taylor's footnote corrects "analysis" to "analogy" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: From the axioms set out, then, since there is one unity, the principle of the whole of things, from which every hyparxis has its existence, this unity must produce from itself, before all other things, a multitude marked by unity, and a number most akin to its cause. For if every other cause sets up offspring like itself before what is unlike, much more must the One bring into light in this way the things after it, since it is beyond likeness, and the One itself must produce by union the things that first proceed from it. For how could the One give existence to its offspring except in a unified way? For nature generates what is second to it naturally, soul as soul does, and intellect intellectually. So the One is the cause of the whole of things by union, and the procession from the One is one-like. But if what first produces all things is the One, and the procession from it is unified, the multitude produced from there must surely be self-perfect henads, most akin to their producing cause. Further, if every monad sets up a number suited to itself, as was shown before, far more must the One generate a number of this kind.
