For in the procession of things, what is produced is often unlike its producing cause through the rule of difference: such are the last of things, far from their own principles. But the first number, born together with the One, is one-like, inexpressible, beyond being, and wholly like its cause. For in the first causes, neither does difference come between to separate the begotten from the begetter and carry it into another order, nor does the motion of the cause, slackening its power, bring the generation of the whole of things out into unlikeness and indefiniteness. The cause of all things, raised in a unified way above all motion and division, has set up about itself a divine number, and united it to its own simplicity. So the One, before beings, has given existence to the henads of beings.
notes: Elements of Theology 113-114: the whole number of the gods is one-like, and every god is a self-perfect henad.

paragraphs.modern: Again, in another way, first beings must share in the first cause through their nearest henads. For second things are each joined to the natures before them through like things: bodies to the soul that ranks as a whole through the particular souls they share in; souls to the universal intellect through intellectual monads; and first beings to the One through unified hyparxes. For being is by its own nature unlike the One. For being, and what needs a union brought from outside, is not fit to be joined to what is beyond being and to the first union, and is far from it. But the henads of beings, since they have their existence from the unshared unity, set apart from the whole of things, are able to join beings to the One and turn them back to themselves.
notes: Elements of Theology 64, 108-112: each order is joined to the order above it through its highest members.

paragraphs.modern: It seems to me, then, that Parmenides, showing these things through the second hypothesis, joins the one with being, sees all things about the one, and shows that this nature that proceeds, and stretches its processions as far as the last of things, is the one. For before true beings the henads had to be set up, since it neither was nor is lawful, says Timaeus, for what is best to do anything but what is most beautiful. And this is, in a remarkable degree, most like what is best. But to the One a unified multitude is most like; since the Craftsman of the universe too, being good, made all things like himself through goodness itself. Much more, then, does the source of all good produce goodnesses united to itself by nature, and set them in beings. So there is one God, and many gods; one henad and many henads before beings; one goodness, and many after the one goodness, through which the making intellect is good and every intellect is divine, whether intellectual or intelligible. And what is first beyond being is the One; and there are many beyond being after the One. Is this multitude of henads, then, unshared, as the One itself is, or is it shared by beings, so that each henad of beings is, as it were, the flower of some being, its summit and centre, about which each being exists? If these henads too are unshared, in what do they differ from the One? For each of them is one, and exists first from the One. Or in what, more than the first cause, were they set up by it? For everywhere what is second, being lower than what is before it, must fall short of the union of its producing cause, and by the addition of something have a lessening of the first's simplicity as a monad. What addition, then, can we name, or what more besides the one, if each of these too is by itself one? For if each of them is one and many, we will seem to carry over to them the character of being. But if each is one only, as the One itself is, why does that rank as the cause set apart from all things, while each of these has a second dignity? So we will neither keep the transcendence of the first over what comes after it, nor can we grant that the henads proceeding from it are unconfused with each other or with their one principle.

flags.taylor: connects the one with being, surveys all things about the one
flags.why: Proclus means the one being of the Parmenides' second hypothesis (142b), "if one is", from which all the orders of gods are drawn. Taylor's two footnotes correct "one" to "being" and "present" to "leading" in the Greek he translated.

notes: Timaeus 29e-30a: the Craftsman was good, and "wanted all things to be as like himself as possible"; "it neither was nor is lawful for the best to do anything but the most beautiful".

paragraphs.modern: Nor will we fail to be persuaded by the Parmenides, who produces the one together with being, and shows that there are as many parts of the one as of being; that each being shares in the one, and the one everywhere exists together with being; in short, who says that the one of the second hypothesis shares in being and is shared by being, the sharing not being the same in each. For the one shares in being, as not being first one, nor set apart from being, but as lighting up truly existing being. And being shares in the one, as held together by it, filled with divine union, and turned back to the unshared One itself. For the shared monads join beings to the One, set apart from the whole of things, as shared intellects join souls to the intellect that ranks as a whole, and shared souls join bodies to the soul that ranks as a whole. For the unlike kinds of second natures cannot be united without middles to the cause set apart from multitude; contact must be made through like things. For a like multitude, so far as it is multitude, shares with the unlike; but so far as it is like the monad before it, it is joined to it. Set, then, in the middle of both, it is united to the whole and to the One before multitude, but holds in itself far processions, of themselves unlike the One. Through itself, too, it turns all things back to that One, and so all things reach towards the first cause of the whole of things, the unlike through the like, and the like through themselves. For likeness by itself leads and binds the many to the one, and turns second natures back to the monads before them. For the very being of like things, as like, comes from the One. So it joins multitude to that from which it has its procession. And for this reason likeness is what it is, making many things akin, in sympathy with themselves, and friends with each other and with the One.

flags.taylor: But neither shall we be persuaded by Parmenides who produces the one together with being
flags.why: The sense required is the opposite: "Nor shall we be persuaded otherwise by Parmenides", or "We shall not fail to be persuaded": Proclus is calling on the second hypothesis, which joins one and being, as evidence that the henads are shared by beings. Taylor's footnote corrects "unlike" to "like" in the Greek he translated.

notes: The Parmenides 142b-144e: the one being has two parts, one and being, each of which is again one and being, so that the one is divided as far as being is.

paragraphs.modern: If we must not only unfold the multitude of gods shared by beings through Parmenides' intellectual reachings, but also show briefly Socrates' account of these things, we must recall what is written in the Republic, where he says that the light that comes from the Good unites intellect and beings. For through this the Good is shown to be set apart from being and what is, as the sun is set apart from visible things. But this light, being in the intelligibles, lights them up, as the sun-like light in visible things does. For visible things become plain and known to sight in no other way than through the light born in them. All intelligibles, then, become good-like by sharing in light, and through this light every true being is most like the Good. If, then, it makes no difference whether we speak of this light or of the one (for this light joins the intelligibles and makes them one, having its existence from the One), the godhead that proceeds from the first is shared, and all the multitude of henads is shared. And what is truly beyond being is the One. But each of the other gods, by his own hyparxis, by which he is a god beyond being, is like the first; yet they are shared by being and what is. By this reasoning, then, the gods appear to us as henads, and shared henads, binding all beings to themselves, and, through themselves, joining the natures after them to the One that is set apart from all things alike.
notes: Republic VI 508d-509b. Taylor's footnote supplies "truly" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Since, then, each of the gods is a henad, but is shared by some being, shall we say that the same being shares in each of the henads, or that those sharing in some henads are more, and in others fewer? And if so, either those sharing in the higher henads must be more and those of the lower fewer, or the reverse. For there must be an order of the henads, as we see that of numbers some are nearer their principle and others further from it; some simpler and others more composite, greater in quantity but lessened in power. And it is well that we have mentioned numbers. For if we must look at the order of the first monads among themselves, and their procession about beings, from these as images, then here too the monads nearer the One will be shared by things simpler in being, and those further from it by more composite beings. For so the sharing will be by analogy: first monads always shared by first beings, and second monads by second beings. Again, if the first is set apart from all things and unshared, and what is born together with the simplest nature, and the One, is more like the unshared than what is born together with a more varied and many-formed nature, with more powers hanging from it, then it is wholly plain that the henads nearer the One must be shared by the first and simplest beings, and those further off by more composite beings, which are less in power but greater in number and multitude. For in short, additions in these henads are takings away of powers; and what is nearer the One, which goes beyond the whole of things by a wonderful simplicity, is more one-like, and exists together with more universal orders. It follows, by the ratio of power, that the simplicity of the first henads is transcendent. For those that are the causes of more effects imitate as far as possible the cause of all things; but those that are the causes of fewer have a being more varied than the natures before them. For this variety breaks into small parts and lessens the power that remains in one. Moreover, among shared souls too, the first and most divine exist in simple and everlasting bodies. Others are joined to simple bodies, and together with these to material bodies too. And others are joined at once to simple, material and composite bodies. The heavenly souls rule over simple bodies, which exist immaterially and unchangingly. The souls that govern the wholes of the elements are clothed in ethereal garments, and through these are carried in the wholes of the elements, which as wholes are everlasting and simple, but as material receive generation, corruption, and composition from unlike natures. And the souls of the third rank are those that give life directly to their vehicles of light, but also draw from the simple element material garments, pour into these a second life, and through these share with composite, many-formed bodies, keeping up through this sharing another, third life.

flags.taylor: their luciform vehicles
flags.why: The soul's "vehicle of light" (augoeides ochēma), the subtle body of light that, for the later Platonists, the soul has always, before it takes on the material body. Taylor's footnote corrects the Greek he translated here ("light-formed" for "self-formed").

notes: Elements of Theology 196-210, on the soul's vehicles. Taylor's other footnote rewrites a corrupt sentence of the Greek he translated ("those that are the causes of more ... imitate the cause of all").

paragraphs.modern: If you are willing to look at the intellectual orders, some of these are set in the souls that rank as wholes, and in the most divine of the souls in the world, which they also govern as is fitting. Others, set in the souls of the higher kinds, are shared directly by the rulers among them, and secondarily by more partial beings. And again they set third intellectual orders in partial souls. And as the power they have is lessened, so the sharing in them is more varied, and far more composite than the sharing of the natures before them. If, then, this is the way of sharing in all beings, it is surely necessary that of the gods too, those nearer the One should be carried in the simpler parts of being, and those that have gone further should be carried in the more composite parts of being. For the sharings of second kinds are divided in this way, by likeness to the gods.

flags.taylor: in the souls of the more excellent genera
flags.why: The "more excellent kinds" are the angels, daemons and heroes, set between the gods and human souls.

paragraphs.modern: Again, then, we may say in brief that after the One, the one principle of the whole of things, the gods appear to us as self-perfect monads, shared by beings. How many orders of beings there are we will unfold later, and show which beings have a simpler and which a more varied hyparxis. The last of all beings, then, is the bodily. For it has its being and all its perfection from another, older cause, and has neither simplicity nor composition, nor everlastingness nor incorruptibility from its own power. For no body is self-existent or self-begotten; everything of that kind, drawing together into one cause and what proceeds from the cause, is bodiless and undivided. In short, what is the cause of hyparxis to itself also gives itself an unlimited power of existence. For never leaving itself, it will never cease to be, nor depart from its own existence. For everything that perishes perishes through being separated from the power that gave it being. But what gives being to itself, since it is not separated from itself, has through itself an everlasting being. No body, however, since it is not the cause of everlastingness to itself, will be everlasting. For everything everlasting has an unlimited power; but body, being limited, is not the cause of unlimited power. For unlimited power is bodiless, because all power is bodiless. And this is plain, because greater powers are everywhere; but no body can be wholly everywhere. If, then, no body gives itself power, whether unlimited or limited, but what is self-existent gives itself the power of being and of existing for ever, no body will be self-existent. From where, then, is being given to bodies, and what is fit to give them being most directly? Must we not say that the first cause of being to bodies is what, by being present, makes the nature of body more perfect than akin bodies deprived of it? This is plain to everyone. For it belongs to what gives perfection also to hold together the being of second natures, since perfection is the perfection of being. What, then, is that by sharing in which bodies are said to be better than bodies that do not share in it? Is it not clear that it is soul? For we say that ensouled bodies are more perfect than those without soul. So soul is first beyond bodies; and we must grant that the whole heaven, and everything bodily, is the vehicle of soul. So these two orders of beings appear to us: one bodily, the other, above it, of soul.
notes: Elements of Theology 40-46 (the self-existent is bodiless and imperishable) and 186-188. Taylor's footnote: about a line and a half of the Greek he translated is so defective that he left it untranslated.

paragraphs.modern: Is soul itself, though, the same as intellect, or different? For as the body that shares in soul is perfect, so the soul that shares in intellect is perfect. And not all things share in the soul that can live by reason; but rational souls share in intellect and the light of intellect, and so do all things that have any kind of knowledge. And soul acts in time, while intellect holds in eternity both its being and its stable activity together. And not every soul is fit to keep its own perfection unchanged and undiminished; but every intellect is always perfect, and has an unfailing power of its own blessedness. So the intellectual kind is above the soul's kind in being; since the first, neither in whole intellects nor in partial ones, lets in the nature of evil, while the second, undefiled in whole souls, in partial souls falls away from its own blessedness. What, then, is the first of beings? Shall we say intellect, or, before this, the extent of life? For soul lives of itself, giving itself life; and intellect is the best and most perfect, and, as we have said, an eternal life. But the life of intellect is in a way intellectual, mixed from the intellectual and the living character. There must, though, be life itself. Which, then, is better, life or intellect? If only knowing beings share in intellect, but beings without knowledge share in life (for we say that plants live), life must surely be ranked above intellect, as the cause of more effects, giving more gifts from itself than intellect. What then? Is life the first of beings? Is to live the same as to be? This is impossible. For if life is what is first being, and to live is the same as to have being, with the same definition of life and being, then everything that shares in life would share in being, and everything that shares in existence would share in life. For if each is the same, all things would share alike in being and life. All living natures have being and existence; but there are many beings without life. So being exists before the first life. For what is more universal, and the cause of more effects, is nearer the One, as has been shown before. So soul is first set above bodies; intellect is beyond soul; life is older than intellect; and being, which is first being, is set above all these. Everything that shares in soul shares far before that in intellect; but not everything that enjoys the working of intellect is fit to share in soul. For only rational animals share in soul, since we say that the rational soul is truly soul. For Plato says in the Republic that the work of soul is to reason and look at beings; and every soul (every rational soul) is immortal, as is written in the Phaedrus, the irrational soul being mortal, according to the Craftsman in the Timaeus. In short, it is clear in many places that Plato takes the rational soul to be truly soul, and the others to be images of souls, so far as these too are intellectual and living, and together with whole souls produce the lives distributed about bodies. In intellect, however, we grant that not only rational animals share, but also such other animals as have a power of knowing, I mean those with imagination, memory and sense; since Socrates too, in the Philebus, refers all such animals to the intellectual series. For taking away intellect from the life of pleasure, he takes away not only the rational life but every power of knowing in the irrational life. For all knowledge is the offspring of intellect, as all reason is an image of soul.
notes: Republic I 353d: the work of soul is to take care, rule and deliberate. The Phaedrus 245c: "all soul is immortal". Timaeus 69c-d: the gods made the mortal kind of soul. The Philebus 21b-d: without intellect, a life of pleasure would have no memory, opinion or knowledge of its pleasure. Taylor's footnote corrects "life" to "soul" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, all things that share in intellect share far before that in life, some more dimly and others more clearly. But not all living things share in intellectual power, since plants are living beings, as Timaeus says, but share in neither sense nor imagination, unless someone says they have a dim feeling of what pleases and pains. And in short, the powers of appetite are everywhere lives, images of the whole of life and its last productions; but of themselves they are without intellect and have no share in the power of knowing. So they are of themselves indefinite and deprived of all knowledge.

flags.taylor: the orectic powers
flags.why: Taylor's "orectic" means of appetite or desire (orexis).

notes: Timaeus 77a-c: plants are living beings that share in the third kind of soul, the appetitive, with sensation of pleasure and pain but no opinion or reason.

paragraphs.modern: Again, all animals receive a share of being, different animals a different share, according to their natures; but not all beings can share alike in life, since we say that qualities, all affections, and the last of bodies receive the last working of being, but we do not say that they share in life. So being is older than life, life than intellect, and intellect than soul. For the causes of more effects, being older and more ruling in order, must preside over causes able to produce and adorn fewer effects. So Plato rightly, in the Timaeus, gives soul its existence from intellect, as second to it by its own nature. In the Laws he says that intellect is moved like a sphere turned on a lathe. For what is moved is moved by sharing in life, and is nothing else than real life about motion. And in the Sophist he sets being apart from all the universal kinds of things, and from motion. For being, he says, by its own nature neither stands still nor is moved. And what neither stands still nor is moved is beyond eternal life.
notes: The Laws X 898a-b: the motion of intellect is most like that of "a sphere turned on a lathe". The Sophist 250c: being, "by its own nature, neither stands still nor is moved". Taylor's footnote corrects the Greek he translated ("on a lathe").

paragraphs.modern: These four causes, then, being before bodily existence (being, life, intellect and soul), soul shares in all the causes before it: it has reason from its own character, but intellect, life and being from older causes. So it gives existence to what comes after it in a fourfold way. By its being, it produces all things down to bodies; by its life, all things said to live, down to plants; by its intellect, all things with a power of knowing, down to the most irrational natures; and by its reason, the first of the natures able to share in it. Intellect, set beyond soul, and existing as the fullness of life and being, adorns all things in a threefold way: it lights up all knowing beings with the power of the intellectual character, but gives sharing in life to still more, and in being to all those to whom first being gives itself. Life, set above intellect, exists before as the cause of the same things in a twofold way: giving life to second natures together with intellect, and filling from itself with the rivers of life the things by nature fit to live; and, together with being, producing being in all things from above. But being itself, which is first being, generates all things by its very existence, all lives, intellects and souls, is present to all things in a one-like way, and is set apart from the whole of things by one cause that gives existence to all things. So it is the most like the One of all things, and unites the embrace of beings in itself to the first principle of the whole of things, through which all beings and non-being exist, wholes and parts, Forms and the privations of Forms; and these privations do not need to share in being, but must certainly share in the One.
notes: Elements of Theology 57: every cause acts before its effect and goes further down than it; the higher a cause, the further its working reaches. Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: These things, it seems to me, persuaded the Stranger from Elea in the Sophist, discussing what perfectly is, to grant that not only being is there, but also life, intellect and soul. For if true and real being is revered and honoured, intellect, he says, is there first. For it is not lawful for what is of itself revered and immaterial to be without intellect. And if intellect is in what perfectly is, intellect will surely be moved. For intellect cannot ever exist without motion, or without rest. But if intellect is moved and stands still, there are in being both life and motion. So from what has been said three things appear: being, life and intellect. Moreover, soul too is found next through these. For life and intellect, which before were by themselves, must, he says, also be in soul. For every soul is a fullness of life and intellect, sharing in both, which the Stranger points to when he adds: "Shall we say that both these are in it, but that it does not have them in soul?" For to have, as someone says somewhere, comes after to be. Soul shares in each of these by its own character, and mixes the rational form of its own hyparxis with the intellectual, life-giving power. But both intellect and life exist before soul, the first as moved and standing still at the same time, and the second as motion and rest. These four monads, soul, intellect, life and being, are mentioned by Plato not only here but in many other places. And as in soul all things exist by sharing, so in intellect the things before it exist, and in life what is before life. For we say that life exists, or has being. Or how could it be said to be ranked in being unless it shared in being? We likewise say that intellect is and lives. For it is moved, and is a portion of being. So it is the third of the more embracing monads. Before shared beings, though, unshared causes must everywhere exist, as was shown before, in keeping with the likeness of beings to the One. Being, then, which is first being, is unshared; life first shares in being, yet is unshared, set apart from intellect. Intellect is filled from being and life, but is unshared by souls and the natures after it. Intellect also presides over soul, giving it by its light a share in life and being; but being unshared, it exists before bodies. The last order of beings, then, is that to which bodies are attached: heavenly bodies first, and bodies below the moon with material garments added. This, then, is the procession of beings, through life, intellect and soul, ending in a bodily nature.

flags.taylor: the former as being moved and standing still at one and the same time, and the latter as being motion and permanency
flags.why: That is, intellect is moved and at rest, while life is motion and rest themselves. Taylor's "permanency" here is rest (stasis).

notes: The Sophist 248e-249b: "Shall we be easily persuaded that motion, life, soul and thought are not present in what perfectly is?"

paragraphs.modern: If, then, the henads of the gods beyond being, which have their existence from the unshared cause of all things, must be shared, some by the first orders among beings, others by the middle, and others by the last, as was shown before, it is clear that some make divine the unshared portion of being, while others light up life, others intellect, others soul, and others bodies. In the last henads not only bodies share, but also soul, intellect, life and being. For intellect is in itself a fullness of life and being. From the henads above the world, intellect hangs, and the power of soul that exists beforehand in intellect. From the henads above these, unshared, intellectual intellect hangs. From those beyond these, the first, unshared life hangs. And from the highest henads hangs first being itself, the most divine of beings. So Parmenides, beginning from the one being, produces from it the whole orders of the gods. These things settled beforehand, let us speak about the divine dialogues, beginning from on high, and producing from the One the whole orders of the gods. And, following Plato, let us first show the several orders from other dialogues, by arguments that cannot be refuted. Then let us join and fit the conclusions of the Parmenides to the divine processions, fitting the first conclusions to the first processions and the last to the last.
notes: Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Again, then, the mystic teaching about the One must be taken up by us, so that, proceeding from the first principle, we may praise the second and third principles of the whole of things. Before all beings, and before the gods who produce beings, there exists one set-apart and unshared cause: a cause inexpressible by all speech, unknown by all knowledge and beyond grasp, bringing all things into light from itself, existing inexpressibly before all things and turning all things back to itself, as the best end of all things. This cause, truly set apart from all causes, which gives existence in a unified way to all the henads of divine natures and to all the kinds of beings and their processions, Socrates in the Republic calls the Good, and through its analogy to the sun reveals its wonderful and unknown transcendence over all intelligibles. Parmenides, again, calls it the One, and through negations shows the set-apart and inexpressible hyparxis of this One, the cause of the whole of things. The account in the letter to Dionysius, proceeding through riddles, praises it as that about which all things are, and as the cause of all beautiful things. And in the Philebus Socrates praises it as what gives existence to the whole of things, because it is the cause of all godhead. For all the gods have their existence as gods from the first God. Whether, then, it is lawful to call it the source of godhead, or the kingdom of beings, or the henad of all henads, or the goodness that generates truth, or a hyparxis set apart from all these things and beyond all causes, both those of fathers and those of generation, let it be honoured by us in silence, and, before silence, by union; and of the mystic end may it give us, by its light, a share fitting our souls.
notes: The Philebus 23c: "we said that god had shown the limit and the unlimited of beings" (quoted in the next chapter).

paragraphs.modern: But let us look with intellect at the twofold principles that proceed from it and come after it. For what else must be set after the union of the whole study than the dyad of principles? What, then, the two principles of the divine orders after the first principle are, we will next consider. For in keeping with the theology of our forebears, Plato too sets two principles after the One. In the Philebus Socrates says that god gives existence to limit and the unlimited, and, mixing all beings through these, has produced them; the nature of beings, according to Philolaus, being made of the joining of limited things and unlimited things. If, then, all beings are made of these, clearly they themselves exist before beings. And if second natures share in these mixed together, these will exist unmixed before the whole of things. For the procession of the divine orders begins not from things ranked together and existing in others, but from things set apart and set in themselves. As, then, the One is before things united, and what is acted on by the One has a second rank after the unshared union, so the two principles of beings, before being shared in and mixed with beings, are by themselves the causes of the whole of things. For limit must be before limited things, and the unlimited before unlimited things, by the likeness to the One of what proceeds from it. For again, if we produced beings straight after the One, we would nowhere find the character of the One existing purely. For being is not the same as the one, but shares in the one; nor is the first really the one, for, as has often been said, it is better than the one. Where, then, is what is most properly and wholly one? So there is a one before being, which gives existence to being and is first its cause; since what is before it is beyond union, a cause without relation to all things, and unshared, set apart from all things. But if this one is the cause of being and sets it up, there will be a power in it that generates being. For everything that produces, produces by its own power, which exists between the producer and what is produced: of the one it is the procession and, as it were, the stretching out; of the other, the generating cause set before it. For being, produced from these, which is not the One itself but one-like, has its procession from the one through the power that produces it and brings it into light from the one, and its hidden union from the hyparxis of the one. This one, then, which exists before power, and first exists from the unshared and unknown cause of the whole of things, Socrates in the Philebus calls limit, and its power that generates being he calls the unlimited. He speaks thus in that dialogue: "God, we said, has shown the limit and the unlimited of beings."

flags.taylor: nor in reality is that which is the first the one; for, as has been frequently said, it is better than the one
flags.why: Proclus means that the first principle is beyond even the name "one"; the one that is the principle of being is limit, the first after the first.

notes: The Philebus 16c (the ancients handed down that things are made of one and many, with limit and unlimitedness in them), 23c-d, 26e-27b. Philolaus, frag. 1-2: "nature in the cosmos was fitted together from unlimited things and limiting things". Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: The first, unified God, then, is called by him God without any addition, because each of the second gods is shared by being and has being hanging from it. But the first, as set apart from the whole of beings, is God, defined by the inexpressible itself, unified alone, and beyond being. But the limit and the unlimited of beings bring that unknown and unshared cause into light: limit as the cause of stable, one-like, holding-together godhead; the unlimited as the cause of power that proceeds to all things and can be multiplied, and, in short, as the leader of every generating distribution. For all union and wholeness and sharing of beings, and all the divine measures, hang from the first limit; while all division, fertile production and procession into multitude have their existence from this most ruling unlimitedness. So when we say that each of the divine orders remains and at the same time proceeds, we must grant that it remains stably by limit, but proceeds by the unlimited, and has at the same time unity and multitude; and we must hang the first from the principle of limit and the second from that of the unlimited. In short, of all the oppositions in the divine kinds, we must refer the better to limit and the lower to the unlimited. For from these two principles all things proceed into being, down to the last of things. Eternity itself shares at once in limit and the unlimited: as the intelligible measure, in limit; as the cause of an unfailing power of existing, in the unlimited. Intellect, so far as it is one-like and whole, and holds together the measures of the patterns, is the offspring of limit; but so far as it produces all things eternally, and exists in keeping with the whole of eternity, giving all things existence at once and always keeping its own power undiminished, it is the offspring of the unlimited. Soul, measuring its own life by returns and periods, and setting a boundary to its own motions, is referred to the cause of limit; but having no rest from motion, and making the end of one period the beginning of the whole of a second circuit of life, it is referred to the order of the unlimited. The whole of this heaven, too, in its wholeness, its holding together, the order of its periods and the measures of its returns, is limited; but in its fertile powers, its various unrollings and the unfailing revolutions of its spheres, it shares in the unlimited. Moreover, the whole of coming to be, since all its Forms are limited and always remain in the same way, and since its own circle imitates the heavenly circuit, is like limit; but in the variety of the particulars it is made of, their unceasing change, and the more and less that come into the sharing of Forms, it is the image of the unlimited. Besides these, every natural thing is like limit in its form, and like the unlimited in its matter. For these hang last from the two principles after the One, and the procession of their productive power reaches as far as these. Each of these too is one; but form is the measure and boundary of matter, and is more one. Matter is all things in potential, as having its existence from the first power. There, though, power generates all things; but the power of matter is imperfect, and needs the reality that generates all things in act. Rightly, then, does Socrates say that all beings come from limit and the unlimited, and that these two intelligible principles first have their existence from God. For what gathers both of them, perfects them, and brings itself into light through all beings is the One before the dyad. Union comes to all things through the first; but the division of the two orders of things comes from these first causes, and through these reaches to the unknown and inexpressible principle. Let it be clear, then, from these things, what the two principles of beings are that appear next after the One, according to Plato's theology.

flags.taylor: by restitutions and periods
flags.why: Taylor's "restitutions" are returns (apokatastaseis): the soul's, and the heaven's, coming back round to the same state at the end of each period.

notes: Taylor's footnotes correct the Greek he translated in five places ("hangs from" for "is set apart from", twice; "to remain", "lastly", and "generative").

paragraphs.modern: Next, let us show what the third thing is that appears from these principles. It is everywhere called the mixed, as having its existence from limit and the unlimited. But if limit is the limit of beings, and the unlimited is the unlimited of beings, and beings are the things that exist from both, as Socrates himself clearly teaches us, it is clear that the first of mixed things is the first of beings. This is nothing else than what is highest among beings: being itself, and nothing but being. My meaning is that this is clear from the things by which we show that what is first being holds all things in an intelligible way, life and intellect too. For we say that life is threefold in the manner of life, and intellect in the manner of intellect, and that these three, being, life and intellect, are everywhere. But all things exist beforehand, first and in the manner of being, in being. For there are being, life and intellect, the summit of beings. Life is the middle centre of being, and is called, and is, intelligible life. Intellect is the boundary of being, and is intelligible intellect. For in the intelligible there is intellect, and in intellect the intelligible; but there intellect is intelligibly, and in intellect the intelligible is intellectually.
notes: The Philebus 23c-d: the third kind, the mixture of limit and the unlimited. Taylor's footnote supplies "third" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Being is what is stable in being, woven together with the first principles and not departing from the One. Life is what proceeds from the principles, born together with unlimited power. And intellect is what turns itself back to the principles, joins the end with the beginning, and makes one intelligible circle. The first of beings, then, is what is mixed from the first principles, and is threefold: one thing it holds is in it in the manner of being, another in the manner of life, and another in the manner of intellect, but all things exist beforehand in it in the manner of being. By the first of beings I mean being in the strict sense. For being itself is the summit of all beings, and, as it were, the monad of the whole of things. In all things, then, being is first; and in each thing what belongs to being is oldest, as having its existence from Hestia, the hearth of beings. For the intelligible is most of all this; since intellect is what knows, life is thinking, and being is intelligible. If, then, every being is mixed, but being is being itself, before all other things being is what exists mixed from the two principles that proceed from the One. So Socrates, pointing out how the way the two principles are generated differs from that of the mixture, says that "god has shown limit and the unlimited". For they are henads that have their existence from the One, and, as it were, shining manifestations of the unshared and first union. But making a mixture, and mixing through the first principles, is as far below bringing into light as making is below unfolding, and generating below manifesting; and by so much the mixed has a procession from the One lower than that of the two principles.

flags.taylor: deriving its subsistence from the Vesta of beings
flags.why: Taylor's "Vesta" is Hestia, the hearth: being is the fixed centre from which all beings have their existence.

flags.taylor: luminous patefactions
flags.why: Taylor's "patefaction" means a laying open, a manifestation: limit and the unlimited are "shown" (Philebus 23c) by the first God, not made.

paragraphs.modern: The mixed, then, is intelligible being, and exists first from the first God, from whom the unlimited and limit come too. But it exists secondarily from the principles after the unified God, I mean from limit and the unlimited. For the fourth cause, which produces the mixture, is again God himself; since if any other cause besides this were granted, there would no longer be a fourth cause, but a fifth would be brought in. For the first cause was God, who brings the two principles into light; after him come the two principles, limit and the unlimited; and the mixture is the fourth thing. So if the cause of the mixture is different from the first divine cause, this cause will be the fifth and not the fourth, as Socrates says it is. Further, if we say that God most of all gives union to beings, and the mixture of the principles is itself a union into the reality of being, God is surely first the cause of this too. Moreover, Socrates in the Republic clearly shows that the Good is the cause of being and the very being of intelligibles, as the sun is of visible things. Must we not, then, if the mixed is first being, refer it to the first God, and say that it receives its procession from him? Again, the Craftsman in the Timaeus makes the being of the soul by itself from an undivided and a divisible being, which is the same as making it from limit and the unlimited (for the soul by limit is like the undivided, and by the unlimited like the divisible being); if, then, the Craftsman mixes the being of the soul from these, and again separately from same and different, and from these, now existing beforehand, makes the whole soul, must we not much more say that the first God is the cause of the first being? The mixed, then, proceeds, as we have said, from the first God; it does not exist from the principles after the One alone, but proceeds from these too, and is threefold. First, it shares from God in inexpressible union and the whole of its existence. From limit it receives hyparxis, the one-like, and a stable character. From the unlimited it receives power, and the hidden power of all things that is in it. For in short, since it is one and not one, the one is in it by limit, and the not-one by the unlimited. But the mixture of both, and its wholeness, come from the first God. So the mixed is a monad, because it shares in the One; it is twofold, so far as it proceeds from the two principles; and it is a triad, so far as in every mixture, according to Socrates, these three are necessary: beauty, truth and proportion. Of these, though, we will speak again.
notes: The Philebus 23d, 26e-27b: the fourth kind is the cause of the mixture. Timaeus 35a: the Craftsman mixes the soul's being from the undivided and the divisible, and then from the same and the different.

paragraphs.modern: How being is what is first mixed we will now explain. For of all things this is the hardest to discover, what first being is, as the Stranger from Elea also says somewhere; for it is most puzzling how being is no less than non-being. How, then, being exists from limit and the unlimited must be shown. For if limit and the unlimited are beyond being, being may seem to have its existence from things that are not being. How, then, can things that are not being produce being? Or is this not so in all other things that exist through mixing with each other? For what is produced from things mixed together is not the same as the things not mixed. Soul is not the same as the kinds from which the father generated it by mixing them; nor is the happy life the same as the life of intellect or the life of pleasure; nor is the one in bodies the same as its elements. So it is not surprising if what is first being, though it is neither limit nor the unlimited, exists from both and is mixed: not that the natures beyond being are themselves taken into its mixture, but second processions from them come together into the existence of being. So being is made of these, sharing in both: it has the one-like from limit, and the generative, and in short hidden, multitude from the unlimited. For it is all things in a hidden way, and so is the cause of all beings. The Stranger from Elea points to this when he calls being the first power, as existing by sharing in the first power, and having hyparxis from limit and power from the unlimited. Later, though, the Stranger defines being as power, as fertile and generative of all things, and as being all things in a one-like way. For power is everywhere the cause of fertile processions and of all multitude: hidden power of hidden multitude, and the power that exists in act and brings itself into light of all-perfect multitude. Through this cause, I think, every being has powers born with it. For it shares in the unlimited, and has its hyparxis from limit but its power from the unlimited. And being is nothing else than a monad of many powers, a multiplied hyparxis; and so being is one-many. The many exist in a hidden way and without separation in the first natures, but with separation in second natures. For the nearer being is to the One, the more it hides multitude, and is defined by union alone. It seems to me, too, that Plotinus and his followers, often pointing to these things, produce being from form and intelligible matter, setting form as answering to the One and to hyparxis, and power as answering to matter. If they say this, they speak rightly. But if they give a certain formless and indefinite nature to intelligible being, they seem to me to stray from Plato's ideas on this subject. For the unlimited is not the matter of limit but its power; nor is limit the form of the unlimited, but its hyparxis. And being is made of both, as not only standing in the one, but receiving a multitude of henads and powers mixed into one being.

flags.taylor: calls being the first power
flags.why: The Sophist 247d-e: the Stranger proposes "that being is nothing else than power" (dynamis), to act or be acted on. Proclus reads it as the power, born of the unlimited, that being holds.

notes: The Sophist 243b-c, 250d-e: being is as hard to grasp as non-being. Plotinus on intelligible matter: II.4.2-5. The Philebus 22a-b: the good life is neither the life of pleasure nor that of thought alone. Taylor's footnote corrects "multitude" to "form" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: What is first being, then, is for these reasons called by Plato the mixed. And by likeness to it, coming to be too is mixed from limit and the unlimited. In this the unlimited is imperfect power, and the limit is the form and shape of this power. So we set this power down as matter, not existing in act, and needing to be limited by something else. But we no longer say it is lawful to call the power of being matter, since it generates activities, produces all beings from itself, and is fertile of the perfect powers in beings. For the power of matter, being imperfect, imitates the power of being in an unlike way; and becoming multitude in potential, it copies the labour with multitude in the power of being. Moreover, the form of matter imitates limit at the last, since it gives bounds to matter and ends its unlimitedness; but it is multiplied and divided about it. It is also mixed with the privation of matter, and represents the highest union of the hyparxis of being by its being always moving towards existence and always tending to decay. For what is in the first natures by transcendence is in the last by deficiency. For what is first being is mixed too, is set apart from the limit of unlimited life, and is its cause; but what is made of the last of forms and first matter is in its own nature without life, since it has life in potential. For there, generating causes exist before their offspring, and perfect things before imperfect; but here, things in potential come before things in act, and joint causes are set below what is produced from them. This happens by nature, I think, because the gifts of the first principles reach as far as the last of things, and generate not only more perfect natures but also those with a more imperfect existence. And for this reason the mixed is the cause of coming to be, and of the nature mixed here. But limit and the unlimited before being are the causes not only of this nature, but of its elements, of which the mixed, as mixed, is not the cause. For limit and the unlimited are twofold: one kind is set apart from the mixed things, the other is taken into the completion of the mixture. For I think that everywhere, before mixed things there must be unmixed ones; before imperfect things, perfect ones; before parts, wholes; and before things in others, things in themselves. And Socrates persuades us to grant this not of one thing only, but of beauty and proportion and all Forms. If, then, the second and third kinds of being and Forms exist before what shares in them, how can we say that limit and the unlimited, which run through all beings, first exist as mixed? We must grant, then, that they are unmixed and separate from being, and that being comes from them and at the same time is made of them. It comes from them, because they exist before; it is made of them, because they exist in being by a second procession.

flags.taylor: concauses are subject to the things which are produced from them
flags.why: Taylor's "concauses" are joint or contributing causes (synaitia), such as matter: in the lower world they come before, and are set below, what is made from them.

notes: Taylor's footnotes correct the punctuation of one sentence of the Greek he translated, and "first" to "last" (of form), since Proclus is speaking of body.

paragraphs.modern: The kinds of being too are twofold: some make beings, others are the elements of the nature of each being. For some exist beforehand by themselves, as having a productive power; others, generated from these, make up each particular being. So let no one any longer wonder how Socrates in the Philebus sets the mixed before limit and the unlimited, while we, on the contrary, show that limit and the unlimited are set apart from the mixed. For each is twofold: one is before being, the other in being; one generates, the other is an element of the mixture. Of this kind too are the limit and the unlimited of the mixed life, each being an element of the whole of happiness. So each needs the other: neither is intellect by itself desirable, nor perfect pleasure. The good, though, must be made of all these: the desirable, the sufficient and the perfect. Limit itself, then, and the unlimited, which are separate, exist as causes before the mixed; but the limit and the unlimited that are mixed are more imperfect than the mixture. From what has been said, then, it is clear what the things are of which the mixture is made.
notes: The Philebus 20d-22b, 61a-64a: the good life is a mixture of pleasure and thought, neither enough alone.

paragraphs.modern: Next we must speak of the triad that exists together with this mixture. For every mixture, if it is rightly made, as Socrates says, needs these three things: beauty, truth and proportion. Nothing ugly, brought into the mixture, will give it rightness, since it will cause error and disorderly excess; nor, if truth is ever separated, will it let the mixture be made of things pure and truly mastered, but it will fill the whole with an image and with non-being. Nor without proportion will there be a sharing of the elements and a graceful company. Proportion, then, is needed for the union of the things mixed and a fitting sharing; truth for purity; and beauty for order, which also makes the whole lovely. For when each thing in the mixture has its fitting place, it makes both the elements and the arrangement that comes from them beautiful. Here, then, in the first mixture, these three things appear: proportion, truth and beauty. Proportion is the cause of being one to the mixture; truth, of the reality of its existence; and beauty, of its being intelligible. So it is intelligible and truly being. What is first being, too, is more one-like, and intellect is joined to it by its closeness to the beautiful. But each shares in existence, because it is being derived from being. The mixed is highest among beings, because it is united to the Good. It seems to me that the divine Iamblichus, seeing these three causes of being, defines the intelligible by these three, proportion, truth and beauty, and through them unfolds the intelligible gods in his Platonic theology. How the intelligible breadth is made of these will be clearest as we proceed. From what has been said, though, it is wholly plain why Socrates says that this triad is found in the vestibule of the Good. For what is first being shares in this triad through its union with the Good. Because the Good is the measure of all beings, the first being becomes itself in proportion. Because the Good is before being, the first being exists truly and really. And because the Good is good and desirable, the first being appears as the beautiful itself. Here, then, the first beauty exists too; and so the One is the cause not only of good but of beauty, as Plato says in his Letters. Beauty is here in a hidden way, since this order holds all things in a one-like way, existing first from the principles, limit and the unlimited. Where and how beauty comes into light, we will soon explain.
notes: The Philebus 64a-65a: the mixture needs measure and proportion, truth and beauty, and "we find the good taking refuge in the nature of the beautiful"; the three stand "in the vestibule of the good" (64c). Iamblichus' Platonic Theology is lost. The Second Letter 312e: the king of all is "the cause of all beautiful things".

paragraphs.modern: Such, then, is the first triad of intelligibles, according to Socrates in the Philebus: limit, the unlimited, and what is mixed from these. Limit is a god proceeding to the intelligible summit from the unshared and first God, measuring and defining all things, and giving existence to every fatherly, holding and undefiled kind of gods. The unlimited is the unfailing power of this god, bringing into light all the generating orders and all unlimitedness, that before being, that of being, and that which proceeds as far as last matter. And the mixed is the first and highest order of gods, holding all things in a hidden way, completed through the intelligible triad that holds together, holding in a unified way the cause of every being, and setting its summit in the first intelligibles, set apart from the whole of things.

flags.taylor: deriving its completion indeed through the intelligible connective triad
flags.why: That is, the mixed is completed through the triad of limit, unlimited and mixed itself, the intelligible triad that "holds together" (synektikē).

paragraphs.modern: After this first triad, existing from the One and joined to it, we will praise the second, proceeding from the first and completed through things answering to the triad before it. For here too being must share, and the one be shared, and this one, which is second one, must generate what is second being. For everywhere shared godhead sets up about itself what shares in it. So whole souls make bodies exist together with their causes, and partial souls generate irrational souls together with the gods. Much more, then, do the gods produce all things together with the One. So as the first of the henads generates the summit of being, so the middle henad sets up the middle being. And everything that generates, makes or produces has a power fertile of what is produced, by which it produces, strengthens and holds together its offspring. Again, then, a second triad will come into light, answering to the first. One thing is its summit, which we call one, godhead and hyparxis; another its middle, which we call power; and another its end, which we say is second being. This is intelligible life. For all things are in the intelligible, as was shown before: to be, to live, and to act by thinking. The summit of the intelligible order is all things as cause and, as we have often said, in a hidden way. Its middle makes multitude shine out, and proceeds from the union of being into plain light. And its end is now all intelligible multitude and the order of intelligible Forms. For Forms have their existence at the end of the intelligible order, since Forms must first exist and appear in intellect. If, then, being remains set apart in the first mixture, but now proceeds and is generated in a twofold way from the monad, there will be motion about it; and if there is motion, there must also be intelligible life. For everywhere motion is a certain life, since someone calls even the motion of material bodies life. The first in this second triad, then, may be called limit; the second, the unlimited; and the third, life. For the second triad too is a god, having fertile power, and bringing into light, from and about himself, what is second being. Here too, though, the triad answers to the first triad.

flags.taylor: some one calls even the motion of material bodies life
flags.why: Aristotle, Physics VIII.1 (250b): motion is "a kind of life for all things that exist by nature". Taylor's footnote corrects "irrational" to "analogous" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: But again we must grasp by reasoning the character of this triad. The first triad is all things, but intelligibly and in a unified way, and, as I may say, speaking as Plato does, in the form of limit. The second triad is all things, but in the manner of life, and, as I may say, following the philosopher, in the form of the unlimited; just as the third triad proceeds by the character of the mixed. For as in the procession in breadth the mixed appears third, so in the procession of intelligibles in depth the third has the rank of the mixed in relation to the higher triads. The middle triad, then, is all things, but marked by intelligible unlimitedness. For the three principles after the first set out for us in order the intelligible kind of gods: limit brings into light the first triad, the unlimited the second, and the mixed the third. It is by unlimited power, then, that the second triad is marked. For, being the middle, it exists by the middle of the first triad, being all things from all. For in each triad there are limit, the unlimited and the mixed; but the character of the monads, different in each, unrolls the intelligible order of the gods. The middle triad, existing in this way (I say "in this way" because it is made of all the things the triad before it is made of), holds and binds the middle of intelligibles by unlimited power. It is filled from a higher union, and fills the union after it with the powers of being. It is measured from there in a one-like way, and measures the third triad by its own power. It remains stably in the first triad, and sets in itself the triad next in order. In short, it binds to itself the intelligible centre and sets up one intelligible coherence, making shine out what is hidden and one-formed in the first triad, and gathering the intelligible multitude of the third triad and holding it on all sides. The being that completes this triad is mixed, as the being of the triad before it is, and receives the character of life. For the unlimited in it generates life.

flags.taylor: as in the progression according to breadth
flags.why: Proclus' two dimensions: "breadth" is the spread of the three terms within one triad (limit, unlimited, mixed); "depth" is the descent of the three triads one below another.

paragraphs.modern: This triad must also share in the three, proportion, truth and beauty. What is first being exists chiefly by proportion, which unites it and joins it to the Good. The second triad exists chiefly by truth: because it shares in what is first being, it is being, and truly being. The third triad exists chiefly by the beautiful: for there intelligible multitude, order and beauty first shine out. So this being is the most beautiful of all intelligibles; but this will be discussed later. As there is a triad, then, in each of the mixtures, proportion most of all holds together the first, truth the second, and beauty the third. And this led the divine Iamblichus to say that Plato defines the whole intelligible order by these three. For all are in each, but one of them rules more in one of the intelligible monads than in another. Moreover, the third triad appears after this. For the end of being must also be made divine, and share in an intelligible henad. For beings are not more in number than the henads, as Parmenides says, nor are the henads more numerous than beings; each procession of being shares in the one; since this universe too, in each part of itself, is governed by soul and intellect. Much more, then, must the intelligible, in its first, middle and last realities, share in the intelligible gods.
notes: The Parmenides 144c-e: the one is divided by being into as many parts as being, so that the one and being are equal in number.

paragraphs.modern: As the first henad, then, after the set-apart cause of all things, brings into light intelligible being, and the second henad intelligible life, so the third sets up about itself intelligible intellect, fills it with divine union, and sets up power as the middle between itself and being, through which it completes this being and turns it back to itself. In this, then, every intelligible multitude shines out to view. For the whole of this being is intelligible intellect, life and being. It is neither all things as cause, as what is first being is, nor does it make all things shine out, as the second being does; but it is, as it were, all things in act, and openly. So it is the boundary of all intelligibles. For since the procession of beings goes by likeness, the first being is most like the One; the second is in labour with multitude and is the origin of separation; and the third is now all-perfect, and brings into light in itself intelligible multitude and Form.

Further, as the first triad remains hidden in limit, and fixes in itself everything stable in intelligibles, and the second at once remains and proceeds, so the third, after procession, turns the intelligible end back to the beginning and rolls the order back to itself. For everywhere it is the work of intellect to turn and converge to the intelligible. And all these are one-like and intelligible: the remaining, the proceeding and the returning. For each of these is not said in the same way among intelligibles. The intelligible kind of gods is unified, simple and hidden, joining itself to the One itself, which is before beings, and brings into light nothing else than the transcendence of the One. For these three triads announce mystically that unknown cause, the first and wholly unshared God: the first announcing his inexpressible union; the second his transcendence, by which he goes beyond all powers; and the third his all-perfect generation of beings. For as they are able to hold the principle that goes beyond both the union and the powers of all beings, so they show second natures his wonderful transcendence, receiving separately the unified power and rule of the first God, and bringing into light intelligibly the cause before intelligibles. For these gods, though they have a simplicity equally set apart from all the divine orders, still fall short of the union of the father. Of this triad, then, which turns all intelligibles back to the first principle and rolls the multitude that appears in it back to the stable union of the whole of things, one thing is limit, henad and hyparxis; another, the unlimited and power; and another, the mixed: being, life and intelligible intellect. But the whole triad exists by being, and is the intellect of the first triad. For the first triad is an intelligible god first; the triad after it an intelligible and intellectual god; and the third triad an intellectual god. These three godheads, triadic monads, complete the intelligible kinds. For they are monads by their godheads, since all other things hang from the gods, powers and beings too. But they are triads by a separate division. For limit, the unlimited and the mixed exist in three ways: in one place all things are by limit; in another all things by the unlimited; and in another all things by the mixed. In one place the mixed is being; in another, intelligible life; and in another, intelligible intellect. In this last, then, the Forms first exist. For the separating of intelligibles unfolds the order of Forms, because Form is being, but not simply being. So what is first being is being itself, and what is being. What is the second being is power, proceeding from the first being, and existing as a dyad, as it were, that generates the multitude of beings, but not yet multitude. And what is the third being is itself the multitude of beings, being there existing with separation. For being is the set-apart cause of the things that the Forms set up dividedly; and of the things that being produces together, the Forms are the cause with separation. For Forms are causes that produce separation in their effects; and also Forms are called the patterns of beings. Being is the cause of all that comes after it, but not their pattern. For patterns are the causes of things separated in existence and having different characters of being. After the One before beings, then, comes what is one-many in a hidden way, the united. So it is what is divided into multitude, and tends from the one-like to the bright. And the last of intelligibles is that from which a certain distribution into parts begins, and which holds intelligible multitude.

flags.taylor: the first triad is an intelligible God primarily. But the triad posterior to it is an intelligible and intellectual God. And the third triad is an intellectual God
flags.why: Not the later orders of the intelligible-intellectual and intellectual gods (Books IV and V), but the three intelligible triads, each named by its character: the third, intelligible intellect, is "intellectual" within the intelligible. Taylor's footnotes correct the Greek he translated in three places.

paragraphs.modern: Socrates in the Philebus, then, gives us such aids to the study of the intelligible triads. But we must not only remain in these ideas; we must also show Plato's theology of these triads from other dialogues, and from them point out one truth suited to the things themselves. Let us take what is written in the Timaeus, follow our leader Syrianus, who unfolded to us the secret mysteries of these triads, and join to the end of what has been said the beginning of the discussion that follows. In the Timaeus, then, Plato, searching for what the pattern of the whole world is, finds that it holds all intelligible living beings, is all-perfect, is the most beautiful of intelligibles, is only-begotten, and is the intelligible of the Craftsman. He also calls it the living being itself, as the intelligible pattern of every living being, and of what is perceptible. So this living being itself, because it is all-perfect and the most beautiful of intelligibles, must be set in the intelligible orders. For though there is an intelligible living being in the Craftsman, it is intellectual rather than intelligible, and not the most beautiful of all intelligibles, but second to them in beauty and power. For first beauty is in the intelligible gods. In the Craftsman too there are not only the four Forms of things in the world but all the multitude of Forms; for in him the patterns of particular Forms exist beforehand. But the living being itself sets up all living beings as wholes by the intelligible tetrad. Again, the Craftsman is not, like the living being itself, only-begotten among beings; he exists together with the life-giving cause, with which he sets up the second kinds of being, mixing them in the mixing bowl for the generation of souls. For of the things that the intelligible living being produces and at the same time generates, the Craftsman has the cause in a divided way, together with the bowl. So, as I have said, the living being itself is set apart from the Craftsman, and is, as Timaeus everywhere calls it, intelligible.

flags.taylor: animal itself
flags.why: Taylor's "animal itself" is the Timaeus' "living being itself" (autozōon), the pattern of the world.

notes: Timaeus 30c-31b, 39e: the world's pattern is "the living being of which all other living beings are parts", "the most beautiful of intelligibles and in every way perfect", and one only. The "four Forms" are the four kinds of living being (39e-40a): the heavenly gods, birds, water creatures and land animals. The mixing bowl: Timaeus 41d.

paragraphs.modern: Yet because Forms are first separated in it, and because it is all-perfect, it exists in the third order of intelligibles. For neither what is first being nor what is second being is all-perfect. The first is beyond all separation; the second generates and is in labour with intelligibles, but is not yet the multitude of beings. If, then, neither of these is multitude, how can either be all-perfect multitude? But if all-perfect multitude shines out in the third triad of intelligibles, as was shown a little before, and the living being itself is the first pattern (for it holds all intelligible living beings, is an only-begotten pattern, and is not joined with any other principle), the living being itself must be set in this order. For either there will be no intelligible pattern (and then how will perceptible things be images of intelligibles, or how will the intelligible gods be the fathers of the whole of things?), or, if there is, it is the third among intelligibles. For the natures before the triad among intelligibles are not all-perfect, since they are set apart from division into multitude. And the natures after it are not only-begotten, for they proceed together with others, the male with the female, and those of a making character with those of a generating one. Nor are they the most beautiful of intelligibles; for beauty is in the intelligible. But the living being itself is all-perfect and at the same time only-begotten. So the first pattern of beings is ranked in the third triad of intelligibles. Moreover, the living being itself is eternal, as Timaeus himself says: "the nature of the living being is eternal". And again elsewhere he says that "the pattern is being through all eternity". If, then, it is eternal, it shares in eternity. And if what shares is everywhere second to what is shared, the living being itself is second to eternity. And if it is being through all eternity, it is filled with the whole power of eternity. If so, it exists next after eternity. For what enjoys the whole of its causes is ranked next after them.
notes: Timaeus 37d ("the nature of the living being was eternal") and 38c ("the pattern is being through all eternity"). Taylor's footnote: the "first life" is intelligible life, life itself.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, if eternity has the same ratio to the intelligible living being as time to the perceptible one, and the universe shares directly in time (for time came to be together with the universe), the living being itself must surely share first in eternity. So eternity is above the first pattern. For eternity measures the existence of the living being itself, and the living being itself is measured and filled with everlastingness from it. Besides, we say that eternity is the cause of immortality to all things. So eternity is what is first immortal. For as what is first being is the cause of existence to all things, and what produces form is itself before other Forms, so what is the cause of everlastingness and immortality is itself first immortal. The daemonic Aristotle also rightly calls eternity immortal and divine, that from which the existence and life of all things hang. If, then, it is first immortal, not by sharing, but is, as it were, immortality and everlastingness, it will be life, having the "always" from itself, scattering the power of everlastingness in abundance and reaching it out to other things, as far as each is by nature fit to receive it. For the immortal is in life and exists together with life. So Socrates in the Phaedo, after many beautiful proofs of the soul's immortality, says: "God, then, my dear Cebes, and the Form of life itself, are far more immortal." So intelligible life, and the god who holds this life together, first have the immortal, and are the source of the whole of everlastingness. And this is eternity. So eternity has its existence in life, and will be set in the middle of the intelligible order.

flags.taylor: The dæmoniacal Aristotle
flags.why: "Daemonic" as high praise: Aristotle, On the Heavens I.9 (279a), calls eternity (aiōn) "immortal and divine", from which "being and life" depend for all things.

notes: The Phaedo 106d: "god, I think, and the Form of life itself, and whatever else is immortal, would be agreed by all never to perish". Taylor's footnote corrects "Phaedrus" to "Phaedo" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Further, we must say that intelligible eternity is one of three things: it exists either by being, or by life, or by intelligible intellect. But being, as the Stranger from Elea says, by its own nature neither stands still nor is moved. For if being is being to all things, and being in the strict sense is of this kind, much more must this be so with intelligible being and what is first being; for they are nothing else than being only. But being unfolds motion and rest, and the other kinds of beings, in its own second and third processions. The first being, then, as we have said, is at once set apart from motion and rest. But eternity, according to Timaeus, remains in one. So too time, in its motion, imitates the intelligible remaining of eternity. Eternity, then, does not exist by what is first being. Nor does it exist by intelligible intellect. For neither is soul time, though it is moved through the whole of time. And in short, among divine beings what is shared is everywhere set above what shares. But the eternal shares in eternity, as the temporal shares in time. So eternity is before intelligible intellect and after being; so that it is set in the middle of the intelligible breadth. And as the living being itself is eternal, so eternity is what always is. For as the living being itself shares in eternity, so eternity shares in being, and is the cause of existence, of everlasting life and thinking, and measures the being, powers and activities of all things.
notes: The Sophist 250c; Timaeus 37d: time is "a moving image of eternity, which remains in one". Taylor's footnote supplies a missing clause ("nor by intelligible intellect") in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Since eternity exists by the middle centre of intelligibles, and the living being itself by their end, the brightest of what is intelligible, what is the first of intelligibles, and how does Timaeus name it? He says of eternity that while it remains in one, time proceeds by number; and that by motion time sketches the remaining of eternity, and by number its stable union. What, then, is that one in which Timaeus says eternity remains? We must say either that it is the one of eternity, or the One that goes beyond all intelligibles, or the one of the first triad. If we say it is the unshared One, how can anything remain in what is set apart from all things, and admits neither relation nor sharing of second natures with itself? For everything that remains in something is in a way held on all sides by what we say it remains in. But it is wholly impossible for the first One either to hold any being or to be ranked with beings. If anyone supposes that it is the one of eternity in which Timaeus says eternity remains, then eternity will be in itself. Yet it must remain in itself by having its existence in remaining in what is before itself. For to remain in what is before is better than the setting of things in themselves, as that is more perfect than placing the better in less excellent natures. If, then, eternity remains in itself, to what shall we first give remaining in what is before itself? For this, being more divine, must have its generation before what is lower than it. If, then, eternity can remain neither in itself nor in the One before beings, it is clear that, remaining in one according to Timaeus, it is set in the one of the first triad, or rather in the whole of that triad. For, as we have said before, the first triad is the cause of stability to all beings, as the middle triad is the cause of their procession, and the third triad of their return to their principle.
notes: Timaeus 37d: the maker made "an eternal image moving by number of eternity remaining in one", which we call time.

paragraphs.modern: Again, then, three orders of intelligibles appear to us, according to Timaeus' teaching: the living being itself, eternity, and the one. Through this one, and its firm setting in it, eternity has fixed the intelligible kingdom; and through eternity the living being itself defines the boundary of the intelligible gods, by an everlasting and unchanging sameness. The living being itself, having proceeded as a tetrad, hangs from the dyad in eternity. For eternity is the "always" together with being. And the dyad in eternity shares in the intelligible monad, which Timaeus for this reason calls one, as the monad and principle of all the intelligible breadth. For indeed he rightly calls the first triad one, because it is most of all marked by limit, naming it from limit. The middle triad he calls, in a twofold way, eternity, joining the names, because this triad is defined by intelligible power. And the third triad he calls the living being itself, carrying the name over to the whole of it from the end of the triad. The first triad, then, is the union of all the intelligibles, being in a way ranked with them; for this union is different from the one set apart from intelligibles and unshared. It is also the giver of stable power, for all things are set firm because of it. But eternity is first being, and what is first set firm.
