So of the remaining of the whole of things, we say the first triad is that because of which this remaining comes about, and the second triad that by which it is produced. For the firm setting of beings is by this second triad, but because of the first. The second triad is the nearest measure of all beings, and is ranked with the things measured. In it at one and the same time are limit and the unlimited: limit, so far as it measures intelligibles; the unlimited, so far as it is the cause of everlastingness and the "always". For according to the Oracle, eternity is the cause of unfailing life, untiring power and unsluggish activity. Yet eternity is marked more by the unlimited than by limit, for it holds in itself unlimited time. Time has limit and the unlimited in a divided way: by its continuity it is unlimited, but by the now it is limited, for the now is a limit. But eternity sets limit and the unlimited in the same. For it is a henad and power: by the one it is limit, by power unlimited; which time too shows, as from images, because the middle triad of intelligibles has limit, the unlimited and the mixed. For from where does time get its limit, except from eternal limit? For the temporal limit too is undivided, as the limit of eternity is one; and the undivided is the image of the one. And from where does the unlimitedness of time's continuity come, except from the power of the unlimited? But the one is a stable unlimitedness, the other a moved one; and as the one stands still by the one, so the other is moved by number. For from where does time's kinship with lives come, except from the first principle of life, eternity? And time proceeds through all life in time.

flags.taylor: eternity is the cause of never-failing life, of unwearied power, and unsluggish energy
flags.why: From the Chaldean Oracles (frag. 49 and 59 are related), where Aion is a god who gives unfailing life and power. Taylor's footnote supplies "time" in the Greek he translated.

notes: "Eternity remaining in one": Timaeus 37d. The "now" as the limit of time: Aristotle, Physics IV.11 (220a).

paragraphs.modern: Again, then, it is clear from these things that eternity exists by the middle of the intelligible gods. For here is unlimited life, the cause of all life, intellectual, of soul, and that which exists divided in bodies. Eternity is the father and giver of unlimited life, since eternity is also the cause of all immortality and everlastingness. And Plotinus, showing in a most divinely inspired way the character of eternity according to Plato's theology, defines it as unlimited life, unfolding into light at once the whole of itself and its own being. For it sets its life in the intelligible centre: through the one it measures its being and fixes it in what is before itself, but through power makes it unlimited; it unfolds the one-like transcendence of the first triad, but defines the end of the gods, and stretches from the middle on all sides to all the intelligible breadth. Moreover, the third triad is filled with intelligible life, and so is an intelligible living being, and the first living being. For it first shares in the whole nature of this life, and brings into light in itself the first of the Forms, to which the making intellect, reaching out, sets up the whole world; and it is itself the intelligible universe, as the visible world is the perceptible universe. So Plato calls the living being itself all-perfect. Or rather, if you are willing, let us speak this way: in this third triad there are limit, the unlimited, and the mixed, which we have called intelligible intellect. So the whole triad is called only-begotten from the father in it. For the cause of limit gives what is unranked with other things and a set-apart transcendence. For what holds, says Timaeus, all the intelligible living beings will never be second with another; for again there would need to be another living being about it. So what holds in one all intelligible living beings is a whole. But everywhere the whole is referred to limit, and parts to the unlimited. So if the living being itself is only-begotten for this reason, it will have this character by limit. But again it is called eternal by its power. For this power belongs most of all to the eternal; for eternity is unlimited power remaining in one and proceeding stably. The living being itself is all-perfect by intellect. For what unfolds in itself all the intelligible separation of being is intelligible intellect; and that intellect, by Plato's decision, will be all-perfect which holds all intelligibles and defines the boundary of the intelligible order. The only-begotten, then, the eternal, the all-perfect, limit, the unlimited and the mixed show the nature of the intelligible living being. So Timaeus too reminds us of the pattern in these three conclusions: in the one that shows that the universe is only-begotten, in the generation of time, and in the all-perfect holding of all living beings.
notes: Plotinus III.7.3-5: eternity is "the life that belongs to what is, in being, all together and full, without extension", "unlimited life". Timaeus 31a-b: "what holds all intelligible living beings would never be second with another". Taylor's footnotes correct the Greek he translated in three places ("character" for "everlastingness", "life", and "towards" for "before").

paragraphs.modern: If Timaeus also says that the living being itself is the most beautiful of all intelligibles, and it has the third order among intelligibles, this will not be surprising. For we said before that everywhere the cause of the best mixture is the triad of proportion, truth and beauty. But beauty shines out chiefly in the third procession of being, and shows its shining nature together with intelligible Forms, as truth shines out in the second, and proportion in the first procession of being. If, however, truth is first, beauty second, and proportion third, it is not at all surprising that in order truth and beauty should come before proportion, but that proportion, being plainer in the first triad than the other two, should shine out third in the second processions. For these three exist in a hidden way in the first triad. Truth, so far as it is intelligible knowledge, is in the second triad; beauty, so far as it is the Form of Forms, is in the third. That this triad exists there first is clear from this: truth is first in what is most of all being, before knowledge; beauty, which reaches as far as the last of beings, must be in the first being, from which the last beings come; and the first proportion is in what is first mixed. For every mixture needs proportion, so that what is produced from it may be one thing. Though these three, then, exist beforehand there (for we take as agreed by all that proportion is there, and the most beautiful of intelligible living beings, as Timaeus says), we will put aside further consideration of them for now, since we have discussed them elsewhere, and tried especially to establish what we take to be Plato's opinion of their order. For we have spoken of these things in a treatise of one book, in which we show that truth is ranked with the philosopher, beauty with the lover, and proportion with the musician; and that as the order of these lives is, so too is the relation of truth, beauty and proportion to each other.

flags.taylor: If, however, truth is indeed the first, beauty the second, and symmetry the third
flags.why: In the Philebus (65a-66b) the order of goods is measure, proportion and beauty, then truth (intellect); Proclus means here the order in the third mixture's list, where truth comes before beauty and proportion.

notes: The Phaedrus 248d: the first soul becomes "a philosopher, a lover of beauty, or one devoted to the Muses and to love". Proclus' one-book treatise on these three lives is lost.

paragraphs.modern: The living being itself, then, may most justly be called most beautiful, so far as it is held, in an eminent way, in intelligible beauty. For beauty is wont to ride on Forms, and is, as it were, the Form of Forms, unfolding what is hidden in the Good, making its loveliness shine out, and drawing to its own splendour the desire hidden about it. To the Good all things have a silent and secret leaning; but we are roused to the beautiful with wonder and motion. For its light and working pierce keenly through every soul, and, as the most like the Good of all things, it turns back every soul that looks at it. The soul, seeing what is secret shining out, as it were, to view, rejoices in what it sees, admires it, and is struck with wonder. And as in the holiest of the mysteries, before the mystic visions, the initiates are seized with wonder, so among intelligibles, before sharing in the Good, beauty shining out strikes those who see it with wonder, turns the soul to itself, and, set in the vestibule of the Good, shows what is in the inner shrine, and what the transcendence of hidden good is. Through these things, then, let it be clear where beauty begins and how it first shines out, and that the living being itself is the most beautiful of all intelligibles.
notes: The Phaedrus 250c-e: beauty alone "has this lot, to be the most visible and the most lovely". The vestibule of the Good: the Philebus 64c.

paragraphs.modern: Timaeus says that the first and intelligible patterns exist in the intelligible living being, and that they are four, coming first into light by the all-perfect tetrad. This being so, we must first consider that, as Forms appear in the intelligible, much more must the kinds of beings exist beforehand among intelligibles. For we cannot grant that the Forms are intelligible, but the kinds only intellectual. But as the Forms exist intelligibly in their first existence, while their fullness shines out in the intellectual gods, divides what is universal into more partial lessenings, brings the one-like out into multitude, and spreads what is set apart into ranked causes, so too the kinds of being are in the intelligibles hidden and undivided, but in the intellectual gods with separation. So the first triad has being as its mixed; the second has life, where there were motion and rest, life both remaining and proceeding; and in the third there are sameness and difference. For the all-perfect multitude is through intelligible difference, and what is united and holds the parts in common, by kinds and by one, is through intelligible sameness. And all these exist in these triads intelligibly, in the manner of being, and in a one-like way.
notes: Timaeus 39e-40a: "as many Forms as intellect sees in the living being that is, so many and such the world must have: and they are four". The "kinds of being" are the Sophist's five great kinds (being, rest, motion, sameness, difference). Taylor's footnote corrects "intelligibles" to "intellectuals" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: First, then, this should be inferred by those who love to look at the nature of things: they should give the intelligible Forms kinds ranked with them. For it neither was nor will be lawful for the kinds to shine out after the Forms. So much more must those who grant that there are intelligible Forms grant that the kinds exist in the intelligible in the way described. Next, besides this, we must see how this tetrad of Forms exists, and how it shines out in intelligible intellect, answering to the principles. It is divided into a monad and a triad. For so far as the Form of the heavenly gods is set before the others, it is defined by a divine cause. It seems to me that intelligible intellect, returning to the principles of the whole of things by its turning back, becomes the fullness of Forms, and is all things intellectually and at the same time intelligibly, holding in itself the causes of beings; and, full of the inexpressible and set-apart cause of all things, it sets up the monad of the gods; which is why, I think, Plato calls it the Form of the gods. Receiving the intellectual causes of the three principles after the One, it shows three Forms after this. One is the cause of the living beings that wander and fly in the air, proceeding in answer to limit. So it sets up gods who are one-like, uplifting and undefiled, united to the heavenly gods, receiving measures second in dignity to theirs, and having the same relation to the gods who govern coming to be, ranked with these, as the heavenly gods have to them by set-apart transcendence. It shows the cause of the gods of the water, ranked with generating and unlimited power, which produces gods who give motion and fertile abundance, and watch over life; since this perceptible water too is ruled by pouring out, unlimited flow and indefiniteness, and so is given to the life-giving powers. And intelligible intellect shows the prior cause of the gods of the earth, who walk on it, in a way suited to the nature of the mixed. It generates gods who hold the end of the whole of things, who are stable, who master the formless nature of matter by the last Forms, and fix the seat of the natures in the world in the one centre of the universe. For, having their existence, as it were, from the first Hestia, the seat of beings, they stably define this seat in the world. So the Forms first come into light in intelligible intellect, having their procession and order by the first principles. Third, besides these things, we must infer, following Timaeus, that by this triad the multitude of intelligible parts shines out, and the whole is divided into an all-perfect order of parts. For that, he says, of which the other intelligible living beings, one by one and by kinds, are parts, is the first and most beautiful pattern of the universe. But if the other intelligible living beings are parts of it, clearly it is a whole, holding in itself the multitude of intelligible parts, and binding all intelligible parts together. We must infer, then, that this triad is the first cause of production and making. For if it holds the first patterns of things, clearly the ordered distribution of second natures begins from it. And if it is a living being that sets up all living beings, every extent of soul and all the extent of bodies proceed from there; and it will also hold the intelligible causes of all the life-giving and making orders.

flags.taylor: the cause of air-wandering and volant animals
flags.why: Timaeus 40a: the four kinds are the heavenly race of gods, the winged kind "that travels in the air", the kind that lives in water, and the kind "that walks on land". Proclus takes them as kinds of gods first, then of daemons and mortals.

notes: Timaeus 30c-d: the pattern is "that of which the other living beings, one by one and by kinds, are parts". Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Such ideas, then, may be taken from what is written in the Timaeus about the three intelligible triads, in agreement with what is said of them in the Philebus, seeing in each limit, the unlimited and the mixed. If you are willing, we will also show from what is scattered in the Sophist that Plato had the same idea as we have about the first principles. The Stranger from Elea in that dialogue, raising doubts against Parmenides' claim that the universe is one, unfolds intelligible multitude and shows how it hangs from the One. First he argues from the one being (being marked by the one), and reminds us that this is acted on by the One and shares in the One, but is not the One itself, nor what is first one. Afterwards he brings out the idea of the distinction between the unshared One and being from the whole. For if the one being is a whole, as Parmenides testifies, and what is a whole has parts, and what has parts is not the One itself, the one being will not be the same as the One. Third, he argues from the all-perfect. For what is wholly divided and binds many parts together can never exist in the same way as what is wholly one. Having gone this far, he shows that what is free of multitude is by its own nature set apart from the one being, proceeding in the proof of this through three arguments, beginning at one time from the one being, at another from the whole, and at another from the all. It is better, though, to hear Plato's own words. That the One is not the same as the one being he proves through these words: "What about those who say the universe is one? Must we not ask them, as far as we can, what they say being is? Certainly. Let them answer this: Do you say that only one thing is? We do. Or will they not say so? They will. What then? Do you call something being? Yes. Is it what you call one, using two names for the same thing? Or how? What will be their answer after this, Stranger?" Through this, then, Plato, separating the One and being from each other, and showing that the idea of the One differs from that of being, and that they are not the same, shows that the most proper and first One is set apart from the one being. For the one being does not remain purely in a hyparxis free of multitude and having the form of the one. But the One itself is set apart from every addition; for by whatever you add to it, you lessen its highest and inexpressible union. So we must set the One before the one being, and hang the one being from what is one alone. For if the One and the one being were the same, and it made no difference to say one and being (since if they differed, the One would again differ from the one being); if, then, the One differs in no way from the one being, all things will be one, there will be no multitude among beings, and it will not be possible to name things, lest there be two things, the thing and the name. For being set apart from all multitude and all division, there will be neither a name of anything nor any speech about it; the name will appear to be the same as the thing. And a name will not be the name of a thing, but the name of a name, if the thing is the same as the name and the name the same as the thing; and the thing will be the thing of a thing. For all things will be about the thing as about the name, through the union of thing and name. If, then, these things are absurd, and the One is, and being too, and being shares in the One, the One and the one being are not the same.
notes: The Sophist 244b-d: if only one thing is, then "being" and "one" are two names for one thing, and even having a name is absurd. Taylor's footnote corrects the order of "name" and "thing" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: That the whole too is not the same as the One, Plato shows afterwards in the same dialogue, beginning thus: "What then? Will they say that the whole is different from the one being, or the same as it? Of course they will say, and do say, it is the same. If, then, it is a whole, as Parmenides says, 'like the mass of a well-rounded sphere, equally balanced every way from the middle; for it must be neither greater nor less here or there', then being, being such, has a middle and extremes; and having these, it must surely have parts. Or how shall we say? Just so. Yet nothing prevents what is divided into parts from having the property of one in all its parts, and being so, as all and whole, one. Of course. But is it not impossible for what has these properties to be the One itself? Why? Because what is truly one, by right reasoning, must be said to be wholly without parts. It must. But such a thing as this, being made of many parts, will not agree with that account." Through these things, then, the Stranger, arguing from wholeness after the one being, and from the division of the parts of wholeness, shows that the all is not one. For if the whole is among beings, as Parmenides testifies in his verses that it is, all things will not be the One. For the One is without parts, but the whole has parts. So the whole is not the One itself; for that goes beyond all things and wholeness, while the whole is acted on by the One. So it is called whole, for it is not the One itself. So all things are not one, without separation and multiplying.
notes: The Sophist 244d-245b, quoting Parmenides frag. 8.43-45.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, the all holds many parts. For the whole is at first made of two parts; but the all has a multitude of parts, and, sharing in wholeness, is at the same time all, as wholly distributed into parts. This, then, is not the One itself, but is acted on by the One. For the One itself is without parts, and without parts in such a way as to be set apart from all parts. So the all is not the same as the One. We have divided the whole and the all, but Plato joins them, when he says: "Nothing prevents what is divided into parts from having the property of one in all its parts, and being so, as all and whole, one." At the same time, though, they are divided in the way described. Through these three arguments, then, the Stranger from Elea separates the One from what shares in the One, and raises doubts against those who say all things are one: the one being, the whole and the all; of which the all shares in the whole, and is a self-perfect multitude made of many parts, and the whole shares in being. For being is not the whole, as Parmenides testifies. These having such an order, must not Plato's arguments be made in keeping with the three intelligible triads? For since Parmenides defined the one being among intelligibles, Plato had to draw from there his proofs of the distinction between the One before intelligibles and the one among intelligibles. For the doubts raised against Parmenides show in many places that the shared one has its existence from the unshared union. So the One is not in these triads, but the one being and the whole. And the all is clearly at the end of the intelligible order, for what is in every way perfect, and all intelligible multitude, exist at that end. The whole is in the middle centre, the bond of the intelligible breadth. For the whole is fit to exist before the all, since the all is a whole, but the whole is not necessarily all. For the all is divided multitude; but what holds multitude in itself, not yet separated, is the whole. And this belongs most of all to eternity. For eternity is the measure of all intelligible multitude, as the whole is the holding together and union of the all. And the one being is in the first triad. For the One is most of all the character of this triad, as Timaeus too has shown; and being, which is being in a hidden and intelligible way, the cause of being to all other things, first shines out there. Again, then, following the Stranger from Elea, three triads appear to us: the first by the one being, the second by the whole, and the third by the all. Looking to these, the Craftsman of the universe adorns the perceptible universe, defining the visible nature by that intelligible all, and time by the intelligible wholeness; which is why time too is continuous. And as the intelligible whole holds two parts but contains them in one boundary, so time too is bounded by the now, but by its twofold parts is unlimited. These things we will discuss more fully shortly, when we speak of the Parmenides. For the Stranger's ideas are the preliminary rites of the mysteries of the Parmenides. Before we turn to the Parmenides, though, let us discuss, if you agree, the three triads from the beginning, gathering Plato's idea from his sayings scattered in many places.

flags.taylor: the proteleia of the mysteries of the Parmenides
flags.why: The proteleia were the preliminary rites before an initiation; the Sophist prepares for the Parmenides as these did for the mysteries.

notes: Taylor's footnotes correct "intellectual" to "intelligible" in the Greek he translated, and supply "the One".

paragraphs.modern: There are three triads, then, as we have often said, and they are divided in this way into limit, the unlimited and the mixed. So there are threefold intelligible limits, threefold unlimiteds, and threefold mixtures. But of every intelligible triad, the limit in each is called father, the unlimited power, and the mixed intellect. Let no one think these names foreign to Plato's philosophy. For it will appear that he uses these names in these triads more than anyone. He calls the first God father and lord in his Letters. It is clear, though, that as the first God goes beyond even the fatherly order, the first fatherly order is in the intelligible gods. For these are most of all akin to the One, and unfold his inexpressible and unknown union intelligibly. If, then, the first God is called one and father from the natures that proceed next from him, then, as the intelligible gods are first henads, so too they are first fathers. For Plato names the inexpressible in two ways, either from the summits of beings or from all beings; for through these the transcendence of the One is known. Moreover, the Stranger from Elea calls being what has power, and power. The first power, then, exists before being and is united to the father; but it agrees most with being, which it also fills. So being, as sharing in power, is called powerful; but as united to it, and producing all beings by it, it is called power. And if both Plato himself and his truest disciples often call all true beings intellect (which is why in many places they make three principles, the Good, intellect and soul, calling every true being intellect), you will have the third in these too as intellect. But we must not fail to see the difference. One kind of intellect is so in relation to hyparxis. For when we call the henad in each triad intelligible, as the object of desire of being and as filling being, then we call the third in the triad intellect. For it is intelligible as being and intellect, not as the intellect of being, but of the father and godhead. For every shared godhead is intelligible, as the fullness of what shares in it. Another kind is the intellect of being, by which we say that the being of the third triad is the intellect of what is first being. For this is intellect of being, having its own being by its very activity. For all things are in it in the manner of being, both the simpler kinds and the first patterns; for it is intelligible intellect. And the third kind is intellectual intellect, which exists answering to intelligible intellect, is joined to it and filled from it, having intellectually what is in the other intelligibly. In short, everywhere the first in each series must have the form of what is before them. So they are called first, and have a certain transcendence of being over the natures ranked with them. Since what is before intelligibles is God, the first intelligibles are gods and henads. Since the intelligible is of being, the first intellects are beings. Since intellect everywhere is intellectual by its own nature, the first souls are intellectual. Since souls are the fullnesses of life, the first of bodies are most alive. And since everlasting bodies are moved in a circle, the summits of material bodies are moved together with everlasting bodies. This, then, is why the henads are often called intelligibles, and beings intelligible intellects.
notes: The Sixth Letter 323d: "the god who leads all things present and to come, and the lord and father of the leader and cause". The Sophist 247e: being is power. "Father, power and intellect" is a Chaldean triad (Oracles frag. 3-4). Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: That Plato knew this triad, father, power and intellect, we will learn by looking at the making order. For in it the triad appears most remarkably. Because of its union with the intelligible it is filled with this triad, and has these things in a more divided way than the living being itself or intelligible eternity. At the very beginning of the making, in the Timaeus, the Craftsman calls himself father: "Of which works I am the maker and father." Shortly after he unfolds his power: "imitating my power in your generation." And this is remarkable, that he has given us the most theological idea of power. First, he calls it the power of the father, when he says "of which works I am the maker and father"; and that the power is his is clear from "imitating my power", so that for Plato power is the father's. Next, he gives this power a character that generates the whole of things, as is clear from "in your generation". Power, then, is the cause of generation and of the procession of beings. And last, he gives the intellectual character of the Craftsman: "Having said this, he poured again into the former bowl, in which he had mixed the soul of the universe, mixing the remains of the former mixture." For to pour, to mix, mixture, and producing soul belong to intellect. But what need is there to say this, since before this he calls the Craftsman intellect: "Whatever Forms intellect, by discursive reason, saw in the living being itself, such and so many he thought this universe must hold." So the Craftsman is father, power and intellect, and he has these as far as possible because of the intelligibles. He is a god as father because of them; he is also power and the generator of wholes, and knows beings intellectually, because of them. For in them intelligible knowledge first exists. Much more, then, are father, power and intellect in the intelligibles; filled from them, the Craftsman too shares in this triad. For Plato takes each of these by analogy. As the fatherly triad among intelligibles gives existence to intelligible eternity, so the Craftsman makes the works of which he is father indissoluble. And as among intelligibles eternity, proceeding by all power, generates the intelligible living being itself, so the making power gives existence to everlasting and divine living beings in the world, and gives the young gods another power, which generates mortal living beings. That anyone can take these names from Plato is clear from what has been said.
notes: Timaeus 41a ("gods of gods, of which works I am maker and father"), 41c ("imitating my power in your generation"), 41d (the second mixing in the bowl), 39e ("as many Forms as intellect sees in the living being").

paragraphs.modern: Since being has a threefold reality among intelligibles, one is first being, before the eternal; another is second being and the first eternity; and another is being last, and is intelligible and eternal intellect. Here there is being, there eternity, and there intellect. And eternity is wider than intellect, and being than eternity. For every intellect is eternal, but not everything eternal is intellect; for soul in its being is eternal. And everything that shares in eternity shares far before that in being; for existence always goes together with everlasting existence. But what shares in existence is not always eternally being; for bodies too share in a way in the nature of existence, but they are not eternal. Intellect, then, as intellect, sets up only intellectual being, since as life and being too it sets up all things. Eternity sets up both intellectual and soul's being, for the mixture in the second triad was intelligible life. And being sets up the intellectual, the soul's and the bodily life. For matter too is being, most dimly: it is potential, a formless being and non-being, falling away from sharing in being. If someone says it is being in potential, still it has this power from being. For potential is the forerunning share of act. So much, then, for these things.

What sufficient means of division does Socrates give us in the Phaedrus concerning these intelligible triads? And how, from what he says, can we go back to the idea of the reality of the most ruling gods? Socrates in that dialogue, inspired by the Nymphs, praises everything divine as beautiful, wise and good, and says that the soul is nourished by these. But if everything divine is of this kind, much more is the intelligible. All these are everywhere, but in the first triad the good chiefly exists, in the second the wise, and in the third the beautiful. For in this is the most beautiful of intelligibles. In the second triad are truth and the first thinking. And in the first is the well-proportioned, which we say is the same as the good. But Socrates in the Philebus says the marks of the good are the desirable, the sufficient and the perfect. The desirable belongs to limit, for it is the union and goodness of the whole triad, and the triad converges about it. The sufficient belongs to the unlimited, for sufficiency is a power able to reach all things and be present to all things without hindrance. And the perfect belongs to the mixed, for this is what is first threefold, since every mixture has its coming together from the triad. The marks of the good, then, unfold to us the first triad, and the marks of intelligible wisdom the second. For everything wise is full of being, generates truth, and turns imperfect natures back to their perfection. The full belongs to the second limit, for this is filled in a one-like way by sharing in the natures before it. For the full everywhere fits limit, as what cannot be filled fits the unlimited. The fertile belongs to the second power and the unlimited. For what does not remain in its own fullness but is fertile and generative of other things shows most of all the divine unlimited. And the turning-back belongs to the mixed. For this, having the end of the triad, turns everything imperfect back to the full, and unites itself before other things to the limit of the whole triad.

flags.taylor: being inspired by the Nymphs
flags.why: In the Phaedrus (238c-d, 241e) Socrates says he is possessed by the Nymphs of the place where he speaks.

notes: The Phaedrus 246e; the Philebus 20d; and Book I, chapters 21-23, on goodness and wisdom.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, the marks of beauty are the distinctive characters of the third intelligible triad. These are, as we said before, the lovely, the delicate and the bright. The lovely, set in answer to the desirable, belongs to limit. The delicate, ranked with the sufficient, belongs to the unlimited power in the beautiful. And the bright is of intellectual character. For it is the beautiful of beauty, lights up all things, and strikes with wonder those able to see it. And as visible beauty, shining most clearly, is seen through the clearest of the senses (for the objects of this sense have many differences, according to Aristotle, and this sense reaches further than the rest), so intelligible beauty appears to the intellect of the soul, shining intelligibly. For it is an intelligible Form. And for this reason the brightness of beauty is plain to intellect. Bright beauty, then, as Socrates calls it, shines out at the end of the intelligible order. For this is the brightest of intelligibles, is intelligible intellect, and sends out the intelligible light that, when it appeared, struck the intellectual gods with wonder and made them admire their father, as Orpheus says. Such, then, is the preparation for the science of the intelligible gods that may be taken from these things. And now it will be clear how beauty is hidden at the end of the first intelligible triad, but exists in the third triad as having come plainly into light. For in the first it exists in one form only, in the third in a threefold way. It is also clear how each of the triads is at one and the same time a monad and a triad. For the first triad, marked by the good, is completed by the three marks of the good. The second, marked by the wise, is held in the triad of wisdom. And the third, existing by the beautiful, is all-perfect through the triad of beauty. If, then, the beautiful is hidden in the first triad and shines out threefold in the third, it is clear that intelligible intellect loves the first triad, and has love joined to its beauty. And this is the intelligible love of the first beauty. From these, then, intellectual love proceeds, together with faith and truth, as we said before. For the three intelligible monads, the good, the wise and the beautiful, set up three powers that lead upward all other things, and before other things the intellectual gods. Of these things, though, we will speak later.

flags.taylor: that when it appeared astonished the intellectual Gods, and made them admire their father, as Orpheus says
flags.why: From the Orphic theogony: when Phanes, the first-born, appeared, the gods marvelled at the light; Proclus sets Phanes at the end of the intelligible order.

notes: Aristotle, Metaphysics I.1 (980a): we love sight above the senses because it shows many differences between things. The Phaedrus 250b-d, on bright beauty, and Book I, chapter 24.

paragraphs.modern: Let us now turn our attention to the study of the Parmenides. But I want to remind the reader again of what we have shown before. It has been shown that the second hypothesis must be divided into the whole processions of the one being, and that this hypothesis is nothing else than the generation and procession of the gods, proceeding from on high, from the highest union of intelligibles, as far as being made divine. For the discussion is not, as some say, about God and the gods in the first hypothesis. For it was not lawful for Parmenides to join multitude with the One and the One with multitude, since the first God is wholly set apart from the whole of things. And in the first hypothesis being, and even the One itself, are taken away from the first God; and that such a taking away does not fit the other gods is plain to everyone. Nor, again, does Parmenides in the first hypothesis speak of the intelligible gods, as some say. They say that the negations are of these gods because they are joined to the One, and in simplicity and union go before all the divine kinds. For how can the like or the unlike, contact and lack of contact, and all the other things denied of the One, be in the intelligible gods? They seem to me right to say that the things taken away are likenesses of the gods, but not right to say that all of them are likenesses of the intelligible gods. Besides, against this claim, the discussion is about the intelligible gods again in the second hypothesis. For what is denied in the first is affirmed in the second. This, then, as I have said, has been shown: that the conclusions have, in relation to each other, the order of before and after, of causes and effects. Proceeding from the beginning, then, we must fit the first conclusions to the first orders, the middle conclusions to the middle orders, and the last to the last, and show that there are as many questions asked as there are processions of the divine orders. And first we must give Parmenides' teaching about the intelligible gods, of whom we have set out to speak, since Plato speaks of them in many places, partly pointing and partly unfolding his meaning clearly.

flags.taylor: some say it is, in the first hypothesis, concerning God and the Gods
flags.why: Proclus' Commentary on the Parmenides (VI-VII) reviews earlier readings: some (perhaps Origen, or Amelius) took the first hypothesis to be about the first God and the gods, others about the intelligible gods. Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: We must, though, gather into one the careful and synoptic study of each order, since it would not be fitting to repeat now the exposition we have given in our commentary on that dialogue. Taking each conclusion by itself, I will try to refer it to the fitting order of gods, following in this the divine inspirations of our leader Syrianus. For with his help we too, with a divine head, have followed these sacred paths in the study of the Parmenides, stirred with a divine frenzy and woken, as from a deep sleep, to this secret mystic teaching. So much for the way of the whole of the conclusions. From here I will pass to the account of what was set out.

flags.taylor: with a divine head pursued these sacred paths
flags.why: A Homeric phrase ("with the head inspired"); Proclus means that he followed Syrianus as an initiate follows the guide, with the highest part of the soul.

paragraphs.modern: The first and unshared One, then, which exists beyond the whole of things, beyond not only the henads that share but those that are shared, is praised through the first hypothesis, shown to be the cause of all things inexpressibly, but not defined itself in any of all things, nor having any power or character akin to the other gods. After this unshared One comes what alone is beyond being and surpassing, unmixed with all hyparxis: a henad shared by being, setting up about itself the first being, and by the addition of this sharing becoming more than what is first one. This is a hyparxis beyond being, the hyparxis of the first intelligible triad. As there are these two in the first triad, the one and being, and the first generates and the second is generated, the first perfects and the second is perfected, the middle of both must be power, through which, and together with which, the one sets up and perfects being. For the procession of being from the one, and its return to the one, are through power. For what else joins being to the one, or makes the one shared by being, but power? For it is the procession of the one and its reaching out to being. So in all the divine kinds powers go before processions and generations. This triad, then, the one, power and being, is the summit of intelligibles: the first producing, the third produced, and the second hanging from the one but growing together with being.

This triad Parmenides gives at the very beginning of the second hypothesis, joining to the one the simplest sharing of being. He calls it the one being, and says that being shares in the one and the one in being. But their sharing is different. The one shares in being as lighting up, filling and making being divine; being shares in the one as hanging from the one and made divine by it. The relation that is the middle of both is not, with them, without being. For not even the relation among perceptible things is in no way being, much less the relation there. This relation is twofold: it belongs to the one and is born together with being. For it is the motion of the one and its procession into being. Parmenides gives this triad, beginning what he says about it thus: "See, then, from the beginning, if the one is, can it be and not share in being? It cannot." And he ends speaking of it with these words: "When someone says in brief that one is, will this be anything else than that the one shares in being? It will not." This, then, is the first intelligible triad: the one, being, and the relation of both, through which being is of the one and the one of being, in a wholly wonderful way; Plato pointing through these that the father is the father of intellect, and intellect the intellect of the father, and that power is hidden between the extremes. For godhead is the father of the triad, and being is the intellect of this godhead. Yet it is not intellect in the way we usually call the intellect of being. For every such intellect stands still and is moved, as the Stranger from Elea says; but what is first being neither stands still nor is moved, as he also teaches. The first triad, then, is called the one being, since power here is hidden. For the triad does not proceed from itself, but exists without separation and in a one-like way, defined first by divine union. So this is the first sharing in being, which shares in the one through power as the middle, which gathers together and separates both the one and being. And it is beyond being, but joined with being. So we must never think that all power is the offspring of being. For the powers of the gods are beyond being, and exist together with the henads of the gods themselves; and through this power the gods generate beings. Rightly, then, does poetry everywhere say that the gods can do all things. For powers of being cannot do all things, since they do not set up natures beyond being. The first triad, then, is unfolded to us by Parmenides through these things.

flags.taylor: the habitude which is the middle of both
flags.why: Taylor's "habitude" is relation (schesis): the link between the one and being, which Proclus identifies with power.

notes: The Parmenides 142b-c. "The gods can do all things": Odyssey X.306. Taylor's footnote corrects "one being" to "one" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Right after this the second triad has its procession, which Parmenides marks by intelligible wholeness, as we showed in the Sophist. For the first triad, being one-like and having all things intelligibly and in a hidden way, hyparxis, power and being (so that power, the cause of division, existing between the one and being, is hidden, and appears through the sharing of the extremes with each other), the second triad proceeds, marked by the first intelligible power, and having the monads in itself distinguished from each other. For while all things are united and undistinguished in the first triad, distinction and separation shine out in this one. Being and power too are more divided from each other. And what is made of these is no longer the one being, but a whole, so that it has the one and being in itself as parts. For above, in the first triad, all things are before parts and wholeness; but in this triad there are both parts and a whole, power bringing itself into light. For since there is separation here, there are parts and the whole made of them. The second triad, then, is called intelligible wholeness. Its parts, the one and being, I call the extremes. And power, being the middle here, joins the one and being, and does not make them one as in the first triad. Since it is the middle of both, through its sharing with being it makes the one a one being, and through its sharing with the one it makes being wholly one. And so the one being is made of two parts: being marked by the one, and the one marked by being, as Parmenides himself says. He begins to speak of this triad thus: "Again, then, let us say, if one is, what will follow. Consider whether this hypothesis must not mean that the one is such as to have parts?" And he ends with these words: "What is one, then, is a whole, and has a part."
notes: The Parmenides 142c-d.

paragraphs.modern: Through these things, then, Parmenides defines the second order of intelligibles as a wholeness. For as existence comes to all things from the first triad, so the whole from the second, and an all-perfect division from the third; but this we will consider later. Wholeness, then, is threefold, according to Plato's teaching: before the parts, made of parts, or in a part. In the Statesman he calls a genus a whole and a species a part, not that the genus is completed from the species, but that it exists before it. And in the Timaeus he says that the world is a whole of wholes. The whole world is completed from parts that are wholes, but each of the parts is a whole not as the universe is, but partially. Wholeness, then, being threefold according to Plato, as we have said, now is given the henad, the intelligible and hidden cause of these, holding and setting up in a unified way three wholenesses: by its own hyparxis, the wholeness before the parts; by its power, the wholeness made of parts; and by its being, the wholeness in a part. For the one is before all multitude; power shares in a way with both extremes and holds their characters in itself; and being in a way shares in the one. So the first of the wholenesses, before the parts, comes from a unified hyparxis. For it is a monad, and itself sets up the parts and the multitude in them. The second wholeness comes from power. For it is completed from parts, as in the power that gathers the one and being, the extremes in a way shine out to view. And the third wholeness comes from being. For being is a part, the offspring of both power and the one, and has each of these partially. After the intelligible, then, three wholenesses are divided among the different orders of beings. But the intelligible wholeness holds the three in a unified way, and is the monad that intelligibly binds this triad together, stretching its powers every way from the middle of the intelligible and hidden order.
notes: The Statesman 262a-263b: a part is not the same as a species. Timaeus 33a: the world is "one whole of wholes". Taylor's footnote corrects "being" to "one" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Right after this triad we can see another proceeding, in which all intelligible multitude shines out, and which Parmenides makes a wholeness, but a wholeness made of many parts. For after the hidden union of the first triad and the twofold separation of the second, the procession of the third comes about, which has its existence from parts, but the parts are many, the multitude with which the triad before it is in labour. For in this triad there are a henad, power and being; but the one is multiplied, and so are being and power. And so the whole triad is a wholeness; but each of its extremes, the one and being, as a multitude joined through gathering power, is again divided and multiplied. For this power, joining unified multitude to the multitude of beings, makes some of these each, by procession, being marked by the one, and others each, by sharing, the one marked by being. For here there are two parts of the wholeness, the one and being; but the one shares in being, for it is joined with it, and being shares in the one. The one of being, then, is again divided, so that the one and being generate a second henad joined to the part of being. And being, sharing in the one, is again separated into being and the one. For it generates a more partial being hanging from a more partial henad. And being is made of more partial divinised beings, and is a more specific monad. The cause of this procession is power. For power makes two things, and works multitude. The one calls out into multitude, and being turns back to sharing in the divine henads. Where, then, does Parmenides begin to teach us about this triad, and where does he end his account of it? The beginning of what he says on it is this: "What then? Can each of these parts of the one being, the one and being, leave each other, so that the one is not a part of being, or being not a part of the one? It cannot." And he ends thus: "So will not the one being in this way be an unlimited multitude? It seems so."
notes: The Parmenides 142d-143a. Taylor's footnote corrects the Greek of the quotation.

paragraphs.modern: First, then, we must understand the manner of procession of the divine kinds: that after the intelligible monad, which we rank by the one being, the dyad after it, which we call a wholeness, proceeds; that it is made of two parts separated by power; and that intelligible multitude appears from the monad and the dyad. For when all things are said to be parts of the one being, that is, second things, which appear through the separating cause of power, then Parmenides gives the union that runs from the monad to the third triad. But when power, separating and joining the henads and beings, completes multitude, then the sharing in the dyad becomes wholly plain, as I think Parmenides shows when he says "so that two must always come to be, and never one". This triad, then, proceeds by both the triads before it, flowing, according to the Oracle, and proceeding to all intelligible multitude. For unlimited multitude points to this flowing, and to the ungraspable nature of power. So, first, I have said that the reality of this triad is shown through these things to hang from the triads before it. And next I say that this triad, according to Parmenides, is first-born. For it first gives the power of coming to be; and Parmenides calls the multitude in it coming to be. For he says: "and the part will come to be from two parts at least". And again: "whatever part comes to be will always have these parts". And in what follows: "so that two must always come to be, and never one". Does not he, then, who so often uses the word coming to be in teaching the procession of intelligible multitude, proclaim that the natures before this order are more united to each other? But this order proceeds further, unfolds the hidden nature of the triads before it, and is first-born, unfolding fertile power in itself.

flags.taylor: flowing according to the Oracle
flags.why: A Chaldean phrase for the procession of the intelligible into multitude.

flags.taylor: this triad, according to Parmenides, is primogenial
flags.why: Taylor's "primogenial" is first-born (prōtogonos): Proclus links the third intelligible triad with Phanes, called Protogonos in the Orphic poems.

paragraphs.modern: Besides this, we must understand the unlimitedness of multitude not as those who take the unlimited in quantity see fit to speak of it. Since in the principles of the whole of things there are limit and the unlimited, the first the cause of union, the second of the separation of multitude, Parmenides calls the first and intelligible multitude unlimited, because all multitude, by its own nature, is unlimited, as the offspring of the first unlimited. All intelligible multitude is of this kind. For it is the first multitude, and multitude itself; and multitude itself is the first offspring of intelligible unlimitedness. Intelligible multitude, then, is unlimited for this reason, as bringing into light the first unlimited; and this unlimitedness is the same as the all-perfect. For what has proceeded to the all, and as far as an intelligible nature should proceed, through the power that generates the whole of things, is unlimited; for it cannot be held by anything else. But intelligible multitude holds all intelligible multitude. For if what is first unlimited were unlimited in quantity, we would have to grant that the intelligible is an unlimited multitude of this kind. But since the intelligible is unlimited power, what shares in the first unlimited must make unlimitedness shine out by the power that holds all prior natures. And if I must give my own opinion: as what is first one is first limit, so what is first multitude is unlimited multitude. For it receives the whole power of the unlimited, and, producing all henads and all beings down to the most individual natures, has unfailing power. So it is more universal than all multitude, and an unlimited that cannot be grasped. So, bringing all multitude into light, it bounds and measures it by unlimited power, and through wholeness brings limit to all things. These things, then, may be taken from Parmenides about the third intelligible triad.

Next, let us speak in common of all the intelligible triads. The first triad, which is hidden and has the intelligible summit among intelligibles, Plato at one time, proceeding from the union in it and its set-apart transcendence over the other triads, calls one, as in the Timaeus: for eternity, he says, remains in one; and reason shows that this one is the first triad of intelligibles. At another time, proceeding from the extremes in it, what is shared and what shares, he calls it the one being, taking the power held in these as inexpressible, since it exists in a one-like and hidden way. And at another time he unfolds the whole of it by the monads in it, limit, the unlimited and the mixed: limit pointing to its divine hyparxis, the unlimited to its generative power, and the mixed to the being that proceeds from this power. Plato, then, as I have said, teaches us the first intelligible triad through these names, unfolding it to our view at one time through one name, at another through two, and at another through three. For there is a triad in it, by which the whole is marked; a dyad, by which the extremes share with each other; and a monad, which shows the inexpressible, hidden and unified nature of the first through its own monads.

The second triad after this Plato calls eternity in the Timaeus, and the first wholeness in the Parmenides. How these have the same character we may learn by considering that everything eternal is a whole, if it is wholly eternal and has the whole of its being and activity present at once. Every intellect is of this kind, setting at once in itself the whole of its intellectual perception. It does not have one part of being and lack another, nor share in activity in part, but holds in sum the whole of being and the whole of thinking. If, though, it proceeded in time in its activities but had an eternal being, it would have the whole of its being, always stably the same, but would have its activity variably, acting differently at different times. Eternity, then, is everywhere the cause of wholeness to the natures to which it is first present. And the whole too everywhere holds everlastingness. For no whole leaves its being or its proper perfection; what first perishes and is spoiled is a partial nature. This is why the whole world is everlasting, because it is a whole; and so with all that the heavens hold, and with each of the elements. For everywhere wholeness holds together what underlies it. So eternity exists together with wholeness, and whole and eternity are the same. Each is a measure: the one of eternal things and all everlasting natures, the other of parts and all multitude. But since there are three wholenesses, one before parts, one from parts, and one in a part, through the wholeness before parts eternity measures the henads of divine natures set apart from beings; through the wholeness from parts, the henads ranked with beings; and through the wholeness in a part, all beings and whole beings. For these wholenesses, being parts of the divine henads, have in a divided way what exists beforehand in the henads in a unified way. Moreover, eternity is nothing else than the "always" shining out from the henad joined with being. And the whole is made of two parts, the one and being, power being what gathers the parts. By both these ideas, then, the dyad of the middle intelligible triad unfolds the one-like and hidden reality of the first triad.
notes: Eternity as "always" (aei) and "being" (ōn): Aristotle, On the Heavens I.9 (279a); Plotinus III.7.4.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, in the Timaeus Plato calls the third triad of intelligibles the living being itself, intelligible, all-perfect and only-begotten. In the Parmenides he calls it unlimited multitude, and a wholeness holding many parts. And in the Sophist he keeps calling it the intelligible distributed into many beings. All these sayings, then, are offspring of one science, and tend to one intelligible truth. For when Timaeus calls this triad the intelligible living being, he also says it is all-perfect, and holds intelligible living beings as its parts, one by one and by kinds. So the living being itself is, by this, a whole holding intelligible living beings as its parts. And Parmenides, when he shows that the one being is all-perfect multitude, shows that it exists together with this order. For the unlimited will be all-powerful and all-perfect, as we said before, holding in itself an intelligible multitude of parts, which it also generates, some more universal and others more partial, and, as Timaeus says, one by one and by kinds. Further, as Timaeus calls the living being itself eternal and only-begotten, so Parmenides first gives the "always" and "coming to be" to unlimited multitude, when he says: "And so, by the same reasoning, whatever part comes to be will always have these two parts; for the one will always hold being, and being the one; so that two must always come to be, and never one."
notes: The Parmenides 142e-143a; the Sophist 245b-d, 246b-c.

paragraphs.modern: Who, then, so clearly reminds us of the eternal living being and the first-born triad as Parmenides, who first takes up, in this order, coming to be and the "always", and uses each of them so continually? The same thing, then, is an all-perfect living being and all-powerful intelligible multitude. For since the first unlimitedness is power, and every intelligible exists by it and receives from it a division into parts, I think it right to call it all-powerful, so avoiding the name "unlimited", which disturbs the multitude. But what in these things is hard to understand, and for which Plato most deserves admiration, we must not leave out, but show to the true lovers of truth. The intelligible living being holds four intelligible Forms, by which it sets up not only the kinds of gods but the higher kinds of beings after the gods, and mortal living beings themselves. For, generating, it stretches out the Form of the beings that wander in the air, the Form of those in the water, and the Form of those on the earth, from the gods down to mortal living beings. Since the living being itself, then, holds four Forms, and through the same patterns produces, as wholes, divine, daemonic and mortal living beings, this rightly raises a question for those who love the contemplation of truth: how, with the same causes and the same first patterns existing beforehand, some of the natures set up are gods, others daemons, and others mortal living beings. For if all these are generated in relation to one Form, how can they not have the same form and nature, since one Form must everywhere generate things of like form? For this is why we grant the hypothesis of Forms: so that the intelligible kind of gods may have and hold, before multitude, monads that produce like natures. This question, so hard, someone may solve logically, by saying that not all things that exist by one Form share the name in the same sense, nor share alike in their common cause, but some first and others last. For each Form leads a certain series, beginning from on high and sinking as far as the last of things. For according to the Oracle, all things begin from on high to stretch their wonderful rays down to the place below. So it will not be surprising that the same Form should exist beforehand as the cause of gods, daemons and mortal living beings, producing all things as wholes, and handing on the more partial separation of things to the making order, as this order hands on the production of individuals to the young gods. For intelligibles are the causes of whole series; intellectual gods, of divisions by common kinds; Forms above the world, of specific differences; and Forms in the world, of things that are now individuals. For they are causes that are moved, and lead their offspring into change.

flags.taylor: all things which subsist according to one form are not synonimous
flags.why: Taylor's "synonimous" is Aristotle's term (Categories 1a): things that share both a name and its definition. Proclus means that gods, daemons and mortals share a Form's name but not in the same sense. Taylor's footnote corrects "unlimitedness" to "difficulty" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: But if we must look at the thing itself by itself, and see how one intelligible Form is the cause of gods, daemons and mortals, Parmenides alone can satisfy us about the parts held in intelligible multitude. For he marks some things by being and others by the one. The one being is taken up by the one, but being that is one is rather taken up by being; and the one being, and being that is one, hold in themselves each of the intelligible living beings. By the one being, then, Parmenides sets up the divine kinds, with a fitting character; by being that is one, the kinds after the gods. By the one being of being that is one, he sets up the kinds of daemons; and by being that is one, the mortal kinds. And again, by the one being of the one being, he sets up the first and highest kinds of gods; and by its being that is one, the second kinds, which have an angelic order. And so all things are full of gods, angels, daemons, living beings and mortal natures. And you see how the middle of the higher kinds is kept. For being that is one is the angelic boundary of the one being that produces the gods; and the one being is the daemonic summit of being that is one, which adorns second natures. As for the unions of second natures, it is not unclear that they come near to multitude and to the procession of the natures set above them. Nor should you wonder that being that is one is the cause of angels, but the one being of daemons. For in one place being that is one is a part of the one being, in another the one being is a part of being that is one. And here the union is of being, but there being has the form of the one. For the summit of being that is one is of this kind. Rightly, then, is intelligible multitude all-powerful, and the intelligible living being all-perfect, as being at once the cause of all things, as far as the last of things; Plato all but crying out, in the words of the Chaldean Oracle: "From there a fiery whirlwind, sweeping along, darkens the flower of fire, leaping at the same time into the hollows of the worlds." For the divine henads, proceeding step by step, generate the multitude of all the natures in the world. This triad, then, is the source and cause of all things; and from it all the life and procession of the gods, of the kinds above us, and of mortal living beings exist. For it produces all things as wholes and in a one-like way, and binds to itself the whole principles of the divided rivers of life-giving and of the production of Forms.

flags.taylor: according to the one being indeed of being which is one, he constitutes the genera of dæmons, but according to being which is one, the mortal genera
flags.why: Proclus' scheme, hard to follow in any language: each part of the one being, "the one" and "being", is again "one being" and "being that is one"; the parts in which the one rules give gods and angels, those in which being rules give daemons and mortals. Taylor's footnote supplies "cause" in the Greek he translated.

notes: "All things are full of gods": Thales (Aristotle, On the Soul I.5, 411a), and the Laws X 899b. The Chaldean Oracles frag. 35 or 37 (the "whirlwind" of the Forms leaping from the Father's intellect).

paragraphs.modern: Again, then, let us go back from the divided study of intelligibles to the all-perfect and one science of them, and say to ourselves that this intelligible kind of gods is set apart in a unified way from all the other divine orders. It is called intelligible not as known by a partial intellect, nor as grasped by thinking together with reason, nor yet as existing beforehand in all-perfect intellect. For it goes beyond both universal and partial intelligibles, and exists before all objects of intellect, an unshared and divine intelligible. So it has the same transcendence over all the intelligible orders as the One over every kind of gods. For this intelligible is unshared, and fills from above the divine and intellectual orders. For if every intellect is intelligible to itself, it has this property through the intelligible gods, since fullness comes to all things from there. And so the intelligible is at once set apart from intellect, existing itself by itself, and at the same time not outside intellect. For there is an intelligible joined with intellect: the ranked coming from the set-apart, the shared from the unshared, what is in another from what exists before, and the multiplied from the one-like. Intelligible simplicity, then, must not be defined like what we usually say of intelligibles. For in these the one becomes equal to multitude, and separation to the one-like sameness of being. But intelligible simplicity is one-like, without separation and hidden, above every divided form of life and intellectual multitude. So I do not set intelligible simplicity in the rank of a Form. For a Form is partial, and below intelligible union. I take it to be the hyparxis of divine natures, generating the whole of the good distributed to all divine natures, in which the gods themselves exist. For the goodness of the gods is neither form nor habit, but the fullness of divine self-sufficiency and divine power, by which the gods fill all things with good. Much more, then, are the intelligible gods, because they are united to the Good, wholly full of goodness beyond being, and, set in this, hold in it their own highest hyparxis. Rightly, then, do we say that the intelligible gods unfold the inexpressible principle of all things, and his wonderful transcendence and union: themselves existing in a hidden way, but holding multitude in a one-like and unified way; reigning over the whole of things in a set-apart way, and unranked with all the other gods. For as the Good lights up all things with light beyond being, and shows the gods who are the fathers of all things, so the intelligible kind of gods, by its likeness to the Good, gives from itself to all the second gods intelligible fullness. So in each distribution of the gods there is a fitting intelligible multitude, just as a monad answering to the Good exists before each of the divine orders. This monad is the leader, existing beforehand, of union to second natures; and intelligible multitude is the source, existing beforehand, of beauty, self-sufficiency, power, being and all intelligible goods. For the gods hold beforehand and intelligibly all intellectual natures, and hold all things in themselves by highest union.
notes: Taylor's footnote: with one correction ("all things by union"), the end of the book is complete, and not cut short, as Portus, the Latin translator, thought.

paragraphs.modern: Let our discussion of the intelligible gods, unfolding Plato's mystic teaching about them, end here. It follows next that we consider in the same way the account of the intellectual gods. But since among intellectuals some are both intelligible and intellectual, those that, as the Oracle says, are thought at the same time as they think, while others are intellectual only, we will begin with those that are intellectual and at the same time intelligible, and first set out what they have in common, which will make the teaching about each of their orders clearer. Let us recall, then, what we showed a little before: that there are three monads as wholes, wholly beyond the gods divided into parts, namely being, life and intellect. And these, before the partial ones, share in the henads beyond being. Being is set apart from the rest; life has the middle rank; and intellect turns the end of this triad back to its beginning. All these are intelligibly in being, intelligibly and intellectually in life, and intellectually in intellect. And as second natures always share in those set above them, while these, before being shared, exist themselves by themselves; and as in each order there are three things, the cause of remaining, the cause of procession and the cause of return, intellect taking its form more by return, life by procession, and being by remaining; this being so, the first intellectual gods, whose being is by life, must join intellect that is not shared to the intelligible kind of gods, holding together the many processions of second natures in a one-like way, and unfolding and spreading out the stable hyparxis of the causes before them. For life that is not shared is of this kind: it surrounds what is first being and intellect, sharing in being and shared by intellect. This is the same as to say that thinking is filled from the intelligible, and fills intellect from itself. For being is the intelligible, and life is thinking. Being is marked by a divine hyparxis, life by power, and intellect by intelligible intellect. For as being is to hyparxis, so intellect is to being. And as intelligible power is to each of the extremes, so life is to the intelligible and to intellect. And as power is born from the One and hyparxis, but together with the one sets up the nature of being, so life proceeds from being and gives existence to a power other than that in being. And as the One itself, which is before being, gives being a second unity from itself, so life, having its existence before intellect, generates intellectual life. For true being and the intelligible, which come before the rest, supply both life and intellect with union. So life that is not shared, but shares in the intelligible monads, is second after being; it generates intellect that is not shared, completes this middle, and holds the bond of intelligibles and intellectuals. It is lit up by gods who have a union second to the hidden existence of the intelligibles, but who, as cause, come before the separation of intellectual natures. For the unitary, undivided, simple and first nature of the intelligibles sinks, through these gods, into multitude and separation and the unfolding, beyond telling, of the divine orders. So, I think, the gods who hold together unlimited life, being the middle of the intelligible and intellectual gods and carried in their own divisions as in a vehicle, are called intelligible and at the same time intellectual: filled from the first intelligibles, and filling the intellectual gods. For we call the intelligible gods intelligible not as ranked with intellect. The intelligible in intellect is one thing, what produces the intellectual gods another. And we call the gods who exist by life intelligible and intellectual at once, not as completing intellect, nor as set in intellectual thinking and giving intellect its power of thinking and the intelligible its power of being thought, but because they have their existence from the intelligible monads and generate all the intellectual hebdomads. And because they are lit up with intelligible life but exist before intellectuals as generating causes, we think it right to name them in common, joining their name from the extremes, as they also have, among the divine orders, a character that gathers wholes together.

flags.taylor: according to the Oracle perceiving intellectually are at the same time intellectually perceived
flags.why: The Chaldean Oracles speak of gods who "think and are thought"; the phrase "intelligible and intellectual" (noētoi kai noeroi) names this whole order.

flags.taylor: generating all the intellectual hebdomads
flags.why: The intellectual gods form a hebdomad (seven): Kronos, Rhea, Zeus, the three Kouretes (the "unpolluted" guardians), and the god who separates (Book V).

paragraphs.modern: It is clear, then, that they exist by this middle, and are next to the intelligible gods, who are both monads and triads. For the intelligible triads are triads in relation to the highest union, which is set apart from all things; but in relation to the divided being of triads they are monads, bringing whole triads out into light from themselves. Since the intelligibles, then, in their threefold procession, do not leave their unitary hyparxis, the intelligible and intellectual gods exist as triads, showing in themselves the separation of the monads, and through divine difference proceeding into multitude and a variety of powers and beings. For natures further from the one principle of all things are more multiplied than those before them: they are lessened in power and in the grasp they have of second natures, but divided into more numbers, further from the monad. They also leave the union that causes what first produces, and take variety in exchange for the hidden hyparxis of those first beings. By this reasoning the intelligible and intellectual separation is greater than the separation that is only intelligible. And the partial orders, again, have far more division than these, so as to unfold a multitude of gods that cannot be held in the numbers within ten. Their characters too cannot be described or unfolded by our thoughts, and are plain only to the gods themselves and to their causes. Such, then, are the intelligible and intellectual gods, and such is the character they have: a character that binds the extremes together, brings into light what comes before, and turns back what comes after. For they think the gods before them, and are thought by the gods after them. So Timaeus too makes the all-perfect living being the most beautiful of intelligibles: because there are intelligibles after it, which it surpasses in beauty, being above them, and because it is the boundary of the first intelligibles, while what comes after it exists intellectually. By this reasoning, then, the first intellectual gods are also intelligible; and we do not bring these things in from elsewhere and pin them on Plato, but say them with his help. This will be clearer from what follows.
notes: Timaeus 30d: the living being itself is "the most beautiful of intelligibles". Taylor's footnote corrects a pronoun in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Next, then, we will discuss how the gods who light up the breadth of unshared life proceed from the intelligible gods. Since the intelligible gods set in themselves in a one-like way what is multiplied, in a hidden way what is divided, and the many kinds of beings by a wonderful transcendence of simplicity, the first intellectual gods, unfolding their undistinguished union and the unknown nature of their existence, and filled through intelligible power and life of being with the fertile abundance of wholes, have a kingdom that ranks second after them. They always produce, perfect and hold themselves together, but receive from the intelligible gods a hidden generation: from intelligible power, a character that generates all things; and from intelligible life, which exists beforehand as cause in the intelligible, the nature spread beneath them. For life is in intelligibles first, in intelligibles and intellectuals second, and in intellectuals third: as cause in the first, in its being in the second, and by sharing in the last. The first intellectual gods, then, proceed from the intelligible gods, multiplying their union and their unitary powers, unfolding their hidden hyparxis, and through generating, holding-together and perfecting causes making themselves like the transcendencies of intelligibles, which are of being, whole and all-perfect. For in intelligibles there were three powers that first produce: one setting up the being of wholes; another measuring what is multiplied; and another producing the Forms of everything generated.
notes: Taylor's footnote supplies "intellectual gods" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: In answer to these the intelligible and intellectual powers exist: one producing, by its very being, the life of second natures with a certain intelligible grasp; another holding together everything divided, and lighting up with the intelligible measure the natures that leave the one union of all things; and another supplying all things with shape, form and perfection. The intelligible and intellectual orders of gods, then, are generated by all the intelligible causes. From power they have the character of procession, and from life they receive the portion of being that hangs from them. For life is joined with power, since life is of itself unlimited (all motion has the unlimited in its nature), and the power of the unlimited generates all things. From the threefold existence of intelligibles they receive their distribution into first, middle and last. For all things must be held by a threefold procession, and before all other things the kinds of gods that are intelligible and intellectual at once. Because they exist as the middle of wholes and complete the bond of the first orders, by their summit they are made like intelligibles, and by their extremity like intellectuals. They are partly intelligible and partly intellectual. For everywhere the processions of the divine kinds come about through unbroken likeness, and the first of what is lower are united to the ends of the causes before them.
