But as the first and the last in this middle of wholes are both intelligible and intellectual, there must be a middle that holds them together, in which the character of these gods appears most of all. For what is intelligible and intellectual at once has more of one in one part, and in another shares equally in both. From these things the continuity of the procession of the divine orders appears wonderful. For the extremity of intelligibles was intellectual, but as among intelligibles. The summit of the intelligible and intellectual gods is intelligible, but has this character in the manner of life. Again, the end of the intelligible and intellectual gods is intellectual, but in the manner of life. And the beginning of intellectuals is intelligible and rules over the intellectual gods, but has the intelligible intellectually. And so all the divine kinds have an unbreakable link and communion, a wonderful friendship, a well-ordered lessening, and a transcendence partly ranked with them and partly set apart. What proceeds is always continuous with the cause that produces it; and second natures, while firmly set in their causes, make a procession from them. And there is one series and kinship of all things, second natures always coming from those before them through likeness. How the intelligible and intellectual gods come into light from the intelligible gods may be recalled through these things.

Next let us show how they are divided in their processions, and how their triads differ from the intelligible triads. These gods too are divided in three, in the way described: joined to the intelligible through their summit, to the intellectual through their end, and, through the middle bond of the extremes, having the character of each equally, reaching both the intelligible and the intellectual kinds of gods as the centre of these two orders, holding the communion of wholes in a one-like way. They are divided in three, too, because in them all things, being, life and intellect, are in the manner of life, as they are intelligibly in the gods before them, and intellectually in the gods who come from them. Being is the intelligible of life; life is the middle and the character of this order; and intellect is its extremity, and what is carried next in the intellectuals as in a vehicle. Since all things exist in these gods, then, there will be a division of them into first, middle and last kinds. And third, they are divided in three because life must remain, proceed and return to its principles, since, among beings, the first triad was said to establish all things, and before other things the second triad. Eternity, then, remains stably in the first triad. The triad after it supplies the whole of things with procession, motion, and life in act. And the third triad supplies the return to the One, and the perfection that turns all second natures back to their principles. So the intelligible and intellectual gods must share first in these three powers: remaining in their own summit, but proceeding from there and reaching out to all things, and again returning to the intelligible look-out, joining the end of their whole procession to the beginning of their generation.

The intelligible and intellectual gods, then, are divided in three, as I have said. Being ranks first in them, life is the middle, and intellect the extremity. But since each of these three is perfect, and shares in the intelligible monads (I mean the being there, intelligible life, and intelligible intellect), they are tripled by sharing in the causes that first produce. The intelligible of their life has being, intellect and life intelligibly; the intelligible-and-intellectual of it has being, life and intellect intelligibly and intellectually at once; and its intellectual part has these intellectually and intelligibly. Everywhere there is a triad in each section, but with its own character. So three intelligible and intellectual triads appear to us, lit up by the divine henads, but each holding an all-various multitude. For since among intelligibles there was an all-powerful and all-perfect multitude, how could this multitude not be far more unfolded and multiplied in the gods second to the intelligible order, by their generative cause? Each triad, then, holds in itself a multitude of powers and a variety of Forms, bringing intelligible multitude into act and bringing into light the generative unlimitedness of the intelligibles. We, setting out from what shares, find the character of the gods beyond being who are shared. But in the order of things the intelligible and intellectual monads generate about themselves beings, all lives, and the intellectual kinds. And through these they unfold their own unknown transcendence, keeping by itself the cause, existing beforehand, of the whole of things. There are, then, as we have said, three intelligible triads; and there are three triads after them, which appear tripled from them by their fertile perfection.
notes: Taylor's footnote supplies words missing from the Greek he translated ("intelligibly and intellectually, and the intellectual of it ... and intelligibly").

paragraphs.modern: But the character of the intelligible triad, and of the intelligible and intellectual triad, must be defined in another way. In the intelligible order each triad had only the third part of being; for it was made of limit, the unlimited, and what comes from both. This was being in the first triad, intelligible life in the second, and intelligible intellect in the third. The natures before them were henads and powers beyond being, which complete the whole triads. But in the intelligible and intellectual order, each triad has being, life and intellect: one intelligibly and intellectually at once, but more intelligibly, as continuous with the first intelligibles; another intellectually and intelligibly, but more intellectually, being carried next in the intellectuals; and another in equal parts, holding both characters in itself. So the first triad, to speak of each, was among intelligibles limit, the unlimited and being, for being was what was first mixed. But here the first triad is being, life and intellect, with their own henads. For being hangs from the first god of this triad, life from the second, and intellect from the third. And these three monads beyond being unfold the monads of the first triad. The second triad after this was, in the intelligible order, a henad beyond being, power, and hidden intelligible life. Here, though, being, life and intellect are all in the manner of life, and hang from the gods who hold the single bond of this whole order. For as the first henads had a power that unifies the middle kinds, so the second henads after them show the holding-together character of the causes that first produce. Then comes the third triad, which in the intelligible order was a henad, power and intelligible intellect; but here it is made of three gods beyond being, who close the boundary of the intelligible and intellectual gods and gird all things round intellectually, I mean being, life and intellect. They also supply divine perfection, imitating the all-perfect intelligible triad, as the gods who hold together imitate the intelligible measure, and the gods before them the generative cause of intelligibles. The three intelligible and intellectual triads, then, are generated in this way, and differ in this way from the intelligible triads.

flags.taylor: the connectedly containing Gods
flags.why: Taylor's "connectedly containing" (synochic) is Proclus' name for the second of these triads: the gods who "hold together" all things. The third are the "perfecting" (teletarchic) gods.

notes: Taylor's footnote corrects "most perfect" to "of perfection" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Returning again to Plato, let us agree with him, and show the science of each of these triads that exists beforehand in him. First let us take what is written in the Phaedrus, and look, from Socrates' own words, at how he unfolds to us the whole ordering of these triads and the differences it holds. In the Phaedrus, then, twelve leaders are said to rule over the whole of the world's affairs, to lead all the gods of the world and all the herds of daemons, and to turn them back to the intelligible nature. Zeus is said to lead all twelve, to drive a winged chariot, to set all things in order and care for them, and to lead all the army of gods that follow him, first to the look-out within the heaven, and to the blessed sights and paths of discursive reason among the intelligibles there; and next to the arch beneath the heaven, which closely girds the heaven and is held in it, and after this to the heaven itself and its back, where divine souls stand and, carried round with the heaven, look at all the being that is beyond it. Socrates adds that before the heaven there is what is called the place above the heaven, in which true and real being, the plain of truth, the kingdom of Adrastia, and the divine choir of virtues exist; and that souls, nourished by thinking these monads, are blessed, following, in their contemplation, the circuit of the heaven.

flags.taylor: blessed spectacles, and discursive energies of the intelligibles
flags.why: The Phaedrus 247a: "many and blessed are the sights and paths (diexodoi) within the heaven". Taylor renders diexodoi "discursive energies", as if it meant the passage of thought; the Greek means ways through, or courses.

notes: The Phaedrus 246e-247e. Adrastia ("the inescapable") is named at 248c, in "the law of Adrastia".

paragraphs.modern: These things are said in the Phaedrus, Socrates being clearly inspired by a god, and speaking of mystic matters. But before other things we must consider what the heaven is of which Socrates speaks, and in which order of beings it is set. For once we have found this, we may also look at the arch beneath the heaven and the place above the heaven. For each of these is taken by its relation to the heaven: the one set first above it, the other ranked first beneath it.

flags.taylor: according to habitude towards the heaven
flags.why: Taylor's "habitude" is relation (schesis). Taylor's footnote supplies "and the place above the heaven" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: What, then, is the heaven to which Zeus leads the gods? If we say it is the perceptible heaven, as some others do, the higher kinds will have to turn to things lower than themselves by nature. For if Zeus, the great leader in the heaven, goes to this perceptible heaven and leads to it all the gods who follow him, he will turn to what is lower and after himself. And with Zeus, so will all the leaders, and the gods and daemons who hang from them; though the same Socrates in the Phaedrus says that even a partial soul, once perfected, travels on high and governs the whole world. How, then, could the leaders of whole souls turn to the perceptible heaven and exchange the intelligible look-out for a lower lot, when through these souls they rule the universe, in order to light up the things of the world with a power that is free and unconstrained? Besides this, what blessed thoughts of the gods are there within this perceptible heaven, and what unfoldings of all knowledge of perceptible things? For in short the gods know perceptible things not by turning to them but by holding their causes in themselves. So, thinking themselves with their intellect, they know perceptible things as their cause, and rule them, not by looking at them and leaning toward what they govern, but by turning lower natures back to themselves through love. It is not lawful, then, for the gods who order the whole heaven and think it worth their providence to be ever placed beneath the circuit of this heaven; there is no blessedness in contemplating the things beneath it; and the souls that turn to this contemplation are not among those who are happy and follow the gods, but rank among those who exchange intelligible food for the food of opinion, such as Socrates says are the souls that are lamed, have broken their wings, and are sunk down. Since these afflictions, then, belong to partial souls, and not to happy ones, how can we credit the ruling and leading gods with turning to the perceptible heaven?

flags.taylor: exchange intelligible for doxastic nutriment
flags.why: The Phaedrus 248b: souls that fail to see true being "use the food of opinion" (trophē doxastē). Taylor's footnote says the sentence after this one is too corrupt in the Greek he translated to render, and he leaves it out.

notes: The Phaedrus 246c: the perfect, winged soul "travels on high and governs the whole world".

paragraphs.modern: Further, Socrates says that souls standing on the back of the heaven are carried round by the heaven's own revolution; but Timaeus and the Athenian Stranger say that souls lead everything in the heavens by their own motions, cover bodies from outside with their motions, and, living their own life through all time, give bodies powers of motion as second causes. How, then, do these things agree with those who make this heaven perceptible? For souls do not contemplate and dance round the intelligibles through the circling of the heavens; it is through the unseen revolution of souls that bodies turn in a circle and make their circuits about them. If anyone says, then, that the perceptible heaven carries souls round, and that it is divided into the back, the depth and the arch beneath the heaven, he must accept many absurdities.
notes: The Phaedrus 247b-c; Timaeus 36e; the Laws X 896e-898c.

paragraphs.modern: But if someone says that the heaven to which Zeus is the leader, and all the gods, and with them the daemons, follow him, is intelligible, he will unfold Plato's inspired accounts in keeping with the nature of things, and will follow the most famous of his interpreters. For Plotinus and Iamblichus hold that this heaven is something intelligible. And before them Plato himself, in the Cratylus, following the Orphic theogonies, calls Kronos the father of Zeus, and Ouranos, Heaven, the father of Kronos. He shows that Zeus is the Craftsman of the whole of things through the names he is called by, looking into the truth about them. He shows that Kronos holds together a divine intellect, and that Ouranos is the thinking of the first intelligibles. For sight, he says, looking at the things above, is Heaven. So Ouranos exists before every divine intellect, with which the great Kronos is full; but he thinks the things above, beyond the order of heaven. The great Ouranos, then, has a kingdom between the intelligible and intellectual orders. For the circuit mentioned in the Phaedrus is thinking, through which all the gods and souls come to contemplate the intelligibles. But thinking is a middle between intellect and the intelligible. We must say, then, that the whole heaven is set in this middle, and holds the one bond of the divine orders, being the father of the intellectual kind but generated from the kings before it, which it is also said to see. On one side of it the place above the heaven must be set, and on the other the arch beneath the heaven.

flags.taylor: sight, says he, looking to the things above, is Heaven
flags.why: The Cratylus 396b-c: ouranos (heaven) is explained as horōsa ta anō, "looking at the things above". Zeus' name (Zēna, Dia) is "through whom (di' hon) life (zēn)" comes; Kronos' is koros nou, "pure intellect".

notes: Plotinus V.8.13 and Iamblichus (in a lost commentary on the Phaedrus) took the heaven as intelligible.

paragraphs.modern: Again, if the place above the heaven is the unshared and hidden kind of the intelligible gods, how can we set so great a divine multitude there, and with separation: truth, science, justice, temperance, the meadow and Adrastia? For neither the sources of the virtues nor the separation and variety of Forms belong to the intelligible gods. For the first and most unitary of the Forms reach out the making intellect of wholes to the intelligible pattern and the grasp of Forms there. But Socrates in the Phaedrus says that a partial intellect contemplates the place above the heaven. For this intellect is the pilot of the soul, as the philosophers before us rightly say. If, then, we must look by this analogy for the difference among intelligibles, as the making intellect is not shared but a partial intellect is shared, so of the intelligible, the one that is the first pattern of the Craftsman belongs to the first intelligibles, but the one that is the first pattern of a partial intellect belongs to the second intelligibles, which are intelligibles but have an intelligible transcendence as existing at the summit of the intellectuals. But if the place above the heaven is beyond the heavenly circuit, but lower than those intelligible triads, since it is more spread out (for it is the plain of truth, and is not unknown, is divided into a multitude of Forms, has a variety of powers, and its meadow nourishes souls and is seen by them, whereas the first intelligibles light up souls with inexpressible union, but are not known by them through thinking); if so, the place above the heaven must exist between the intelligible nature and the heavenly circuit. And if Plato himself grants that being that truly is exists in this place, how could he not grant that it is intelligible, and shares in the first intelligibles? For because it is being it is intelligible; but because it truly is, it shares in being.

flags.taylor: a partial intellect contemplates the supercelestial place
flags.why: The Phaedrus 247c: being in the place above the heaven "is seen only by intellect, the soul's pilot". A "partial" intellect is the individual intellect of a soul, as against the one making intellect of the whole.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, having in itself a multitude of intelligibles, it will not be ranked with the first triad; for there is the one being, not the multitude of beings. Having the many-sided life that the meadow points to, it is lower than the second triad; for intelligible life is one and without separation. And again, since it shines out with divided Forms, all-various orders and fertile powers, it falls short of the all-perfect triad among the intelligibles. If, then, it is second to these in dignity and power, but set above the heavenly order, it is intelligible, but the summit of the intellectual gods. This is why souls get their food from there. For the intelligible is food, since the first intelligibles too, the beautiful, the wise and the good, are said to nourish souls. By these, Socrates says, the soul's wing is nourished, and by their contraries it is spoiled and destroyed. These things, though, the first intelligibles do in a set-apart way, through union and silence. But the place above the heaven is said to nourish through thinking and activity, and to fill the happy choir of souls with intelligible light and the fertile rivers of life.
notes: The Phaedrus 246e.

paragraphs.modern: After the place above the heaven and the heaven itself comes the arch beneath the heaven, which plainly must be ranked under the heaven, not in it. For Plato does not call it the heavenly arch, but the arch beneath the heaven. That it lies next beneath the heavenly circuit is clear from what is written about it. But if anyone would make the arch, being such, the same as the summit of the intellectuals, and not as the end of the intelligible and intellectual gods, he must now consider what follows. The summit of the intellectuals sets itself apart from the kingdom of the heaven, but the arch beneath the heaven is held by it on every side. And the summit sets up the whole of intellect, intellectual multitude, and, as Socrates says, the blessed paths of the gods; but the arch only bounds the heavenly series, and supplies the gods with the way up to the heaven. For when the gods rise to the feast and the banquet, and are filled with intelligible goods, they go up to the arch beneath the heaven, and through it are raised to the heavenly circuit. So if you say that the arch perfects the gods and turns them back to the whole heaven and the place above the heaven, you will not stray from Plato's meaning. For the gods are fed by the intelligible, by the meadow and by the divine Forms that the place above the heaven holds; but they are filled with this food through the arch beneath the heaven. For through it they also share in the heavenly circuit. So they return through the arch, receive a vigorous thinking from the heavenly order, and are filled with intelligible goods from the place above the heaven. It is clear, then, that the place above the heaven has the intelligible summit, the circuit of the heaven the middle breadth, and the arch the intellectual extremity. For all things are in it. Intellect turns back, but the intelligible is what is desired. And divine thinking completes the middle, perfecting the returns of divine natures and binding them to the first, but unfolding their reachings toward the intelligibles, and filling second natures with the goods that come before them. I think, though, that through these things we have reminded the reader enough of the order of these three.

flags.taylor: the arch, the intelligible extremity
flags.why: Taylor prints "intelligible" here; the sense (the place above the heaven is the intelligible summit, the arch the extremity where intellect turns back) seems to want "intellectual", and the Workshop renders it so. This is a reading from the sense, not from the Greek.

notes: The Phaedrus 247a-b: "when they go to the feast and the banquet, they climb up to the arch beneath the heaven".

paragraphs.modern: Perhaps someone may ask us why we mark the whole procession of the intelligible and intellectual gods by its middle, and why we call one of the extremes "above the heaven" and the other "beneath the heaven", from their relation to the middle, pointing to the set-apart transcendence of the one and the close, joined lessening of the other. We may answer him briefly that this whole kind of intelligible and intellectual gods binds both extremes together, being the cause of return to the one, and to the other of being unfolded into light and being present to second natures. As we call all the intelligible gods fatherly and unitary, marking them from their summit, and say that they are the boundaries of the whole of things, those that make being, those that cause everlastingness, and those that are sources of the production of Forms; so we unfold these middle gods from the middle in them, as the leaders of all bonds. For this whole middle order gives life, holds together and perfects. Its summit unfolds the impressions of the intelligibles and their inexpressible union. Its end turns the intellectuals back and joins them to the intelligibles. And its middle gathers into itself and fixes, as in a centre, the whole kinds of the gods. For to the extremes too, by reference to the middle, we give the relation of transcendence and lessening, calling one above and the other beneath the middle.

Through these things, then, as I have said, we may answer briefly anyone who is puzzled about these names. But here we should admire Plato's divine science, because he has told of the way all things go up to the intelligible in keeping with the highest of the initiators. For first he raises souls, and the gods themselves, to the source gods through the free leaders. For the blessed and most abundant sights and paths are chiefly in these sources, in which the theurgists also place all their hope of salvation. They are blessed through the undefiled monads, most abundant through the cause of divine difference, and sights and paths through the intellectual and fatherly powers. Second, Plato raises souls and gods from the sources, and through the sources, to the leaders of perfection. For after many divided thinkings the good of the perfecting gods shines out, spread from above from the intellectual gods themselves, and lighting up us, and before our souls whole souls, and before these the gods themselves. From the perfecting gods Plato raises souls and gods to the gods who hold together all the intellectual orders. For the perfecting gods hang from these gods, exist together with them, and are held by them. So close is the communion and union of these gods that some of the most famous interpreters of Plato have supposed an all-perfect, undivided sameness among them, being unable to grasp by reasoning the separation in them. Here too it may seem to someone that Plato calls the extremity of the heavenly circuit the arch. But this is not so. For he does not call the arch heavenly, but beneath the heaven. As what is above the heaven is in its being set apart from the heaven, so what is beneath the heaven is lower than the kingdom of the heaven. For the first points to transcendence, the second to a lessening ranked next below.

flags.taylor: through the liberated leaders
flags.why: The "liberated" (apolytoi, "unbound") leaders are the twelve gods who lead in the Phaedrus, ranked by Proclus among the gods above the world; the "source" (fontal) gods are the intellectual gods, sources of the orders after them. The order of the ascent runs from the lowest of these orders upward.

notes: The "theurgists" are the Chaldean priests and their followers, for whom the soul is saved by rites that join it to the gods.

paragraphs.modern: After this circuit, which holds together the whole of things, Plato raises souls and the gods to the place above the heaven and the intelligible union of the intellectuals, where the gods, remaining, are fed, are in a happy state, and are filled with inexpressible and unitary goods. For with the theurgists too, the way up to the inexpressible and intelligible powers that are the summits of all intellectuals is through the gods who hold together. How the gods are here joined to the first intelligibles, though, Plato no longer unfolds in words; for the contact with them is inexpressible, and through what cannot be spoken, as he teaches in what he says of them in the Phaedrus. Through this order the mystic union with the intelligible and first-producing causes comes about. With us, then, the way of joining is the same; and through this the way of theurgic ascent is the more credible. For as wholes go up to the principles set apart from them through the natures placed next above them, so parts too, imitating the ascent of wholes, are joined through middle steps to the simplest and inexpressible causes. For what Plato has said in this dialogue about whole souls he afterwards unfolds about ours. First he joins them with the free gods; then through these he raises them to the perfecting gods; then through these to the gods who hold together; and in the same way up to the intelligible gods. Socrates, then, telling how we go up to intelligible beauty, and how, following the gods, before bodies and generation, we shared in that blessed sight, says: "For then it was lawful to see beauty shining, when with that happy choir we saw this blessed vision and sight, we following Zeus, others with some other god, and were initiated into the mysteries which it is right to call the most blessed of mysteries." How, then, were we once joined with intelligible beauty? Through being initiated, he says, into the most blessed of mysteries. What else does this say, than that we were joined with the perfecting leaders and initiated by them, so as to be filled with beauty? And what goods does the initiation bring? "Which rites we celebrated," he says, "when we were whole and untouched by evils, and were initiated into, and became watchers of, whole, simple, still and happy visions." The whole, then, comes to souls from the heavenly circuit. For this holds all the divine kinds together, and our souls too. Everything that holds parts in a whole also holds what is divided, and gathers what is many into union and simplicity. But the whole, still and simple visions are unfolded to souls from above, from the place above the heaven, through the gods who hold together. For the mystic impressions of the intelligibles shine out in that place, and the unknown and inexpressible beauty of their characters. For muesis and epopteia, being initiated and becoming a watcher, are symbols of inexpressible silence, and of union with mystic natures through intelligible visions. And most wonderful of all: as the theurgists order the whole body to be buried except the head in the most mystic of initiations, Plato too foresaw this, moved by the gods themselves. "For being pure," he says, "and freed from this garment around us, which we now call the body, we were initiated into and saw this most blessed sight, full of intelligible light." For the pure brightness he mentions unfolds intelligible light as a symbol. So when we are set in the intelligible we shall have a life wholly freed from the body. But raising the charioteer's head to the place beyond the heaven, we shall be filled with the mysteries there and with intelligible silence. It seems to me, too, that Plato unfolds well enough the three causes that lead up, love, truth and faith, to those who read him with care. For what but love joins us with beauty? Where is the plain of truth but in this place? And what but faith causes this inexpressible initiation? For initiation is not through thinking or judgement at all, but through the unitary silence that faith gives, which is better than every act of knowing, and which sets both whole souls and ours in the inexpressible and unknown nature of the gods. These things, though, have run to this length from my sympathy with such matters.

flags.taylor: muesis and epopteia
flags.why: The two grades of the Eleusinian mysteries: muēsis, initiation (from muein, to close the eyes), and epopteia, the final "watching". Taylor's footnote quotes Hermeias' commentary on the Phaedrus: in muesis the soul no longer takes in the divine mysteries by sense but with the pure soul itself, and in epopteia it is set in them and becomes their watcher.

flags.taylor: theurgists order the whole body to be buried, except the head
flags.why: A Chaldean rite of "immortalisation", known only from this passage and a few others: the initiate was buried to the neck, as if the body were already dead.

flags.taylor: elevating the head of the charioteer to the place beyond the heaven
flags.why: The Phaedrus 248a: the best souls "raise the head of the charioteer into the place outside".

notes: The Phaedrus 250b-c. Taylor's footnote supplies a word missing from the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Returning again to the theology we set out, let us unfold the ideas Plato points to about each order of the intelligible and intellectual gods. The place above the heaven, then, is intelligible. So Plato says it is being that truly is, and is seen by the intellect of the soul. It is also the one grasp and union of the intellectual gods. For it is not intelligible in the way the living being itself is, nor the first eternity, nor what is itself first the one being. For as these are first intelligibles, they are set apart from all other intelligibles and exist beforehand by themselves. But the place above the heaven is set next above the heavenly circuit and is its intelligible, yet it is not simply intelligible. That we say this rightly Socrates too bears witness, giving the thinking of this intelligible to souls too, through the heaven. For in this period, in which they are carried round with the circuit of the heaven, they see justice, they see temperance, they also see science, and each of the beings that truly and really are; so that if the place above the heaven is intelligible and real being, it is still intelligible as being above the heaven. The first intelligibles, though, are intelligible by their own being, and by the set-apart, first-producing cause of all intellectual natures. For the great Kronos too, though an intellectual god and the fullness of intellect, is intelligible in relation to the Craftsman; for he is the summit of the intellectual triad. So in this way the place above the heaven also has an intelligible transcendence over the heavenly circuit, and is intelligible as among the first intellectuals. So it also exists in answer to the first triad of intelligibles. That triad, though, was simply intelligible. For the intelligible among intelligibles exists at once before all second and third intelligibles. But the place above the heaven is not simply intelligible; for it is the summit of the intellectuals, not of the intelligibles. So Plato calls the first triad of intelligibles the one being, but names the place above the heaven being that truly is. The first goes before all beings in a wonderful simplicity and the hidden unity of being. For that being is the intelligible itself: not intelligible in one respect and intellectual in another, nor what is acted on by being, but the seat and most ancient monad of being. This order, the place above the heaven, falls short of the union of that triad: it shares in being, but is not simply being. So Plato calls it being, and being that truly is, as receiving this intelligible and being-like nature from what is first being. And the first triad of intelligibles was fatherly, for it exists by divine union and limit, and is the hidden and highest boundary of all intelligibles. But the place above the heaven is motherly, existing by the unlimited and the power of the unlimited. For this order is feminine and fertile, and produces all things by intelligible powers. So Plato calls it a place, as the receptacle of the fatherly causes, bringing forth and bringing out the generative powers of the gods into the existence of second natures. For having called matter too a place, he calls it the mother and nurse of the forming principles that proceed into it from being and the fatherly cause.
notes: The Phaedrus 247c-e. Timaeus 49a, 51a, 52a-d: the receptacle, "nurse" and "mother" of becoming, and "place" (chōra). Taylor's footnote corrects "intellectual as among the first intelligibles" to "intelligible as among the first intellectuals" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: By this analogy, then, Plato names the place above the heaven, as feminine, and as the cause in a motherly way of those things of which the intelligible father is the cause in a fatherly way. Matter, though, only receives Forms; but the mother and nurse of the gods not only receives but also sets up and generates second natures, together with the father. Nor does this generating goddess bring out her offspring from herself into a place outside and separate them from her own embrace, as things that generate here bring their offspring into the light outside themselves; she generates, holds and sets all things in herself. So she is also their place, as a seat that holds them on every side, and as, by her fertile and first-producing powers, taking beforehand into herself and holding all the processions, multitude and variety of second natures. For all beings exist in the gods and are held and kept safe by them. For where could they go away from the gods and from the embrace in them? And how, if they left them, could they remain even for the smallest part of time? But the powers that generate divine natures are in a special way said to hold their offspring, being their nearest causes, and setting up their being with fuller division and a more particular providence. For fatherly causes produce second natures in a one-like way, set apart and unranked with them, and hold their own offspring in a unitary way. In simplicity they take beforehand their variety, and in union their multitude. It is clear, then, from what has been said, that the place above the heaven is intelligible, and how it is intelligible. It is clear besides how it is feminine; for place fits the generating gods for the reasons given. And the meadow is the source of a life-giving nature, as will soon be shown. Socrates also takes all the divine natures in this place to be of this kind, feminine, I mean science itself, justice itself, temperance itself, truth itself, and Adrastia; which may be taken as a special sign that Plato, and not only the other theologians, gives the feminine to this order.

What, then, is the reason why Plato first praises this god by denials, in answer to the One? And what are the denials? He calls it without colour, without shape and without contact, and takes from it these three hyparxes, colour, shape and contact. I say, then, that this order, being the summit of the intellectual gods, is unknown and inexpressible in its own character, and is to be known only through intelligible impressions. For as the summit of the intellectuals it joins itself with the intelligibles. For how could intellectuals be joined with intelligibles unless they first set up an intelligible transcendence of their own? And what link and communion of the whole orders of things could be seen, unless the extremities of the first had a certain likeness to the beginnings of the second? Because of this likeness these grow together, and all things exist in one series. As the end of the intelligibles was intellectual, then, so the beginning of the intellectuals has an intelligible hyparxis. Each of these is intelligible; but the one is simply intelligible, and the other is not intelligible without the addition of the intellectual. These exist together with each other. The one is the fatherly cause of the whole of things, as intelligible, and the intellectual in it is spread out intelligibly. The other sets up the same things in a generating way, because it is intellectual and intelligible good rules in the intellectual kind. All things, then, come from both: in a set-apart way from the intellectual of the intelligibles, and in a ranked way from the intelligible of the intellectuals. Both delight in unknown hyparxes, and are known only, as Plato says, by intelligible, mystic and inexpressible impressions. So he calls it boldness to try to unfold the secrets about them and explain in words their unknown union.
notes: The Phaedrus 247c: "being without colour, without shape, without contact"; and "one must be bold enough to speak the truth".

paragraphs.modern: From the end of the intelligible order, though, the summit of the intellectuals has its unknown character. For as far as it joins itself to the first intelligibles and is filled with their unitary, inexpressible and fatherly hyparxis, so far it exists in an unknown way before the intellectuals. So it cannot be grasped by the natures after it, but is known by those before it, reaching up over itself into an unbroken union with them. It knows the natures before it intelligibly; but this does not differ at all from one-like and inexpressible knowledge. For intelligible knowledge is the union, cause, summit, and unknown and hidden hyparxis of all knowledge. Since, then, the one and united triad is, if we may say so, the intellectual image of the unknown union of the intelligibles, and rules over the same one-like and unknown power in the intellectuals as its own cause does, Plato unfolds it in a mystic way through denials. For everywhere the highest and the unknown answer to the unitary God. As we are taught to praise this God through denials, so we try to unfold the one-like and unknown summits of the second orders by denial. And in short, since Socrates in the Phaedrus makes the ascent as far as the place above the heaven, setting it, in this order and in the ascent of souls, in answer to the first, he praises it by denials. For in the Timaeus Plato holds that the one Craftsman, through whom every making kind of gods exists, is inexpressible and unknown; and everywhere the highest has this transcendence over second natures. For it imitates the cause that is at once set apart from all beings in a unitary way. We praise this cause through denials alone, as existing before all things; but we unfold the summits that proceed in answer to it by affirmation and denial at once. As sharing in the natures before them, we praise them by affirmation. For Plato calls the place above the heaven being that truly is, the plain of truth, the meadow, and the gods' intelligible look-out, and does not only call it without colour, without shape and without contact, so mixing affirmations with denials. For this order is a middle between the intelligible gods and the first intellectual divine orders, holding the bond of both. It keeps watch intellectually, by a one-like and unknown transcendence, but passes on the fullnesses of the intelligibles as far as the last of things. It raises all things at once, by one common union, up to the intelligible father, and generates and brings them out as far as matter. Set between the unitary and the multiplied gods, then, it is unfolded by denial, through the unknown way in which it goes beyond second natures, and by affirmation, through its sharing in the first natures. For the first Craftsman is called in the Timaeus maker and father and good, and all such names, so far as he shares in the causes that exist before him; but so far as he is the monad of all making, Plato leaves him unknown and inexpressible, set apart from all the makers of things. For he says, "it is hard to find him, and, having found him, impossible to declare him to all." So Plato unfolds the place above the heaven by affirmation, as filled from the first causes, calling it at one time being that truly is, at another the plain of truth, and at another something else of this kind; but so far as it goes beyond the intellectual gods, and so far as it is highest and unitary, he praises it by denial, as he does the principle set apart from all things.

flags.taylor: the one and united triad
flags.why: Proclus' name for the first of the intelligible and intellectual triads, the place above the heaven: one and "united" (hēnōmenē) as the image of the hidden union of the intelligibles.

notes: Timaeus 28c: "the maker and father of this universe it is hard to find, and having found him, impossible to declare to all". Taylor's footnotes correct a pronoun and supply "but" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Next, then, we should consider what the denials are, and from which orders they are generated. In the Parmenides, the denials of the One are produced from all the divine orders, because the One is the cause of all of them. Everything divine shares, by its own hyparxis, in the first principle; and the One, being beyond these, is far more set apart from the natures after them. For all things proceed from these, since they receive their characters in a divided way. This is clear from the other hypotheses, in which the same conclusions come round again, joined at one time by denial and at another by affirmation. For what could exist that was not first held as cause in wholes? But in the Phaedrus, the things denied of the intelligible summit of all intellectuals are the natures set next after this summit: the sacred kinds that hold together, that perfect, and the fatherly kinds of what are properly called intellectuals. For this summit, being set apart from these, also goes beyond all the intellectual gods. For what every kind of the gods is to the One, the three orders after this summit are to it. Plato, then, calls colour the heavenly order that holds wholes together and lights them up with intelligible light, because the visible beauty of this perceptible heaven too shines with colours of every kind, and with light. So he calls that heaven intellectual colour and light. For the light proceeding from the Good is, in the orders above the heaven, unknown and hidden, remaining in the inner sanctuaries of the gods; but in this order it shines out and from unseen becomes plain. So it is likened to colour, the offspring of light.

Further, if the heaven is sight looking at the things above, its intelligible may very fitly be called colour, which is joined with sight. The cause of the intelligibles in the heaven, then, is without colour, but set apart from them; for perceptible colour is the offspring of the sun's light. Plato calls figure the order that comes next after the heavenly order, which we have called the arch beneath the heaven. For "arch" is itself the name of a shape. And in this order, in short, Parmenides too sets intellectual shape. But Plato first gives contact to the summit of the intellectuals, as is clear from the conclusions of the Parmenides. For in the first hypothesis, taking shape away from the One, he uses this as a middle term, that the One does not touch itself. "But the one," he says, "does not touch itself." And the conclusion is plain. Here, then, contact first exists, and exists as cause. For of those things of which the Craftsman is the nearest cause, the father before him is the cause as pattern. In this order, then, contact is the pattern of the free gods. So these three orders follow one another: colour, shape and contact. And from these the place above the heaven is set apart in its being. So it is without colour, without shape and without contact. Nor does it go beyond these three by lacking them, but by the excellence of a cause. For it gives colour a share of light from the intelligibles; on shape it lights up intellectual limit; and into contact it puts, from above, union and continuity, and perfects all things by its power: what is touched through union, what is shaped through sharing in limit, and what is coloured through the lighting-up of light. And it draws upward and lures to itself everything in an inexpressible way and through intelligible impressions, and fills everything with unitary goods.

flags.taylor: But the one,” says he, “does not touch itself
flags.why: The Parmenides 138a: the One is "neither in itself nor in another", so it neither touches itself nor anything else; Proclus takes the denial of contact as one of those that come from a definite order of gods. Here "the one" is Parmenides' one.

paragraphs.modern: If we say these things rightly, then, we must not accept the reading of those who busy themselves with perceptible colours, contacts and shapes, and say that the place above the heaven is set apart from these. For these are trifles, and do not fit that place at all. For even nature, not only nature as a whole but partial nature too, is set apart from perceptible colours, visible shapes and bodily contact. What, then, is so venerable in this, if it belongs even to natures? But we must stretch colours, shapes and contacts from on high down to the last of things, and show that the place above the heaven is set apart from all of these alike. For soul and intellect too share in shape; and contact is often among bodiless natures, by the communion of first with second beings, and it is usual to call these communions contacts, and to call the touchings of intellectual thoughts graspings. We should not, then, be carried from the first things to the last, or compare the highest order of the intellectuals with the last of beings, above which both soul and nature are set. For in doing so we shall go wrong, and not attend to Plato, who cries out that it is boldness to say these things about it. For where is the boldness, and what the unknown power beyond our thoughts, in contemplating the truth about perceptible colours, shapes and contacts? Such an existence is known by natural philosophers, not by the sons of the theologians. Such, then, is the power of the denials through which Plato praises the place above the heaven.

flags.taylor: known by physiologists
flags.why: Taylor's "physiologists" are the natural philosophers (physiologoi), the students of nature, as against the theologians.

paragraphs.modern: Again, then, let us next look at the affirmations, and how they exist by sharing in the first intelligibles themselves. The place above the heaven is said to be being that truly is, because it shares in what is first being. For to be, and truly to be, belong to all things as the offspring of intelligible being. For as the one comes from the first principle, which is before the intelligibles, so the nature of being comes from the intelligibles. For the one being exists there, as Parmenides taught us a little before. But the place above the heaven is seen by the pilot of the soul, because it has an intelligible transcendence over the other intellectual gods. So its intelligible good is made plain by its being known by intellect. This intelligible, then, like what truly is, comes to it from the unitary gods. For they are first, unshared intelligibles, and the first producing causes of all intelligibles. These two also go together, what truly is and the intelligible. For every intelligible truly is, and everything that truly is is intelligible. For intellect is intelligible by the being in it, but by its power of knowing it is intellect. So every intellect supplies knowledge, and every intelligible supplies being. For what each is first, it lights up on the orders after it.

Third, then, the kind of true science is said to be set about the place above the heaven. For two things go up to the contemplation of that being: intellect, the pilot of the soul (this is a partial intellect, set above souls, and raising them to their fatherly harbour), and true science, which is the perfection of the soul. Science acts about that place, going round in harmonious measures about being step by step; but intellect contemplates it with simple thinking. Further, the science in us is one thing, and that in the place above the heaven another. The first is true, the second is truth itself. What, then, is it, and where does it come from? It is a goddess who is the source of all intellectual knowledge, and the first cause of undefiled and steady thinking. But it shines out in the first triad of the intellectuals, because this perfects all other things, and divine souls too. For they, going up to this one-like power of all knowledge, perfect their own knowledge. For each of the undefiled souls, Socrates says, going round with Zeus and the heaven, sees justice, temperance and science. So these three sources are there, being intelligible goddesses and the sources of the intellectual virtues, and not, as some think, intellectual Forms. For Plato usually marks the Forms by the word "itself", as "science itself" and "justice itself", as Socrates says somewhere in the Phaedo. But here, when he says justice herself, temperance herself and science herself, he seems to unfold to us certain self-perfect and intelligible goddesses who exist as a triad. Of these, science is the monad, temperance has the second rank, and justice the third. Science supplies undefiled, firm and unchanging thinking; temperance gives all the gods the cause of their return to themselves; and justice gives them the cause of distributing the whole of good as each deserves. Through science each of the gods thinks the natures before him and is filled with intelligible thinking; through temperance he turns back to himself, and enjoys a second union and a good that goes with the return to himself; and through justice he rules the natures after him, "on a silent path", as they say, measures what they deserve, and gives each its fitting share. These three sources, then, hold all the activities of the gods. Science proceeds in answer to the first triad of intelligibles; and as that triad gives being to all things, so this lights up the gods with knowledge. Temperance proceeds in answer to the second triad of intelligibles. For temperance imitates the holding-together and measuring power of that triad, since it measures the activities of the gods and turns each of them back to itself. And justice proceeds in answer to the third triad of intelligibles. For it too separates second natures by what each deserves, as that triad separates them intelligibly by the first patterns.

flags.taylor: elevating them to their paternal port
flags.why: "The fatherly harbour" (patrikos hormos) is a Chaldean phrase for the soul's home in the intelligible, to which it returns.

flags.taylor: in a silent path, as they say
flags.why: Euripides, Trojan Women 887-888: justice "leads all mortal things aright, going on a noiseless path".

notes: The Phaedrus 247d-e. Taylor's footnotes correct "union" to "thinking" twice and restore "as each deserves, as that triad" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: After these things, then, we may look at another triad that exists beforehand in this place, which Socrates also praises: the plain of truth, the meadow, and the food of the gods. The plain of truth is spread out intellectually to intelligible light, and shines with the lights that proceed from there. For as the One sends out intelligible light, so the intelligible gives second natures a share that produces being. The meadow is the fertile power of life and of forming principles of every kind, the grasp of the first causes of life, and the cause of the variety and generation of Forms. For the meadows here too produce forms and forming principles of every kind, and bear water, the symbol of life-giving. And the cause that nourishes the gods is a certain intelligible union, holding in itself the whole perfection of the gods, and filling them with vigour and power, so that they may care providently for second natures, and have an unchanging intellectual thinking of the natures that are first. Above, though, the gods share in these in a one-like way, but in their processions in a divided way.
notes: The Phaedrus 248b-c: "the plain of truth", and "the fitting pasture for the best part of the soul comes from the meadow there".

paragraphs.modern: As to the food, Plato calls one kind ambrosia and the other nectar. "For the charioteer," he says, "stopping the horses at the manger, puts ambrosia before them, and after it gives them nectar to drink." The charioteer, then, being fed with intelligibles, shares in a unitary way in the perfection lit up by the gods; but the horses share in it in a divided way, first in ambrosia, and afterwards in nectar. For from ambrosia they must remain steadily and without straying in the higher natures; but through nectar they must provide unchangingly for second natures. For they say ambrosia is solid food and nectar liquid, which Plato too points to when he says that the charioteer puts ambrosia before the horses and afterwards gives them nectar to drink. So the food of nectar shows the unconstrained and unbreakable nature of providence, and its going to all things without defilement; and the food of ambrosia shows stability and a firm seat in the higher natures. From both it is clear that the gods both remain and proceed to all things, and that neither is their unstraying nature, which does not turn toward lower beings, barren, nor is their fertile power and procession unstable; but remaining they proceed, and, set in the gods before them, they provide for second natures without being stained. Nectar and ambrosia, then, are the perfections of the gods so far as they are gods; other things are the perfections of intellect, nature and bodies. So Plato, having taken these into souls, calls the souls nourished with them gods. For so far as they too share in the gods, so far they are filled with nectar and ambrosia. In their processions, though, these are divided in two: one supplies the gods with stable and firm perfection, the other with unstraying providence, free governance, and an ungrudging, abundant giving of good, by the two principles of the whole of things that rule over such a distribution. For we must grant that ambrosia answers to limit and nectar to the unlimited. So nectar is as if moist, and not bounded from itself, and ambrosia as if solid, and having a boundary from itself. Nectar, then, is fertile, perfects the gods' secondary presence, and is the cause of power, of a vigour that provides for the whole of things, and of an unlimited and unfailing supply. Ambrosia is stable perfection, like limit, the cause to the gods of their being set in themselves, and the giver of firm and unstraying thinking. Before both, though, is the one source of perfection and seat of all the gods, which Plato calls food, and the feast and the banquet, as perfecting in a unitary way the divided multitude of the gods, and turning all things back to itself through divine thinking. For dais, "feast", shows the divided distribution of divine food, and thoinē, "banquet", the united return of the whole of things to it. For it is the thinking of the gods so far as they are gods. But the food holds both these powers together, being the fullness of intelligible goods and the one-like perfection of divine self-sufficiency.

flags.taylor: the one is as it were humid, and not bounded from itself; but the other is as it were solid
flags.why: Here "the one" is nectar and "the other" ambrosia, though ambrosia was named first in the sentence before; the next sentences show it. The modern version names them.

notes: The Phaedrus 247e; 247a ("to the feast and the banquet").

paragraphs.modern: Enough, then, about these things for the present study. Next we should discuss the division of the place above the heaven into three. For the intelligible summit of the intellectuals is, as we observed before, a triad. Right at the first idea of this place, then, Plato unfolds its threefold nature, taking three denials: without colour, without shape, and untouchable. Having also set three goddesses in it, science, temperance and justice, our teacher and leader, Syrianus, thinks right to divide this triad into three monads, and shows this in keeping with the Orphic theologies. But if we must find the definite characters of these three goddesses from what has already been laid down, we must understand that the plain of truth, the meadow, and the cause that nourishes the gods are set there. To nourish, then, belongs to intelligible perfection. So the soul's wing is given its upward drive, and intellectual perfection too, by the food that flows from there into the soul. The character of the meadow is to have a power that generates forming principles and Forms, and the causes of the production of living beings. So souls too graze about the meadow; and pasture (nomē) is food, but in a divided way.
notes: Taylor's footnote corrects "image" to "causes" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: The plain of truth, though, is the spreading-out and showing of intelligible light, the unfolding of inner forming principles, and perfection going out everywhere. This, then, is the character of the third monad. Fertility is the character of the second, and intelligible fullness of the first. For the whole place above the heaven is lit up with the light of truth; so all the natures in it are called true. And Socrates says "that whatever soul, following a god, has seen any of the things that truly are, shall be free from harm until the next circuit." For everything in that place is truly being and intelligible, and full of divine union. In the first monads, though, this intelligible light exists gathered in, and set as if hidden in the inner sanctuary; but in the third monad it shines out, spread out together and divided together with the multitude of powers. From these things, then, we may see the differences of the three monads in keeping with Plato's hypotheses. And if science belongs to the first monad, temperance to the second, and justice to the third, the triad will be wholly plain from these too. Does not science, which is steady, the one-like thinking of wholes, and existing together with intelligibles, belong to the power that is united to the intelligible father, and neither proceeds nor separates its union from the godhead of that father? Does not the kind of justice belong to the power that divides, separates the intellectual kinds, leads intelligible multitude into order, and lights up a distribution by desert? And does not the kind of temperance belong to the power that is the middle of both, turns back to itself, and holds the common bond of this triad? For the harmonious, and a communion with the extremes by reason, are the shining good of this middle power.

flags.taylor: In the first monads however [i.e. in the plain of truth and the meadow,] this intelligible light subsists contractedly
flags.why: Taylor's brackets take "the first monads" as the plain of truth and the meadow, and "the third" as the cause that nourishes the gods. The sentence before says the opposite (the plain of truth is the third monad); Proclus means the first two monads, food and meadow, with the light shining out in the third, the plain of truth.

notes: The Phaedrus 248c. Taylor's footnote explains "perfection going out everywhere".

paragraphs.modern: Not to be long, then, since what has been said is enough to remind us of Plato's meaning: we praise these three goddesses who divide the place above the heaven. All of them are intelligible as among intellectuals; they are summits, and gather all things into one intelligible union. But one does so steadily, another generatively, and another by turning back, having a power that first produces among the intellectuals. For one unites the monads of all the gods and gathers them about the intelligible; another does this about the processions of the gods; and another about their returns. All of them together, though, gather into one the whole of a hyparxis that always remains, proceeds and returns. So Plato also raises the gods distributed in the world to this one place, and turns them back, acting about it, as about what gathers the whole orders of the gods into sharing in the intelligibles. These monads, then, lead out intelligible Forms, fill them with a share in divine union, and call back the natures that have proceeded and join them to the intelligibles. About this whole triad, though, what has been said may be enough.

It remains, then, to pass to the discussion of Adrastia, since Socrates points out that she holds her kingdom in this place. For what sets the measures of a blameless life for souls, from the vision of these intelligible goods, surely has its first unfolding into light there. For the cause that leads up, being second to the objects of desire, can raise both itself and other things to the place above the heaven by turning back. But what sets and measures for souls the fruits of the vision of the intelligible, since it has its hyparxis in the intelligible, lights up blessedness for them from there. It is set, then, as I have said, in that place. But it rules all the divine laws in a one-like way, from on high down to the last of things. It binds to its own one ordinance all the ordinances: those of intellect, those above the world, and those of the world. Whether, then, there are laws of Kronos, as Socrates in the Gorgias says there are, when he says, "This law, then, which was in the time of Kronos, is still now among the gods"; or laws of Zeus, as the Athenian Stranger says, when he says, "But justice follows Zeus, avenger of those who leave the divine law"; or laws of fate, as Timaeus teaches, when he says, "that the Craftsman declared to souls the laws of fate"; of all these the ordinance of Adrastia holds them together by one intelligible simplicity, and at the same time gives them all existence and the measures of their power. And if I must give my own opinion, the inescapable guarding power of this triad, and the unchangeable embrace of order that runs everywhere, exist beforehand in this goddess. For these three goddesses not only unfold and gather all things but are also guardians, according to the Oracle, of the works of the father and of one intelligible intellect.

flags.taylor: the sacred law of Adrastia
flags.why: Taylor's "sacred law" is thesmos, "ordinance", as against nomos, "law". Adrastia ("she whom none escapes") was in the Orphic poems the nurse and guardian of the infant Zeus.

notes: The Phaedrus 248c; the Gorgias 523a; the Laws IV 716a; Timaeus 41e.

paragraphs.modern: This guarding power, then, the ordinance of Adrastia points to, which nothing can escape. For as to the laws of fate, not only the gods are above them, but partial souls too, when they live by intellect and give themselves up to the light of providence. The gods of Kronos are, in their being, set apart from the laws of Zeus, and the gods who hold together and who perfect from the laws of Kronos; but all things obey the ordinance of Adrastia, and all the distributions of the gods, all measures and all guardianships exist because of it. In Orpheus she is said to guard the Craftsman of the universe, and, taking bronze drumsticks and a drum of goatskin, to make so loud a sound that she turns all the gods to herself. And Socrates, imitating this mythical sound, which sends a kind of proclamation to all things, likewise brings out the ordinance of Adrastia to all souls. For he says, "This is the ordinance of Adrastia: that whatever soul has seen anything of the truth shall be free from harm until another circuit," all but voicing the Orphic sound in this proclamation, and saying it as a hymn to Adrastia. For first, he calls it thesmos, an ordinance, and not nomos, a law, as he does the laws of Kronos and of Zeus. For thesmos goes with godhead and belongs more to the intelligibles than to the intellectuals; but nomos, pointing to intellectual distribution, fits the intellectual fathers. Second, he speaks of it in the singular, not the plural, as Timaeus does of the laws of fate. Third, he extends it to all the kinds of souls, and shows that it is the common measure of their happy and blessed life, and the true guard of the souls that can remain on high free of all being acted upon. For such is the meaning of the words, "and if it can always do this, it shall always be free from harm". This ordinance, then, holds all the undefiled life of divine souls, and the temporary blessedness of partial souls. The first it guards intelligibly, and the second it measures by the vision of intelligible goods. And so much about Adrastia.

flags.taylor: receiving brazen drumsticks, and a drum made from the skin of a goat
flags.why: Orphic fragment (Kern 105, 152): Adrastia stood before the cave of Night and beat a bronze drum, so that the gods heard her laws. Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated ("a kind of proclamation").

notes: The Phaedrus 248c.

paragraphs.modern: For what remains, then, we shall say in sum that the place above the heaven is the first triad of the intelligible and intellectual gods, with three characters: unfolding into light, gathering, and guarding. It holds all these intelligibly and in an unknown way: joining intellectuals to intelligibles, calling out the fertile powers of the intelligibles, receiving into itself the fullness of the Forms from the intelligible patterns, and bringing out its own meadow from the summit of the source there. From the one intellect it gives existence to the three virtues, perfects the whole of itself with intelligible impressions, and receives in its inexpressible bosom the whole of intelligible light. At one and the same time it remains in the hidden nature of the intelligible gods and proceeds intelligibly from there, shines out to the view of the intellectuals, and turns back and draws up by inexpressible powers all the images of its own union that it has sown in everything. To this place too we must go up in a mystic way, leaving on earth all the life that brings generation, and the bodily nature with which, coming here, we were surrounded as by a wall, and waking only the summit of the soul to share in the whole of truth and the fullness of intelligible food.

flags.taylor: producing its own meadow from the fontal summit which is there
flags.why: Proclus means the source of life in the second intelligible triad (eternity), from which the meadow, the life-giving power of this place, is drawn.

paragraphs.modern: After this intelligible and unknown triad, which rules over all the intellectual kinds, let us look at the triad that holds their bond together, intelligibly and intellectually at once. For before intellect and the intellectual gods the cause of holding together must be in these gods; and, set in the middle of the intelligible and intellectual order, it must reach all the divine multitudes, all the kinds of beings, and all the divisions of the world. For what is it that first holds things together? If, as some say, it is the nature of breath and local motion, body itself, which holds other things together, will need holding together. For every body, by its own composition, can be scattered and divided; as the Stranger from Elea too points out to those who make bodily principles, saying that the being they praise so much is broken up and scattered. Body, then, is not fitted by nature to hold other things together; and even if a power of this kind belonged to bodies, breath could not give it to us, since it is always flowing away and scattered, and spreading beyond what bounds it. But if we suppose that the states and holding forms divided about bodies light up what underlies them with holding-together, they must surely do so by being present to them; but how will these states and forms hold themselves together? It is hard to see how this could be done. For being distributed about masses of matter and divided along with what underlies them, they need a boundary and a holding-together. But they are not fitted by nature to be bounded or held together by themselves, since they do not have a self-begotten and self-existent being. What neither produces nor perfects itself cannot hold itself together. Moreover, every state and every material form is moved by another, and depends on another, more ancient cause; and so it cannot be separated from what underlies it, being unable to turn to itself.

flags.taylor: the nature of spirit and local motion
flags.why: The Stoics held that pneuma ("breath", Taylor's "spirit"), a fiery air pervading bodies, holds them together by its "tensile motion". Taylor's footnote corrects "intelligibles" to "intellectuals" in the Greek he translated.

notes: The Sophist 246b-c: the giants' "bodies", which their opponents break into small pieces.

paragraphs.modern: But if, leaving these, we should say that souls, which are bodiless and self-begotten, are the first causes of holding-together, where shall we place the divisible and at the same time undivided nature of souls, mixed from the divisible and the undivided, sharing in the kinds of being, and divided into harmonious forming principles? For souls hold bodies and natures together, because they share in an undivided character; but they need another holding nature, which may give the first principle of mixture to the kinds, and of holding-together to the divided forming principles. For the self-moving nature of souls, passing step by step and spread out in time, needs what may hold its one life together and make it whole and undivided. For the whole that holds parts together exists before the parts, since the whole made of parts receives its holding-together brought in from something other than itself. But if, going with reasoning beyond souls, we look at intellect, whether the intellect that is shared or, if you like, the unshared and divine one, and in short if we look at once at the intellectual kind of gods, and if this first holds beings together, we shall find in it too an all-various multitude, divisions of kinds, and, as Socrates says, "many blessed sights and paths". For the separation of divine natures and the variety of Forms appear among the intellectuals, and so do the mythical cuttings and generating powers. How, then, can what holds together be first here, where the dividing kind shines out? And how could intellectual multitude not refer its share of holding-together to another, more ancient cause? For intellectual multitude is what is first held together (since it is what is first divided, and what needs holding together is divisible, while the undivided itself is beyond the holding hyparxis); but it is not what first holds together. For everything held together is held together by another thing that first has the power of holding-together. It is clear, then, from what has been said, that the holding order of beings is set before the intellectual gods.

flags.taylor: fabulous sections
flags.why: The mythical "cuttings", the castration of Ouranos by Kronos and of Kronos by Zeus in Hesiod and the Orphic poems, which Proclus reads as the separation of the intellectual orders.

flags.taylor: discussive energies
flags.why: The Phaedrus' diexodoi again (247a), the "paths" of the gods (see IV.4).

paragraphs.modern: The intelligible and hidden hyparxis supplies union to all things, as existing next after the One, and being undivided and one-like. But holding-together is the drawing of multitude into undivided communion; so it exists as second to the intelligibles. For the middle there was intelligible, and the united cause that first produces holding-together. But the holding-together of the intelligible and intellectual gods imitates the unifying power of the intelligibles. For there the three threefold monads were the unions of wholes: one by transcendence, another by the middle centre, and another by return. But in the intelligible and intellectual orders these three triads are second after those unions, and grow together with multitude. So one of these triads gathers, another holds multitude together, and another is of a perfecting nature. For what is gathered, held together and perfected is multitude. Whether it is intellectual, or above the world, or of the world, or any other multitude, then, it is gathered, held together and perfected through these three triads. When gathered, it is raised to the union of the intelligibles and firmly set in them. When held together, it remains undivided and unscattered in its offspring. And when perfected, it receives its completion from its own parts or powers.
notes: Taylor's footnote corrects "holding" to "held together" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: But since beings, remaining, proceeding and returning, must enjoy this threefold providence, there are three gathering monads existing beforehand, three that hold together, and three that perfect. And we do not say that the first natures are divided so, and rule over so many orders and powers, for the sake of the good of second natures; they are always the first causes of good to the lower things, while we go back from the lower natures to the causes of wholes. The intelligible and intellectual triads, then, perfect things in a threefold way, and always hold them together and gather them into union. But the intelligible monads generate their remainings, processions and returns without separation and in a unitary way. About other things, though, we have partly spoken and shall partly speak again.

Let us speak now, then, about the triad that holds together. This Socrates, in the Phaedrus, calls the circuit of the heaven. Because it has the middle centre of unshared life, and is what is most alive of life itself, he calls it a circuit, as holding all other lives and divine thinkings round about on every side. Because of this, souls raised to it are perfected in their thinking and joined with intelligible sights. The circuit of the heaven, though, is always the same; for it is an eternal, whole, one and united thinking. But the circuit of souls comes about through time, is more partial, and is not a grasp of the intelligibles gathered all at once. So souls are carried round in a circle and come back to where they started, while the heavenly circuit always remains the same. But because it completes the bond of the intelligible and intellectual gods, and holds together all the orders in their remaining, procession and return, Socrates calls it heavenly. For Timaeus says that this perceptible heaven too presses together on every side the elements beneath it, so that no room is left for a void. As the visible heaven, then, holds together all things beneath it, and is the cause of their continuity, coherence and sympathy (for a void coming between would break the continuity of things, and the overturning of this continuity would destroy the sympathy of bodies), so that intellectual heaven binds all the multitudes of beings into an undivided communion, lighting up each with its fitting portion of holding-together. For intellect shares in the holding cause in one way, the nature of soul in another, and bodily being in another. Through the highest share of holding-together intellect is undivided; through second measures of sharing, soul is divisible and undivided by one mixture; and through a last lessening, bodies, which have a divisible existence, still remain held together, and do not perish by being scattered, but enjoy their own division and weakness. The whole triad that holds together, then, is called heaven by its own hyparxes; but the breadth of life spread beneath it is called circuit. For among visible things the revolution of the heavens is motion, and as it were the life of body.
notes: Timaeus 58a: "the circuit of the whole ... presses together and leaves no empty place".

paragraphs.modern: But if we must find its threefold nature from what has been laid down, we must use the way of analogy. Since Plato himself calls the back of the heaven one thing and its depth another, it is clear that the heavenly arch is the third; for the arch beneath this he plainly calls "beneath the heaven". And as we say that the place above the heaven is set above the back of the heaven, so we must grant that the arch beneath the heaven is different from the heavenly arch. For the heaven is bounded above by the back, and below by the arch. It is held by the place above the heaven, and holds the arch beneath the heaven. It is clear from these things, then, that the heaven shows itself as a triad: by its back holding all things together in one simplicity; by its arch bounding the whole triad; and by its depth proceeding into itself, and setting up the middle breadth of holding-together and coherence. The back of the whole heavenly order is an intelligible god, perhaps getting this name from that. But it is intelligible as in the triad that holds together, pressing from outside and holding together all the kingdom of the heaven. It lights up all the gods with a one-like and simple grasp of second natures, and is filled from above with intelligible union. So too divine souls, led through all the heavenly depth, stand on the back of the heaven, and the circuit carries them round as they stand; and so they look at what is called the place above the heaven. Their standing, then, is the setting of souls in the intelligible watch-tower of the heaven, giving souls sameness, undefiled power and unstraying thinking. The carrying round is the sharing in a life full of vigour and the keenest activity. And the presence of both together holds the fertile activity, the quiet motion and the steady thinking of the intelligibles. The heavenly depth is the one continuity of the whole triad, and the middle god who joins the whole heavenly order, proceeding from the intelligible grasp but ending in the heavenly arch, which sets the boundary of the whole heaven.
