There is, then, one union and holding-together of all this triad, and an unbroken procession from the back to the arch, through this middle god, who grows together with both extremes, unfolding the multitude that holds together but bounded on each side by the extremes, one holding it from above and the other bounding its procession from below.
notes: The Phaedrus 247b-c. Taylor's footnote corrects "of wholes" to "the whole" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: The heavenly arch, then, remains, which is the lower boundary of the triad; so too is the intellect in it, filled by life but united by the intelligible, and turning the whole triad back to its principle. For the arch too is like the back of the heaven, though less in extent. By being beneath, then, it is lessened; but by likeness it turns back to the heavenly summit. And this is the heavenly intellect, the nearest sunocheus, holder-together, of the arch beneath the heaven. So each arch is called the intellectual boundary of the intelligible and intellectual gods. The whole triad that holds together, then, is divided like this: the back (nōton) by the intelligible (noēton), the depth by life, and the arch by intellect. But the whole of it is one and continuous, because what holds all other things together should much more hold itself together. For each character of the gods begins its activity from itself: the gathering character fixes itself in a gathered way in the highest union; what turns wholes back turns itself back to its principle; and the undefiled keeps itself pure of matter before other things. So the character that holds together also, before what shares in it, holds itself together intelligibly and intellectually; and through this holding-together the nature of the heaven is said to be one and continuous. For the whole triad converges on itself, and keeps its own wholeness united and most like itself by nature. The arch holds all the intellectuals together most nearly, and presses them on every side. But before this the heavenly depth itself, which also holds the arch, binds together the whole orders. And before these the heavenly back, in a one-like way, holds by one sweep of simplicity the whole heavenly kingdom itself and all things beneath it, and binds them to itself by its holding power and hyparxis. For among visible things too the concave circumference of the heavens presses the elements most nearly, and does not let them scatter and blow away in their unbounded motions on every side. Before these, the heavenly mass presses all things hard and drives them to the middle, leaving no empty place. But there is one embrace of all these, the back of the heavens, which is the cause of likeness to the heavens, and to the elements of contact with the heavens. For the smooth and even nature of the back of the heavens, as Timaeus says, makes the whole heaven like itself; and always the natures that embrace hold together the natures embraced. From visible things, then, we must carry the likeness over to the father of the intellectual gods, Ouranos, and see how he is both one and three: above and below having the intelligible and intellect, and in the middle having life, which, as the cause of processions, intervals and generating powers, we have rightly set, by interval, under the heavenly depth; since Plato too calls the summit the back. "For those called immortals," he says, "when they go beyond and reach the top, stand on the back of the heaven." He calls the summit of the heavenly order, and "beyond", the back of the heaven; and these are in a remarkable way the privileges of the first of the Synocheis. For, holding all things together in the one summit of his hyparxis, according to the Oracle, he exists wholly "beyond", and is united to the place above the heaven and to its inexpressible power, closed in by it on every side, and shutting himself in the one-like grasp of the intelligibles. For what difference is there between saying that the first of the Synocheis is shut in the intelligible look-out, and showing that he is held most nearly by the place above the heaven, which was intelligible but spread out among the intellectuals? If what is "beyond" is the first, the summit is plainly ranked with the rest and set apart from them. But if the first is of this kind, set at the intelligible summit and lighting up the other gods with contact with the intelligible and the fatherly harbour, there must be a middle and an extremity: the first by the heavenly depth, the second by the boundary of the whole circuit. And if the circuit of the whole heaven is one and continuous, the character of this order must be given as the cause of this. For holding together the whole orders of the gods, and before other things itself, and being as it were the centre and bond of the divine kinds, it first binds and holds itself together and stretches itself to one life. The heaven, then, is one and at the same time three, and proceeds into three monads, both unseen and seen and what is between them, imitating the intelligible gods who settle into intelligible triads.

flags.taylor: the proximate sunocheus of the subcelestial arch
flags.why: Sunocheus is "holder-together", one of the Synocheis, the Chaldean name for the gods of this order. Taylor's footnotes explain the word, correct a gender to agree with "arch", and gloss "interval" as the heavenly depth.

flags.taylor: the back (το νωτον) according to the intelligible (κατα το νοητον)
flags.why: A play on words in the Greek: nōton (back) and noēton (intelligible) differ by one letter.

notes: The Phaedrus 247b-c ("they go outside and stand on the back of the heaven"); Timaeus 34b ("smooth and even"). The Chaldean Oracles speak of a god who "holds all things together in one summit, being himself wholly beyond".

paragraphs.modern: If you are willing to see the character of this order from what is written in the Cratylus, first take this as an argument that the Synocheus is set in the middle: a twofold relation of it is given, one toward the intelligibles and the other toward the intellectuals. For it is said to see the things above and to generate a pure intellect. So it is the thinking of intelligibles, and the intelligible of intellectuals. For the cause of intellect exists before an intellectual cause; and what is both at once most of all completes the middle order of intelligibles and intellectuals. For the gathering god, thinking the intelligibles, or rather united to them, does not first give existence to a divine intellect. And the perfecting god, producing intellectuals together with the middle god, most nearly thinks the heavenly order, not the intelligibles before the heaven. But the middle god alone, holding the intelligible and intellectual centre, reaches equally to both; thinking the intelligibles intellectually, it is the cause of the intellectuals intelligibly. But since the relation to its causes comes before its power of generating intellectuals, Socrates, starting from this relation, gives also a second power as hanging from it. Sight turned to the things above is very fitly given the name heavenly (ourania), as seeing the things above (horōsa ta anō). This, then, perfectly defines for us a relation more ancient than the order that holds together, taking it as intellectual in relation to the intelligibles and as sight in relation to what is seen, though it thinks itself and is intelligible in itself. But its intelligible, in relation to what is first intelligible, has an intellectual rank. What follows, though, unfolds the relation of this middle to the intellectuals. For Socrates adds: "Hence also, Hermogenes, those who study things on high say that Ouranos generates a pure intellect, and that the name is rightly given." The order of Ouranos, then, is spread as a middle in the middle, intelligible and intellectual gods, holding the intelligible and intellectual at once in one undivided holding-together, standing alike toward each, and equally distant from the first intellectuals and the unitary intelligibles. So it is said to think the things above and so to produce a pure intellect.
notes: The Cratylus 396b-c. Taylor's footnote corrects "powers" to "power" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Taking this, then, first from what has been laid down, we should next note this: the heavenly order being threefold, and the whole of it thinking intelligibles and producing intellectuals, the first monad thinks intelligibles in a special way. For it mingles itself with intelligibles, knows intelligible intellect, is united to the natures before it, and is undivided as among undivided things, reaching up over itself toward intelligible simplicity. The third monad most of all generates intellectuals, since it is the intellect of the whole triad that holds together. And with the Orphic theologians too, Ouranos, father of Kronos, is the third. The middle monad produces the intellectual order of the gods together with the third, but is joined, together with the first, to the intelligibles, and is filled with intelligible union from the first, and fills the third with fertile powers. Do you not see, then, how Plato, through the character of the extremes, unfolds to us the whole heavenly order? He joins its intelligible hyparxis to the intelligibles, its intellectual hyparxis to the intellectuals, and gives us the means of gathering its hyparxis that is the middle of both and proceeds by a common character. For if you also wish to take this from what has been said, the heavenly light is joined to the light of the intelligibles; for sight is nothing else than light. The middle order, then, by its own light and its divine summit, is joined to the first natures; but by an intellectual nature, and the boundary of the whole triad, it generates intellect, and all the undefiled godhead of the intellectuals. For it does not produce intellect alone, but together with purity. For Socrates himself says: "Hence they say that a pure intellect is generated from it." So the heavenly order is the first cause of the intellectual hyparxis and of undefiled power. But if purity must not be in intellect by accident, it is the godhead of beings set apart from second natures, and the giver of unchangeable power; and the great Ouranos, producing it together with intellect, is at the same time the cause of the gods who are the sources of purity and of the intellectual fathers. These signs, then, of the truth about the gods who hold together may also be taken from the Cratylus.

flags.taylor: Heaven the father of Saturn is the third
flags.why: In the Orphic theogony there are three kings before Kronos (Phanes, Night, Ouranos); Ouranos is the third. Taylor's footnote corrects "first" to "third" in the Greek he translated.

flags.taylor: the Gods who are the sources of purity
flags.why: The "undefiled" (amiantoi) gods, the Kouretes who guard the intellectual fathers, which Proclus discusses in Book V.

paragraphs.modern: It remains, then, following what is written in the Phaedrus, to look at the arch beneath the heaven and the character of the gods there. Before we begin the teaching about it, though, I want to say this first: that some of the most famous interpreters before us, taking this arch beneath the heaven as a divine order ranked under the heaven, have thought fit to rank it right after the first God, calling the first God Ouranos. Others have set both the heaven and the arch beneath the heaven in the breadth of the intelligibles. For the philosopher from Asine, Theodorus, persuaded by Plotinus, calls what proceeds next from the inexpressible the arch beneath the heaven, as he reasons about these things in his treatise on names. But the great Iamblichus, taking the great heaven as a certain order of the intelligible gods (and in one place he takes it to be the same as the Craftsman), says that the order set next under the heaven, and as it were girding it, is the arch beneath the heaven. He writes these things in his commentaries on the Phaedrus. Let no one think, then, that we make any innovation in the theology of this order, or that we are the first to divide the arch beneath the heaven from the heaven; we are chiefly persuaded by Plato, who distinguishes these three orders, the place above the heaven, the heavenly circuit and the arch beneath the heaven; and after Plato by those who have studied his thought with inspiration, Iamblichus and Theodorus. For why need I speak of our leader, Syrianus, who was truly a Bacchant, possessed by the god as the followers of Dionysus are, in a remarkable way in all that concerns Plato, and who made the wonder of Plato's thought, and the amazement that goes with it, shine out down to our day?

flags.taylor: who was truly a Bacchus
flags.why: A Bacchant (bakchos), one possessed by Dionysus: Plato's Phaedo 69c, "many carry the wand, but few are Bacchants", meaning true philosophers.

notes: Theodorus of Asine (4th century), a pupil of Iamblichus and of Porphyry; his treatise on names is lost.

paragraphs.modern: Syrianus, then, in his treatise on the harmony of Orpheus, Pythagoras and Plato, has unfolded most perfectly the character of this order, the arch beneath the heaven. The two wise men just named differ very much from each other in their thought. For Theodorus, calling the first cause Ouranos, can no longer let the heaven be sight that sees the things above, as Socrates in the Cratylus explains the name. For the first God neither sees nor is sight, nor is lower than anything. So Theodorus does not accept this explanation of the name, nor does he praise the place above the heaven, as Socrates does under divine inspiration. For there is no place, nor intelligible, of the One, nor any multitude of Forms, nor does the kind of souls go up beyond the first God, since there is nothing beyond him. The divine Iamblichus, since he supposes that Ouranos exists, undefined, after the first cause, and has not given the character of its hyparxis, is free of the doubts just mentioned; but he should teach us what the heavenly order is, how it exists, and what kind of gods before the Craftsman completes it. But the one who has perfected everything on this subject, and confirmed all he said with arguments that cannot be beaten, is our teacher Syrianus, who looked at all the orders between the first God and the kingdom of the heaven, beheld the character of this order with his intellect, and gave us, his initiates, the exact truth about it. In this way, then, our fathers and grandfathers differ from one another; but all of them in common distinguish the arch beneath the heaven from the heavenly circuit.

flags.taylor: our fathers and grandfathers
flags.why: Proclus' teachers (Syrianus) and their teachers (Iamblichus, Theodorus), in the succession of the Platonic school. Taylor's brackets supply the end of the first sentence, which is broken off in the Greek.

paragraphs.modern: This too, then, we must suppose, and besides this, that this order of gods, the arch beneath the heaven, is set next under the heaven. So, since the heaven, being one and three, has the order that holds together, and the place above the heaven the highest order of the intelligible and intellectual gods, the arch beneath the heaven must surely end the middle procession of the gods, close this whole order and turn it back to its principle; it must receive an order second to the heaven, but one which it turns round to the highest union; it must grow together with the middle kinds, but exist before the intellectuals. For these separate their kingdom from the heavenly power; but the arch beneath the heaven is united to the heaven and held by the heavenly order, which is also why it is called "beneath the heaven". As it is joined, then, to the heavenly circuit and exists next from it, it turns all second natures back to the intelligibles and perfects them by the intellectual look-out. For since the intellectual gods are generated by return, and turned round to themselves by one spherical union, the perfecting rule must be set next above them.

So I wonder at those who do not know this divine order, and do not keep the whole source of perfection; some of them betake themselves to entelechies, of whom we accept only this, that they too join the perfect with the form of holding-together. They do not know, then, the perfection that is separate from what underlies it, gladly embrace the likenesses of true perfections, and busy themselves with these. Others again give soul as the cause of perfection, not knowing that they are not claiming a perfection existing beforehand in eternity, and starting from the life that acts in time and has its perfection in periods. But a perfection whose whole exists at once must come before what is divided, and stable perfection before what is moved. For motion in time itself needs an end and an object of desire, and is unrolled about it part by part. Third, after these, others go back to intellect, and suppose that the first perfection is intellectual. For intellect is activity and intellectual perfection; but it longs for divine perfection, exists about it, and turns back to itself through it. So the cause of return must exist before the intellectual kinds that turn back to divine perfection, and the leader of the one perfection must be spread out above the natures that are perfected.

flags.taylor: betake themselves to entelechias
flags.why: Aristotle's entelecheia, "being-at-the-end", the actual completeness of a thing (his definition of soul in On the Soul II.1); Proclus means the Peripatetics, who find perfection only in forms in their subjects.

paragraphs.modern: Rightly, then, does the arch beneath the heaven, before all intellectual natures, set up an order of gods that turns back and perfects all the second divine kinds. That is why Plato raises the gods and daemons who follow Zeus to this arch, and through it to the heaven and the place above the heaven. For when they go to the feast and the banquet, they climb up to the arch beneath the heaven. So through this they are perfected, share in the circuit of the heaven, and reach out to the intelligible. For the intelligible is what feeds and fills all things. The perfecting order, then, is set beneath the order that holds together. It perfects all the natures that go up to the intelligible, opens souls wide to receive divine goods, and lights up intellectual light. And holding in its bosom the second kinds of the gods, it sets all things in the holding circuit of wholes.

Through these things, then, Socrates too says shortly after that the souls raised with the twelve gods to intelligible beauty are initiated, that is, made perfect, in the most blessed of the mysteries, and through this initiation receive the mysteries with a pure soul, and are set in, and become watchers of, things inexpressible. So the initiation of the gods is there; the first mysteries are there. Nor is it at all surprising if Plato also lets us call the gods of this order teletarchs, rulers of initiation, since he says that the souls there are initiated, the gods themselves initiating them. For how else could we name the first sources of telete, initiation, than teletarchs? For I, seeing the gods so much at work even in the names themselves, do not see how they could be called otherwise. But initiation being one and three (for the perfecting gods are divided along with the gods who hold together), Plato calls its one union the arch beneath the heaven, as he calls the order that holds together Ouranos. And he points to the depth in it by granting that there is in it an extreme lowness and a steep path to the top of the arch. As in the order before this, then, we thought it right to set the intelligible at the summit, life at the depth, and the intellectual at the extremity that bounds the whole heavenly circuit, so in this perfecting order we must take the intelligible of the arch as its summit, naming it in the same way as the back of the heaven, because these are ranked with each other; take the depth, through which souls go to the summit, as ranked with life; and take the extremity that closes the whole arch as ranked with intellect.

flags.taylor: Teletarchs
flags.why: "Rulers of initiation" (teletarchai), the Chaldean name for the gods of this third triad.

notes: The Phaedrus 247a-b ("steep is the way up to the arch beneath the heaven"), 250b-c.

paragraphs.modern: This whole order, which is united to the one before it, we must divide by analogy. For the perfecting gods are spread under the whole triad that holds together. One of them supplies the gods with stable perfection, setting all the gods in themselves and uniting them to themselves. Another is the first source of a perfection that generates wholes, stirring what comes first in being to providence for second natures. And a third leads the return to causes, turning everything that has proceeded back to its own principle. For through this triad everything perfect is self-sufficient and exists in itself; everything that generates is perfect, and generates full of vigour; and everything that longs for its own principle is joined to it through its own perfection. Whether, then, you take the power of nature that perfects what is generated, or the perfect number of the soul's restorations to where it began, or the perfection of intellect set in one by activity, all these hang from the one perfection of the gods, and, referred to it, some have a greater and others a smaller portion of perfect hyparxis; and every perfection proceeds from there. In short, perfection is threefold. One is before parts, such as the perfection of the gods. For this has its existence in unity, existing beforehand self-perfectly before all multitude. For such is the one of the gods: not like the one of souls or of bodies, since these are joined in kinship with multitude and mingled with beings. But the henads of the gods are self-perfect and exist before beings, generating multitudes and not generated along with them. Another perfection is made of parts and completed through parts, such as the perfection of the world; for it has its all-perfectness from its fullnesses. And a third, other perfection is that in parts; for so too each part of the world is perfect. For as this universe is a whole made of wholes, so it is perfect from the perfect parts in it, according to Timaeus. And in short, perfection is divided in the same way as wholeness; for, as Timaeus says, they are joined with each other.
notes: Timaeus 32d-33a: the world is "whole and perfect from wholes and perfect parts". Taylor's footnote corrects "generative" to "stable" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: So the perfecting kind grows together with the holding kind, and the perfecting monad is ranked beneath all the holding kinds. And as the wholeness of the heaven that holds parts together is threefold, so perfection is threefold. And if I must give my own opinion, all the perfections come from all the leaders; but the perfection before parts belongs more to the first leader, that made of parts to the middle, and that in a part to the third leader. Before this triad, though, is the intelligible triad, which is one-like perfection and an all-perfect hyparxis, and which Timaeus too calls "perfect in all respects". There the three perfections existed beforehand in a united way, or rather there was one source of every perfection. As the holding triad, then, is the unfolding of intelligible holding-together, and the gathering triad of the unifying and first in the intelligibles, so the perfecting triad is the image of the all-perfect triad. For the intelligible and intellectual gods proceed in answer to the intelligible triads. Perfection, then, is threefold: before parts, from parts, in a part. In another way, too, perfection is stable, generative, and turning back. And in another, there is one perfection of intellectual and undivided beings, another of the beings of soul, and another of the natures divided about bodies. Very rightly, then, there are three leaders of perfection before the intellectual gods, who make one order beneath the heavenly circuit, raise through themselves all second natures to the intelligible, perfect them with intelligible light, turn them back and join them to the kingdom of the heaven, give an unflagging activity to the natures perfected, and guard their undefiled perfection.
notes: Timaeus 31b: the living being itself is "perfect in all respects". Taylor's footnote corrects "that" to "holding" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Such are the ideas that may be taken from Plato about the third triad of the intelligible and intellectual orders, which at one time he calls the arch beneath the heaven, with a summit, middle and extremity, and at another a blessed mystery, the most ancient and holy of all mysteries, through which he raises souls and joins them to the mystic fullness of the intelligibles. For this triad opens the heavenly paths, being set beneath the heavenly circuit, and shows the self-shining appearances of the gods, which are whole and firm, and open out to the mystic beholding of intelligible sights, as Socrates says in the Phaedrus. For telete, being perfected, comes before muesis, closing the eyes, and muesis before epopteia, watching. So in going up we are initiated (teleioumetha) by the perfecting gods. We see with closed eyes, that is with the pure soul itself (muoumetha), whole and steady appearances, through the gods who hold together, among whom is intellectual wholeness and the firm setting of souls. And we become set in, and watchers of (epopteuomen), the intelligible watch-tower, through the gods who gather wholes. We speak of all these in relation to the intelligible, but we gain a different thing by a different order. For the perfecting gods initiate us into the intelligible through themselves, and the gathering monads are, through themselves, the leaders of the beholding of intelligibles. There are many steps up, but all of them reach to the fatherly harbour and the fatherly initiation. In this may the teletarchs, the leaders of all good, also set us, lighting us up not by words but by deeds. May they think us worthy to be filled with intelligible beauty under the great Zeus, and free us wholly from the evils of generation with which we are now walled round. And may they light up for us this most beautiful fruit of the present study, which, following the divine Plato, we have given well enough to those who love the contemplation of truth.
notes: The Phaedrus 250b-c. Taylor's head for this chapter explains the three grades of initiation, as his note on IV.9 does.

paragraphs.modern: Let us now again follow Parmenides in another way, who after the intelligible triads generates the intelligible and intellectual orders, and unfolds the continuous procession of divine natures through conclusions that follow one another. For the link of the words and their dependence on each other imitate the unbreakable order of things, which always joins middles to extremes, and proceeds through middle kinds to the last processions of beings. This, then, we must look at before the particular ideas: how the intelligible and intellectual triads proceed in answer to the intelligible triads, so that we may grasp by reasoning the well-ordered arrangement of things. There were three intelligible triads, then: the one being, the whole, and unlimited multitude. And three intelligible and intellectual triads have also appeared to us: number, the whole, and the perfect. So from the one being comes number; from the intelligible whole, the whole in these; and from unlimited multitude, the perfect. For the unlimited there was all-powerful and all-perfect, holding all things but itself not held. To the all-powerful and all-perfect, then, the perfect answers, having a perfection that is intellectual and second to the first-producing and intelligible perfection. The whole that is both intelligible and intellectual is akin to the intelligible whole, but differs from it, in that the intelligible whole has wholeness by the one union of the one being; but in this one the one appears by itself to be a whole made of unitary parts, and being appears made of many beings. These wholenesses, then, being divided, differ from the wholeness that comes before by union and is intelligible. For the wholenesses of this whole are parts of the intelligible wholeness.
notes: The Parmenides 142b-145a: the one being, the whole, unlimited multitude, number, the whole with parts, the limited and unlimited, beginning, middle and end, shape.

paragraphs.modern: Third, then, we must consider number as answering to the one being. For the one being is there in a hidden, intelligible and fatherly way; but here, together with difference, it generates number, which sets up the separation of Forms and forming principles. For difference itself first shines out in this order: among intelligibles it was power and the dyad, but here it is motherly, a fertile source. For there power gathered the one and the one being, which is why it was inexpressible, existing hidden in the one and in hyparxis. But here difference separates being and the one. After this it also multiplies the one, which proceeds generatively, and calls being out into second and third processions, breaking being into many beings and dividing the one into more partial henads, each of these completing the lessenings while the wholes remain. Rightly, then, does Plato draw the denials of the One from here. For here the many exist, through difference, which divides being and the one; since the whole too which is denied of the One is intellectual and not intelligible. The denial, then, says that the One is not a whole, so that the affirmation is that the one is a whole. This whole, though, is intellectual and not intelligible. Parmenides also denies the many, thus: "The One is not many"; and the opposite of this is that the one is many. The multitude of intelligibles, though, does not make the one many, but makes the one being many. And in short, every intelligible is marked by the one being. For in the intelligible, being and the one are folded together and grow together, and being is most unitary. But when each of these proceeds into multitude, they are separated from each other and show a greater difference toward each other. Each of these too is divided into multitude by the fertile nature of difference. From these things, then, it is clear that the intelligible and intellectual orders, answering to the intelligible orders, proceed with lessening.

flags.taylor: The negation therefore says that the one is not a whole
flags.why: The Parmenides 137c-d: in the first hypothesis the One "is not a whole" and "is not many"; in the second (142d, 143a) the one being is a whole and is many. Proclus' rule is that each denial in the first denies of the One what the second affirms of an order of gods. Taylor's footnote corrects a word of the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: After this, let us discuss each of them, beginning as nature does. First, then, the intelligible and intellectual number appears to us, which is joined with multitude. For every number is multitude. But of multitude, one kind exists in a united way and another with separation. Number is separated multitude, for there is difference in it. For in the intelligible there was power and not difference, and this power generated multitude and joined it to the monads. Number, then, is continuous with intelligible multitude; and this is necessary. For the monad was there, and the dyad too; since the whole too was there, and was always monadic, and, becoming two, never ceases. So the monad and the dyad were there, which are the first, set-apart principles of numbers. And in them multitude was in a united way; since the monad, the source of numbers, and the dyad hold all multitude as cause, the first in a fatherly way and the second in a motherly way. That is why intelligible multitude is not yet number, but is set intelligibly in the one-like principles, I mean the monad and the dyad: generatively in the dyad, and in a fatherly way in the monad. For the third god was father and mother; since if the living being itself is in it, the cause of male and female must also exist there first. For these are in living beings. So according to Timaeus and according to Parmenides the motherly and fatherly causes are there, and in them the intelligible living beings and intelligible multitudes are held. From these first principles number, with difference, proceeds, and they generate the monads and dyads in number, and all numbers. For both the generative and the fatherly exist in these in a feminine way.

flags.taylor: the third God was father and mother
flags.why: In the Orphic theogony Phanes, whom Proclus sets at the third intelligible triad (the living being itself), is male and female at once.

paragraphs.modern: All the monads of this triad too are fatherly. So before other things they share in the monadic cause, but by the power of difference. For there, I mean in the intelligible, the motherly was in a fatherly way; but here the fatherly exists in a motherly way, just as there the intellectual exists intelligibly, and here the intelligible intellectually. From that order, then, the first number exists next, but being generated in answer to the first triad of intelligibles, it plainly proceeds from it too. So Parmenides, beginning his account of number, reminds us of the first supposition through which he generates the one being, saying that the one shares in being and being in the one, because this exists by that triad. And rightly. For being intelligible and intellectual, so far as it has an intelligible rank among intellectuals it proceeds from the summit of the intelligibles, and so far as it comes before the intellectual orders, from the intellectual of the intelligibles. In that intelligible triad, though, the one was of being and being of the one, through the inexpressible and hidden union of these two and their existence in each other. But in the intelligible and intellectual triad, difference appears, the image of the hidden and inexpressible power in the first triad of intelligibles, and, putting forth its own activity in the light, separates the one from being and being from the one, leads each into divided multitude, and so generates number as a whole. For number, as we have often said, is divided and not united multitude, and exists from the principles by a second procession, not set hidden in the principles. So it is simply different from multitude. Among intelligibles there is multitude, among intellectuals number. For there number is as cause, but here multitude is by sharing. For there division exists intelligibly, but here union exists intellectually. If number, then, proceeds from these and has such a rank, Parmenides rightly mentions these triads especially, saying that the one shares in being and being in the one, and that through these the many appear. For one of these is the shining property of the first triad, and the other of the third. In the first triad the sharing was the existing-beforehand of the union of the one and being; but in the third triad many intelligibles appear, Plato all but proclaiming that the most splendid of intelligibles exists by intelligible multitude, though multitude is there in a hidden and one-like way. For in each order of divine natures multitude is generated, as is fitting, at the extremities.
notes: The Parmenides 143a. Taylor's footnotes supply "and being of the one" and correct "or" to "the" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: The intelligible number of the intellectual kinds, then, proceeds from these and through these. It has properties that human reasonings cannot grasp, but which divide into two first-producing powers: the power that generates wholes, and the power that gathers all processions into union. By the monad it gathers intellectual multitude and joins it to the intelligibles; by the dyad it brings multitude out and separates it by difference. By the odd number it gathers the many orders into undivided union; by the even number it brings all the kinds of gods fertilely into light. For being set as the middle of the intelligible and intellectual gods, and completing their one bond, it is carried in its summit by the intellectuals as in a vehicle; but united to the intelligibles, it unfolds intelligible multitude, and calls its hidden and unitary nature out into separation and fertile generation. It also gathers the intellectual into union and undivided communion. And not only this: generating all things down to the last of things, by the cause, beyond grasp, of the dyad and the nature of the even number, it again unites the natures that proceed, and turns them round by the monad and the sameness of the odd number. Through unity and the dyad it produces, gathers and binds all things intelligibly, in a hidden and unknown way, to the intelligible, and does this even in the last matter and the traces of Forms it holds. Through the even and odd number it sets up the two columns: the life-giving and the unchanging, the fertile and the effective; all the undivided kinds of making and life-producing powers; the powers that rule over divided life or divided production; the more intellectual and single natures of the world, which belong to the better column; and the more irrational and multiplied natures, which complete the lower series. And again, through this divided generation we may see that each of the natures that proceed is at once united and multiplied, undivided and divided in its causes, and separated from them by lessening. We give the better and simpler things to the nature of the odd number, and the less good and more various to the nature of the even. For everywhere the odd number leads undivided, simple and unitary goods, while the even is the cause of divided, various and generative processions. And so we may see all the orders of beings woven together by divine number, which is most ancient, intellectual, and set apart from all the kinds that are counted. For number must exist before what is numbered, and before what is separated there must be the cause of all separation, by which the kinds of the gods are divided and distinguished in order by their fitting numbers.

flags.taylor: the two coordinations
flags.why: The two "columns" (systoichiai) of opposites in the Pythagorean table (Aristotle, Metaphysics I.5, 986a): limit and unlimited, odd and even, one and many, and so on, the better column and the worse. Taylor's footnote supplies "brings out" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: If, then, among intellectuals there are divisions, contacts and separations of the natures that proceed, and communions too of the natures ranked together, there must be number before intellectuals, which divides and gathers all things intelligibly by its own powers. And if all things exist in a hidden, intelligible, unknown and set-apart way in this summit, there is a number of them, and a character unitary and without separation. Number, then, exists in the middle bond of intelligibles and intellectuals, spread out above the intellectuals through intelligible goods, but beneath the intelligibles through intellectual separations. It is made like the intelligibles by the power that gathers many things into union, and like the intellectuals by the power that generates the many from the one. And from this highest look-out of the intellectual gods it sets up the first intellectual numbers themselves, which have the nature of Forms, are universal, and rule over all generation and production. It also sets up the second numbers, which are above the world and life-giving, and measure the gods in the world. As third numbers it sets up these heavenly governors of the everlasting circuits, who turn all the spheres round by their intellectual causes. And as the last numbers it sets up the powers that, in the region beneath the moon, hold together and bound the unlimited and unstable nature of matter by Forms, numbers and forming principles, through which the wholes and parts of all mortal natures are made various with their own numbers. Everywhere it binds the leading and more perfect kinds of gods by the odd number, and the lower and second kinds by the even. So in the intellectual orders it produces the female and fertile by the even, but the male and fatherly by the odd. In the orders above the world it marks likeness and the unchanging by the odd number, but unlikeness and the procession into second natures by the even. For so the Athenian Stranger too orders that in sacred worship odd things be given to the heavenly powers and even to those of the earth. And in each of these kinds, what is more ruling must be referred to the odd number, and what is lower to the even.
notes: The Laws IV 717a-b: "the even and the left" to the gods below, "the odd and the right" to the Olympians. Taylor's footnote supplies "in this summit" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: The nature of number, then, runs from on high down to the last of things, ordering all things and holding them together with fitting Forms. For how could a perfect number hold the period of the whole world, as the Muses in Plato say it does? How could numbers, some of which bring fertility and others barrenness, hold the descents of souls? How could some of them set the ascents of souls in shorter periods and others in longer, as Socrates says in the Phaedrus, where he gives us restorations of three thousand and ten thousand years? Or how could time itself, which holds in a unitary way the measures of souls, proceed by number, as Timaeus says it does, unless divine number existed before all these, giving all things a ruling cause of order by numbers? Since all things, then, exist through numbers and Forms, numbers have their procession from the intellectual summit. But Forms have their generation from intelligible Forms. For Forms exist first in the third triad of intelligibles, but numbers are first in the first triad of intellectuals; since also in their effects every number is a Form, but not every Form is a number.

flags.taylor: the Muses in Plato
flags.why: The Republic VIII 546a-d: the Muses' riddle of the "perfect number" that holds the period of a divine generated thing, and the "geometrical number" that rules better and worse births. Taylor's footnote corrects "intellectual" to "intelligible" in the Greek he translated.

notes: The Phaedrus 248e-249a (ten thousand years; three thousand for the philosopher); Timaeus 37d ("an eternal image moving according to number").

paragraphs.modern: If, though, we must plainly unfold the truth, numbers are also before Forms. For there are numbers beyond being, but there are no Forms beyond being. And by this reasoning every Form is a number, as the Pythagoreans said. For Timaeus, being a Pythagorean, says not only that there are intelligible Forms but intelligible numbers too; for he says the intelligible Forms are four. There, though, number is intelligibly and monadically, as cause. For the intelligible living being is a monad, holding the whole of number in a hidden way. But in the summit of the intellectuals number exists separately, unfolding the number that exists beforehand in the monad as cause and one-like. For there is a difference, I think, between saying multitude in its cause and multitude from its cause, and between saying united and separated multitude. The first comes before number; the second is number. So according to Timaeus there are intelligible numbers with Forms and before Forms; and according to Parmenides number is after multitude. For Timaeus calls the one-like and hidden multitude the number of the Forms. But since number is first in the gods, and Forms share in the divine henads, he calls the first Forms four. For the monad and triad were first in the gods themselves, and secondarily in the intellectuals: beyond being in the first, in the manner of Forms in the second. Among intelligibles, then, multitude was in a unitary way, but among intellectuals it exists separately. And where there is separation there is number, as we have often said. So all the kinds of gods are generated from here too. And they are divided: the fatherly and generative among intelligibles and intellectuals; the making and life-giving among intellectuals. The kinds that bind through likeness are divided among the natures above the world; those both set apart and distributed, among the liberated gods; and the heavenly and sublunary kinds among the gods of the world. In short, all the columns of beings receive their distinction and separation from this order. From these things, then, it is clear what characters the intelligible and intellectual number has, and what it causes for the gods.

flags.taylor: there are indeed superessential numbers, but there are not superessential forms
flags.why: The henads, the gods, are numbers beyond being (Proclus, Elements of Theology, props. 113-118); the Forms all belong to being. Taylor's footnote corrects "beneath the heaven" to "heavenly" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Next, we must say also that the first number is of a feminine nature. For in it difference first shines out, separating the one from being, dividing the one into many henads and being into many beings. What, then, is this difference which is the cause of these things to the gods? If we should call it a kind of being, first, how is it before being? For, separating being and the one, it is ranked between both. Existing as a middle, it calls the one out into generations, and fills being with a generating cause. If, then, it is before being, how will it be some one kind of being? And second, the different that is a kind of being is everywhere of being, and is in no way in natures beyond being. But difference itself is present first to the henads themselves, and separates and brings out many henads from one. How, then, could difference beyond being ever be the same as the difference that completes beings?
notes: The Sophist 254e-255e: the "different" (to heteron) is one of the five greatest kinds of being. Taylor's footnote supplies "number" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Third, that different, which is a kind of being, appears among intellectuals by the making order. But difference itself is the intelligible summit of the intellectuals. The first exists together with sameness; the second exists by itself in the intelligibles of the intellectuals. Besides this, in what follows, Plato as he goes on mentions the different, and generates it together with sameness. How, then, would he draw the same conclusion twice? For he uses no such repetition in any of the other conclusions. The whole which he seems to take twice is not the same whole: the intellectual is not the same as the intelligible, but these, as we have said, differ from each other. For how could he unfold to us the different processions of divine natures if he gathered the same conclusions twice? By all these ideas, then, we must separate the difference that generates numbers from the kind of beings.
notes: The Parmenides 146a-147b: the one is "the same as and different from itself and the others".

paragraphs.modern: But if difference itself is not the nature of the different, but a power that generates beings, it will gather being and the one. For power everywhere has a hyparxis of this kind. For through power the one shares in being and being in the one. Power, then, was the cause not of division but of communion, of contact without separation, and of the relation of the one to being and of being to the one. So this difference must be ranked neither with intelligible power nor with the intellectual difference of beings; but, being the middle of both, it must exist in answer to intelligible power, and generate at the extremities of the intellectuals the portion of the different. What else, then, is it than the feminine nature of the gods? So it imitates intelligible power, and is fertile of many henads and many beings. And how else could it separate number from itself, and the Forms and powers of number, unless it were the cause of the divine processions in a feminine way? Multitude, then, is in a fatherly way among intelligibles, but in a motherly way among intellectuals. So in the first it exists monadically, but in the second by number. Rightly, then, in the second kinds of gods too, union comes from the male gods, and separation from the female. Limit proceeds from the males, and the unlimited from the females. For the male answers to limit, the female to the unlimited. The female, though, differs from unlimited power, in that power is united to the father and is in him, but the female is divided from the fatherly cause. For power is not only in the female gods but is also before them, since the intelligible powers are in the male gods, according to Timaeus, who says that the power of the Craftsman is the cause of the generation of everlasting natures. For the Craftsman says to the young gods, "imitating my power, produce and generate living beings." Power, then, is before the male and the female, in both, and after both. For it runs through all beings, and every being shares in power, as the Stranger from Elea says. For power is everywhere. But the female shares more in its character, and the male in union by limit. That the first number, then, which appears out of the intelligibles, is of a feminine nature, is clear through these things.
notes: Timaeus 41c; the Sophist 247d-e.

paragraphs.modern: It remains, then, to speak of its division into three, following Parmenides. Three things have appeared to us from the beginning, by the separation of the one from being: the one, difference and being; difference not being the same as either the one or being. For though the one and being were among intelligibles, difference first exists here. But since power above, among intelligibles, gathered, while here it separates the extremes, there are not only three monads but three dyads too: the one with difference, difference with being, and the one with being. For difference is also the cause of a separation of this kind, not keeping the union of the one being in its pure state. There are, then, three monads and three dyads. But these may also become three triads, when we begin at one time from the one, at another from being, and at another from difference. So this triad exists both monadically and triadically. But this is the same as to say that difference, the first feminine nature, generates in itself monads, dyads and triads. For taking them apart generates different monads for us; taking them together, dyads and triads, some ruled by the one, some by difference and some by being. And so far the first god appears, fertile of the first numbers: by the one, of unitary numbers; by difference, of generating numbers; and by being, of numbers of being.
notes: The Parmenides 143a-d.

paragraphs.modern: But since from this god, which is intelligible, what is after it proceeds, the monad, dyad and triad must plainly each have fertile power. These powers Parmenides calls once, twice and thrice. For each of these is a power that causes the beings already mentioned, which produce either separately or together. For there, as to their generations, some are wholly their own and others common to second natures. Their offspring, then, are the oddly odd, the evenly even and the evenly odd. Of these the oddly odd, as we said before, gathers the divine processions into union. The evenly even generates wholes, and proceeds down to the last of things. The evenly odd is mixed, existing from both the even and the odd. So we must set the first as answering to limit, the second to power, and the third to being. And you may see how in the first order all things existed first, monad, dyad and triad, but in this order all things exist secondarily and lower. And the mixture, the triad, existed there in one way, but here the evenly odd exists in another. For there the extremes were odd, because they were intelligible; but here the even is more abundant, and only the intelligible summit is odd. For the middle of the triad answers to power. There is the monad, which has all the Forms of odd numbers as cause; the dyad, which is all the Forms of even numbers in a hidden way; and the triad, which is number first. But here both odd and even number now exist in two ways, in one place unmixed and in another mixed. All things, then, are here fertilely, but there in a fatherly and intelligible way. That monad, though, does not proceed from the intelligibles, but exists in them in unproceeding union. So after these and from these we may see the whole of number existing by a third procession. "For these things," says Parmenides, "being there, no number will be lacking." Every number, then, is generated through these in the third monad, and both the one and being become many, difference separating each of them. Every part of being shares in the one, and every henad is carried as in a vehicle in some portion of being. Each of these, though, is multiplied, separated intellectually, divided into the smallest parts, and proceeds without limit. For as among intelligibles we give unlimited multitude to the third triad, so here we give unlimited number to the third part of this triad. For everywhere, in short, the unlimited is the extremity, as proceeding in an all-perfect way, holding all second natures, but itself shared by none of them. In the first monad, then, there were powers, but intelligibly. In the second there were processions and generations, both intelligibly and intellectually. And in the third there was all-powerful number, unfolding the whole of itself into light, which Parmenides also calls unlimited. It is especially clear, too, that this unlimitedness must not be carried over to quantity. For how can there be an unlimited number, since unlimitedness is hostile to the nature of number? And how are the parts of the one equal to the smallest parts of being? For among unlimited things there is no equal. But this has been thought worth attention by those before us.

flags.taylor: the oddly-odd, the evenly-even and the evenly-odd
flags.why: The Parmenides 143e-144a: "even times even, odd times odd, even times odd, odd times even", products of two and three. Proclus maps them on limit, power and being. Taylor's footnote supplies "the evenly odd" in the Greek he translated.

notes: The Parmenides 144a ("no number will be lacking"), 144e (the one is "divided by being" into as many parts as being).

paragraphs.modern: The division into three, then, having been shown by us, we shall briefly note that the one appears to be many by this order, the one itself proceeding into a multitude of henads, and being likewise coming to be together with the one. For those three monads are the intelligible grasps of all orders; they rule at once over all the processions from the intelligibles, produce them all in a set-apart way, and gather them to the intelligible causes. But since Plotinus places number before the living being itself, and says that first being produces number from itself, and that number is set as a middle between the one being and the living being itself, and is the base and place of beings, it is worth speaking briefly about this too. If he says that the living being itself has intelligible and hidden number, as held in the monad, he speaks rightly and agrees with Plato. But if he says that the living being itself holds number already separated, existing in many forms, the offspring of difference, intelligible multitude is not of that kind. For there the one is being, and being is the one. So the living being itself is perfect in all respects. But in number the one is separated from being and being from the one, and each of the parts is no longer an intelligible whole, as the living being itself is. For that is a whole of wholes; everywhere in its parts the one was with being, and the living being itself was only-begotten. But number proceeded after the two columns, I mean the monad and dyad, the odd and the even. How, then, can we place the first number in the living being itself? If someone says that number is there, it is there as cause and intelligibly; but it is separated intellectually by difference. Further, besides these things, if someone looks at the living being itself in the making order, and calls it the fullness of the Forms and the intelligible of the making intellect, it will in this way have intellectual number, as ranked near the intellectual end. But if he calls the intelligible living being number, there will be separation and difference in the gods whom we have said are set above the whole of things by highest union. For all cutting and division begins from the intellectual gods, since here difference proceeds, ordering things together with the one and being. How, then, does the division of the henads into the smallest parts, or the many-formed nature of beings, belong to the intelligibles? And how can the multitude of all Forms agree with the first living being itself? For the tetrad was there, divided by the monad and triad, a division of this kind fitting the third order of intelligible Forms. For as the one being is a monad, and eternity is a monad and dyad (for being is joined with "always"), so the living being itself is a monad and triad. But since it holds in itself the cause of all number, Timaeus calls it the tetrad that holds the four first-producing causes. For the tetrad itself exists beforehand as the source of all the production of Forms. But among intelligibles the monad, dyad and triad exist in a unitary way, and among intellectuals in a divided way.

flags.taylor: Plotinus admits that number is prior to animal itself
flags.why: Plotinus VI.6.8-9 (On Numbers): number, "the base and place of beings", comes after being but before the living being itself, which is "a numbered living being".

notes: Timaeus 31b ("only-begotten"), 39e-40a (four Forms).

paragraphs.modern: Difference, then, necessarily generates all these for us with separation. For everywhere the first of the lower natures have the proper form of the natures that exist before them. So the first multitudes proceed from the One, but they are unitary, without separation and without number, imitating the one principle of the whole of things. Rightly, then, does Parmenides set multitude among intelligibles at the end of the intelligible order, but number among intellectuals at the beginning of the intelligible and intellectual order. And these are joined to each other. Parmenides also sets unitary and intelligible multitude beforehand as the cause of intellectual numbers. And Timaeus shows that the living being itself is only-begotten because it was the cause of the whole of things monadically, not dyadically, nor by divine difference. That number, though, is the first thing among intellectuals we have shown at length.
notes: Taylor's footnote corrects the Greek of the first sentence ("the first of the lower natures have the proper form of the natures that exist before them").

paragraphs.modern: Parmenides begins to speak about number thus: "Go on, then, and consider this further. What? We say that the one shares in being, so far as it is. We do. And for this reason the one being appeared many." He completes his account of the first monad thus: "Are not three odd and two even? How not?" Of the second monad thus: "Then there will be even times even, odd times odd, odd times even, and even times odd." And he completes his account of the third and all the following triad thus: "Then not only is the one being many, but the one itself, distributed by being, must also be many. Altogether so." The first triad, then, of the intelligible and intellectual gods is unfolded to us by Plato through these things. By the first monad it has the first powers of numbers, I mean the odd and the even, and is completed through those principles that were among intelligibles in a hidden way, the monad, dyad and triad. By the second monad it has the second powers of numbers, which exist from the first powers. For the cutting of the Forms of the even number has a second rank, and the oddly odd is lower than the first odd numbers. And by the third monad it has the more partial causes of divine numbers. So here are separation into the smallest parts, unlimitedness, all-perfect division, and number both unitary and of being: receiving the unitary and the being-like from unity and being, but the separation of number from difference. For everywhere difference is in the three monads, but it unfolds the multitudes of numbers especially by the third monad, generates more partial gods, and divides being together with the gods. For neither is godhead in these unshared, because unity is not separate from being, nor is being without godhead, because being too is not without the one.
notes: The Parmenides 143a-144e.

paragraphs.modern: Since all things, though, are in each of the monads, but in a unitary and intelligible way in the first, generatively and by the character of difference in the second, and intellectually and by being in the third, Plato, when he unfolds the first monad to us, rightly begins from the monad and goes on as far as the triad; when he teaches about the second, he begins from evenly even numbers and goes on as far as those that are evenly odd, both of which belong to the nature of the even number. And when he adds the third monad, he begins from being and goes back through difference to the one. For having shown that being shares in number, he leads us round from there to unitary number, using the way of return in thinking this monad.

But if we must look at the unknown character of divine numbers, and at how the first order of the intelligible and intellectual gods, and the number that exists by this order, is the most ancient of all numbers, first we should consider the unlimitedness Parmenides mentions, and see whether he does not say that intelligible multitude is unlimited on account of this number, because it is unknown and cannot be grasped by partial thoughts. For the all-perfect and all-powerful character of divine numbers is set apart from the grasp of divided natures such as ours. They are unknown, then, and so are said to be beyond unfolding and not to be searched out. For number, and multitude, even in the last of things have the unknown along with the known; and we cannot grasp the procession of every number, being overcome by unlimitedness. The ungraspableness of this power, which is unknown to the activity of step-by-step reasoning, is then held as cause in intelligible numbers and multitudes. For there would be no such thing in the last of numbers, unless the unknown existed beforehand in intelligible numbers, and unless the last numbers were the final imitations of the set-apart ungraspableness of the first.

flags.taylor: unknown according to a discursive energy
flags.why: Taylor's "discursive energy" here is step-by-step reasoning (dianoia), unlike the "discursive energies" of the Phaedrus in IV.4.

paragraphs.modern: Second, after this, we may add that unitary numbers are also unknown in themselves. For they are more ancient than beings, simpler than Forms, and, generating them, exist before the Forms we call intelligible. The most venerable of divine works show this, since they use numbers as having an inexpressible power, and through them accomplish the greatest and most secret works. And before these, nature, inexpressibly, by sympathy, gives different powers to different things, solar powers to some and lunar to others, and makes their productions agree with numbers. For in these monadic numbers too, the Forms of numbers, such as the triad, the pentad and the heptad, are one thing, and the unions of the Forms another. For each of these Forms is both one and multitude. So form is unknown by its highest union.

flags.taylor: the most venerable of divine operations
flags.why: Theurgy: the Chaldean rites, which used numbers (and stones, plants and names) for their hidden sympathy with the gods. Taylor's footnote corrects "each other" to "other things" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: If monadic number, then, shares in some unknown power, much more must the first number have this character, set apart from the whole of things in a unitary way. And besides this, we may also take up the power of numbers to lead upward: not only because they set the periods of natural restorations, bounding our unbounded course with fitting measures, perfecting us by these measures, and joining us to our first causes, but because number also has in a remarkable way a certain power of drawing toward truth, as Socrates says in the Republic, leading us from a perceptible nature to the intelligibles. If the last number has this character, then, what should we say of the first? Is it not that it unfolds intelligible light, persuades us most of all to be set among intelligibles, and announces to us through its own order the one-like power of the principles? If we say these things rightly, we shall admire Timaeus the more, who, having set time over the perfections of souls and of the whole world, through which it would become more like the living being itself, says that time proceeds by number, and measures by number the existence of whole souls. And as among intellectuals number is set above the heavenly circuit, gathering it and making it one, so among perceptible things Timaeus says that time, being number, measures the heavenly periods, and holds in itself the first causes of the perfection of the periods. And if Socrates in the Republic, in the speech of the Muses, speaks of the one whole period of the universe, which he says a perfect number holds, does it not appear through these things that divine number perfects wholes, restores them to where they began, and measures all periods? The power of gathering imperfect things to the perfect comes to all things from number, which raises souls from things seen to things unseen, lights up the whole world with the perfection of motion, and sets for all things measures and the order of periods. But if not only does a perfect number hold the period of a divine generated nature, but another, second number after it is master of better and worse births, as the same Socrates says, number will not only restore things to where they began but will also be generative. Plainly these exist in a divided way by the second and third periods of numbers, but at once and gathered together in the first of numbers. The first number, then, generates, measures and perfects what is generated.

flags.taylor: a divine generated nature
flags.why: The Republic VIII 546b: "for a divine generated thing there is a period which a perfect number holds". Taylor's footnote says Plato means every body that moves in an everlasting circle, as the heavens do.

notes: The Republic VII 523a-525b: number "draws toward being". Timaeus 37d-39d, on time. Taylor's footnote corrects the Greek to "leading us to the intelligibles from the perceptible nature".

paragraphs.modern: The first order of the intelligible and intellectual gods, then, is seen by Parmenides in this way. After this the order that holds the middle place of intelligibles and intellectuals, which a little before we called the order that holds together, appears. It is named in three pairs: one and many, whole and parts, limited and unlimited. For since the separation of henads and beings by number reaches it, the one and being, which we said difference divides, become wholes; and the things that proceed from them are their parts. Wholeness holds the parts together, and they are held by their wholeness, in one way by the one and in another by being. For there, I mean in the summit of the intellectual gods, unity was the cause of multitude while set apart from multitude, and generated the many. But here unity is ranked with multitude. So it is a whole that relates to many henads as to parts. But since the order that holds together is threefold, one part intelligible, another intelligible and intellectual, and another intellectual, the first monad exists by the one and the many, the second by whole and parts, and the third by the limited and the unlimited. For where the first triad ends, the second begins. So in the triad before this Parmenides concludes that the one is many; and in this triad he concludes the same together with what remains. There, though, the one generated unlimited things; but here the one holds the many, the whole the parts, and the limited the unlimited. So there unity is set apart from the many, but here it is ranked with multitude. So the first ranking generates the whole with the parts; and the existence of whole and parts produces what is limited and unlimited at once. For these follow one another: the one, the whole, the limited, and the things set as it were in the opposite column: the many, parts, unlimited things. The one itself is the principle of the rest. The whole now has a relation to parts and an image of the dyad, and proceeds into a ranking in relation to the parts. The limited is now multitude, sharing in limit and the one, and is as it were a triad. For it is neither limit alone, like the monad, nor unlimited alone, like the dyad, but shares in limit, which is first a triad. Everything limited, then, is a whole, but not every whole is limited. For the unlimited is a whole, whether multitude or magnitude. And every whole is one, but not every one is a whole. For what has no relation to multitude is not a whole. The one, then, is beyond the whole, and the whole beyond the limited.
notes: The Parmenides 144e-145a.

paragraphs.modern: In the same way, unlimited parts are said to be the parts of what is limited. For the unlimited has no existence of itself, which also shows that the unlimited is not in quantity in act but in potential. Not all parts, though, are unlimited; for by limit they are marked by one of the parts. And again, parts are many, but the many are not altogether parts. The many, then, come before parts, and parts before unlimited things. So as the many are to the one, so are parts to the whole, and unlimited things to the limited. And these three monads that hold together complete the middle order of the intelligible and intellectual gods. For unity supplies all the second orders with stable and intelligible holding-together. Wholeness holds together the processions of divine natures and produces one relation of the ordering of wholes. And the limited monad lights up the returns of second natures with holding-together to the natures before them. One of these answers to the one being, which is why it is intelligible; another answers to the third order, in which there was the one and the dyad that generates unlimited multitude. Such is the triad that holds together, which Parmenides shows us through these things. The one, then, is one and many, whole and parts, limited and unlimited multitude. Let no one be troubled that Plato calls the one, or being, unlimited multitude. For he calls the one and being unlimited in multitude when they have proceeded and are divided. For all multitude is referred to the intelligible unlimited; but divided multitude, which has proceeded perfectly, is unlimited most of all.
notes: Aristotle, Physics III.6: the unlimited exists only potentially. Taylor's footnote supplies "in act" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Since, then, all the first causes of the intellectuals are in this triad, and all things are sown in its bosom, the first Synocheus holds these causes as multitude, being himself an intelligible unity and as it were the flower of the triad. The second holds these causes secondarily, but ranked and multiplied together with them. And the third, with all-perfect division, holds together the multitude held in himself. Each of them holds together, but one as bounding, another as completing a whole, and another as uniting. Plato, then, made, and makes as he goes on, his proofs about the one. For the whole study is about the one. But plainly being is divided together with the one. For it has been said before, in general, that every godhead proceeding from there is shared, and every portion of being shares in godhead. But we must not stop at the one alone, but consider the same character as given to being in the second degree, since Plato too brings out the one itself by itself by the differences of the divine orders. This makes me wonder at those who think that all the conclusions of the second hypothesis are about intellect, and do not see that Plato, leaving being aside, looks at the one itself by itself as proceeding and generated and receiving different characters. For how, speaking about intellect, could he leave aside being, by which intellect has its existence, power and activity? For the one is beyond the nature of intellect; but being gives intellect its hyparxis, and intellect is nothing else than being. This opinion of theirs, though, may be refuted by many other arguments. But if the three gods who hold together are divided in the way described, and the intelligible holding god is one-many, the intelligible and intellectual is whole and parts, and the intellectual is limited and unlimited, each of them is rightly called "many". For each of the Synocheis by his own character is a multitude. For the first, about the many, receives many more partial Synocheis; the second receives them by parts; and the third by unlimited things. If, then, there are partial gods who have this character, they are held in this first triad.

flags.taylor: those who think that all the conclusions of the second hypothesis are concerning intellect
flags.why: Plotinus and Porphyry, among others, took the second hypothesis' "one that is" as Intellect, the second hypostasis, rather than the whole series of the gods. Taylor's footnote corrects "everlastingness" to "character" in the Greek he translated.

paragraphs.modern: Moreover, anyone can easily see how these things agree with what is written in the Phaedrus. For the holding one agrees with the back of the heaven, which holds these. For the one and the back are the same, holding the whole circuit in one simplicity. The whole is the same as the depth of the heaven, and as it were its mass. For the heavenly depth is a whole stretched from the back as far as the arch. And the end is the same as the arch. This, then, is clear beyond all things, and each of the other conclusions is to be referred to the same ideas. So from what has been said we may gather that these three things belong in a special way to the Synocheis: the one, the whole, and the end or limited. For what can so hold multitude together as the one ranked with it? What so holds parts together as the whole? And how could the end, the limit, not be the cause of binding together things carried toward the unlimited? It ends, then, their procession, and brings back their scattered cutting into the one being of holding-together. And so much about the triad that holds together.

But the third, as they say, to the saviour: let us also, following Plato in what remains, praise the perfecting order of the gods. Because the end of the order that holds together was the limited, the perfecting order has extremes. For the end, or limit, is the extremity. There the one was said to be limited, but here it is said to have an extremity, as receiving by sharing what can bound many things. And there the one was the end or limit, which also holds the unlimited together; but here, having an extremity, it will also have a middle and beginning, and will be perfect. For what is completed by all these is perfect. Here, then, the perfection that is made of parts appears. For the completing of the parts produces the perfect. Moreover, because such a one has a middle and extremes, it will have the shape of a circle, or be straight, or be mixed from the straight and the round. For all these need a middle and extremes, some simply and others with linking. Three characters, then, again appear to us: the first, which we said was to have extremes; the second, by the perfect; and the third, by shape. And there are also three perfecting leaders of wholes: one intelligible, another intelligible and intellectual, and the third intellectual.

flags.taylor: But the third, as they say, to the saviour
flags.why: A proverb from the Greek drinking custom: the third libation was poured to Zeus the Saviour, so "the third, to the saviour" meant "third time lucky", the last and best. Plato uses it (the Philebus 66d, the Republic IX 583b).

notes: The Parmenides 145a-b: the one "has extremes", "beginning, middle and end", and "some shape, straight or round or mixed of both".

paragraphs.modern: The intelligible leader, then, is said to have extremes, being ranked directly beneath the end of the gods who hold together, and holding all the intellectual orders intelligibly in his own boundaries. The intelligible and intellectual leader is defined by the perfect, holding in himself the beginnings, middles and ends of beings, and completing the middle bond of the whole perfecting triad. And the intellectual leader proceeds by threefold shape, being the cause of limit and divine perfection, giving bounds to things unbounded and intellectual perfection to things imperfect. This triad is produced by the triad that holds together; for the end in them is the cause of having the extremity. But it is also produced from itself. For what has extremes, having become a whole, sets up the perfect through its end or limit. And the perfect, holding beginnings, middles and ends, unfolds shape. And so the perfecting triad proceeds from above down to the last of things, reaching all things and perfecting both whole and partial causes.

Do you not see how each of the triads joins its own summit to the ends set above it? For the one-many was the end of the gathering and unknown triad, and the same is the beginning of the triad that holds together. The end of the triad that holds together was the limited, and this again is the beginning of the perfecting triad. For to have extremes shows what is made of ends or limits. And so the whole middle order is held together with and united to itself, and is truly the bond of the orders as wholes: it sets up a wonderful communion with itself, joins the intellectuals to the intelligibles, and turns them round to one undivided union, having above the intelligible and unknown triad, producing in the middle the triad that holds processions together, and at the end the rule that turns back, through which it turns the intellectual gods most nearly to the intelligible gods.

For why does intellect look to itself and is in itself? Is it not because it is bounded on every side, converges on itself, and turns its own activities round about itself? But why is it perfect and full of intellectual goods? Is it not because it shares first in the perfection of the leaders just named, and exists by them, having a self-perfect being and thinking? And how is it said to be a sphere, both by Plato and by other theologians? Is it not because it is the first to share in shape, and is shaped intellectually by it? All return, then, all perfection and every intellectual shape come to the intellectual gods from the perfecting triad. For the intelligible leader of perfection gives perfection to the ends, summits and hyparxes of wholes.
