The intelligible and intellectual leader bounds their processions, which reach from on high down to the last of things. And the intellectual leader holds in his own perfection the returns of all the gods, and bounds and perfects through shapes their processions without limit.
notes: Intellect as a sphere: Plotinus V.1.9, VI.5.10; Parmenides frag. 8.43 (being "like the mass of a well-rounded sphere").

paragraphs.modern: Looking to this division, then, we may see as causes many things found among other theologians. For why is one of the gods of the unknown triad carried in the first of the worlds, another in the middle breadth, and another in the extremity? Because the first of these was one-like, the second proceeded by difference, and the third by the unlimited number of beings. But why, of the three gods who hold together, is the first of the empyrean, the second of the aether, and the third of matter? Because the first exists by the one and holds the one world together; the second exists by the whole and divides the aethereal world; and the third, by the limited, rules over material unlimitedness. And why again are the teletarchs divided together with the Synocheis? Because the first, having extremes, guides like a charioteer the wing of fire. The middle, holding beginnings, ends and middles, perfects the aether, which is itself threefold. And the third, which holds by one union the round, the straight and the mixed shape, perfects matter, which is without shape and form: giving form (morphōsas) to the sphere of the fixed stars and the first matter by the round, to the sphere of the planets and the second matter by the mixed shape (for the spiral is there), and to the region beneath the moon and the last matter by the straight. For motions in a straight line are in this region. So the first triad is, in a one-like way, the cause of the division of the worlds. The second shows more of cutting and of procession into parts, yet does not show us the multitude of the worlds. And the third unfolds the seven worlds, the monad with two triads. So great is Plato's divine thought that from these things we may see the causes of what became plain after his time.

flags.taylor: one of the deities of the unknown triad carried in the first of the worlds
flags.why: The Chaldean Oracles' worlds: the empyrean (of fire), the aethereal and the material, divided again into seven (one empyrean, three aethereal, three material). The "gods who hold together" (Synocheis) and the "rulers of initiation" (teletarchs) are Chaldean names, set by Proclus in these orders.

flags.taylor: the wing of fire
flags.why: A Chaldean image: the soul's "wing of fire" that carries it up. Taylor's footnote supplies "the mixed" in the Greek he translated.

notes: "The spiral": the planets' motion, compounded of the circle of the same and the circle of the different (Timaeus 39a); "after his time" means the Chaldean Oracles (2nd century AD), which Proclus took as revealed.

paragraphs.modern: This, from what has been said, appears most wonderful: in each of the triads the middle marks the whole triad. So in the unknown triad difference is set as the middle between the one and being. In the triad that holds together the whole is the mark, which is the middle of the one and the limited. And in the perfecting triad the perfect is the mark, which is itself set as the middle between what has extremes and shape. For difference is the feminine itself and the fertile nature of the gods. The whole is itself the form of holding-together, binding many parts. And the perfect is itself the good of perfection, having beginning, middle and end, and joining the end to the beginning by the character of return. Being nothing else than a perfect governor, it is the cause of the character of these gods existing everywhere by the middle centres. So the whole order of the intelligible and intellectual gods may be seen as existing in the middle. For the intelligible gods are defined above all by hyparxes and summits, which is why they are called fathers and unitary gods; for the one and the father are the same in them. But the intellectual gods are defined by ends or extremities, and so all of them are called intellects and intellectual. The intelligible and intellectual gods, though, being middles, appear especially by the middles of the triads.

Further, this too may be considered in common about all these triads: that each, by its end, proceeds to the unlimited. For the end of the first triad is number; of the second, the unlimited in multitude; and of the third, the straight, which itself shares in the nature of the unlimited. The cause of this is that each triad, by its extremity, rides in the material worlds as in a vehicle, and holds by one cause the unlimitedness of the natures generated in them. Besides what has been said, we may see the order of the triads from their ends. For the end of the first triad is number; of the second, the limited and the unlimited; and of the third, the round, the mixed shape and the straight. It is clear, then, that the first triad is monadic, the second dyadic and the third triadic. The first answers to the one being, the second to the intelligible whole, and the third to the all-perfect whole. That these have this order toward each other has been noted before. In short, then, every intelligible and intellectual triad is joined by its summit to the intelligible, unfolds its own power by its middle, and holds by its end the unlimitedness of second natures. And here we shall end the teaching about the intelligible and intellectual gods.

chapters.head: That the subcelestial arch is the boundary of the intelligible and intellectual Gods, evinced from the peculiarities of it.
chapters.title: The arch beneath the heaven ends the intelligible and intellectual gods

chapters.head: Why Plato characterizes this order of Gods from the middle which it contains, and delivers the names of the extremes according to the habitude to this middle.
chapters.title: Why the order is named from its middle, the heaven

chapters.head: That Plato delivers the same mode of ascent to the intelligible, as is delivered by initiators into the mysteries.
chapters.title: Plato's way up to the intelligible is the initiates' way

chapters.head: What the supercelestial place is. How it proceeds from the first intelligibles. How it is supreme in intellectuals. And how Plato demonstrates its prolific power.
chapters.title: The place above the heaven: intelligible, and the mother of the gods

chapters.head: How Plato has indicated the unknown peculiarity of the summit of intelligibles and intellectuals, and why he celebrates it at one and the same time affirmatively and negatively.
chapters.title: Why the place above the heaven is praised both by denials and by affirmations

chapters.head: What the negations are of the supercelestial place. That they are produced from the divine orders. What kind of negations also designate the uncoloured, what, the unfigured, and what, the privation of contact.
chapters.title: What the three denials deny

chapters.head: What the things are which Plato affirms of the supercelestial place, and from what intelligible peculiarities, he ascribes to it affirmative signs.
chapters.title: What is affirmed of the place above the heaven

chapters.head: What the three deities of the virtues, viz. science, temperance, and justice, are in the supercelestial place; what order they have with respect to each other; and what perfection each of them imparts to the Gods.
chapters.title: Science, temperance and justice in the place above the heaven

chapters.head: What the plain of Truth, and what the meadow are. What the unical form of intelligible nutriment is. What the twofold nutriment of the Gods is which is distributed from this intelligible food.
chapters.title: The plain of truth, the meadow, and the food of the gods

chapters.head: Many admonitions that the supercelestial place is triadic. And what the signs are of the three hypostases in it.
chapters.title: The place above the heaven is a triad

chapters.head: Who Adrastia is. What the sacred law of Adrastia is. That she ranks in the supercelestial place. And on what account she does so.
chapters.title: Adrastia and her ordinance

chapters.head: A summary account of what is said about the supercelestial place, unfolding the peculiarities of it.
chapters.title: The place above the heaven in sum

chapters.head: Demonstrations that the connectedly-containing order is in the intelligible and intellectual Gods. And that it is necessary there should be three connective causes of wholes.
chapters.title: Why there must be gods who hold together, before the intellectual gods

chapters.head: That according to Plato the celestial circulation is the same with the connective order.
chapters.title: The heaven's circuit is the order that holds together

chapters.head: How we may obtain auxiliaries from what is said by Plato of the triadic division in the connective deity. And why he especially venerates the union in this triad.
chapters.title: The heaven is one and three: back, depth and arch

chapters.head: What the theology in the Cratylus is concerning Heaven. And how it is possible to collect from it by a reasoning process the middle of the intelligible and intellectual Gods.
chapters.title: Ouranos in the Cratylus: the middle of the middle gods

chapters.head: That the most divinely-inspired of the interpreters have defined the subcelestial arch to be a certain peculiar order. And that our preceptor has unfolded it in the most perfect manner.
chapters.title: Earlier interpreters on the arch beneath the heaven

chapters.head: Many admonitions that the peculiarity of the subcelestial arch is perfective, from what Plato has delivered concerning it, and from the souls that are elevated to it.
chapters.title: The arch beneath the heaven perfects: the teletarchs

chapters.head: What the triadic division is of the perfective order, which Plato has delivered in the subcelestial arch.
chapters.title: The three perfecting gods

chapters.head: What the elevation is of souls separate from bodies to the intelligible and intellectual triads. What the most blessed telete is. What muesis, and epopteia are. What the entire, simple, and unmoved visions are. And what the end is of all this elevation.
chapters.title: The ascent of souls, and a prayer to the teletarchs

chapters.head: How Plato unfolds in the Parmenides, from intelligibles the intelligible and intellectual orders. And what that which is common, and that which is different are, in the theology concerning these.
chapters.title: The Parmenides' second triads: number, whole and the perfect

chapters.head: How the intelligible and intellectual number proceeds from intelligibles. And in what it differs from intelligible multitude.
chapters.title: Number comes from the intelligibles and differs from intelligible multitude

chapters.head: How divine number adorns all beings. And what the powers in it are which are symbolically delivered from the division of number.
chapters.title: How divine number orders all beings: the monad and dyad, odd and even

chapters.head: How Parmenides has delivered the feminine and generative peculiarity [of first number] in what he says concerning number.
chapters.title: First number is feminine

chapters.head: How we may discover in what is delivered concerning number, the triadic division of the summit of intelligibles and intellectuals.
chapters.title: The first triad in the Parmenides: monads, dyads and triads, and every number

chapters.head: Whether it is proper to place number prior to animal itself, or in animal itself, or posterior to it.
chapters.title: Is number before the living being itself?

chapters.head: Whence Parmenides begins to speak about number. How far he proceeds in what he says about it. And how he unfolds the different orders in it.
chapters.title: Where Parmenides' account of number begins and ends

chapters.head: What the unknown is in divine numbers. What the generative is in them. And admonitions of these things from what is elsewhere said by Plato concerning numbers.
chapters.title: The unknown in divine numbers, and their power to lead up and to generate

chapters.head: How Parmenides delivers the middle order of intelligibles and intellectuals through the one, whole, and finite. And what the peculiarities are of these.
chapters.title: The middle triad in the Parmenides: one and many, whole and parts, limited and unlimited

chapters.head: Whence Parmenides begins to speak about this order. And how far he proceeds in what he says about it. How he likewise unfolds the three monads in it conformably to what is said in the Phædrus concerning them.
chapters.title: The middle triad in the Parmenides agrees with the Phaedrus

chapters.head: How Parmenides delivers the third order of intelligibles and intellectuals. And how he unfolds the perfective peculiarity, and triadic division of it.
chapters.title: The third triad in the Parmenides: extremes, the perfect, and shape

chapters.head: An admonition what the union is of the three intelligible and intellectual triads, from the conclusions of Parmenides.
chapters.title: How the three triads are joined

chapters.head: How many theological dogmas we may assume, through the order of the conclusions delivered by Parmenides in his discourse concerning the intelligible and intellectual Gods.
chapters.title: What Parmenides' order teaches about the Chaldean worlds

chapters.head: How the intellectual orders proceed from the intelligible and intellectual Gods. And according to what peculiarities they subsist.
What the division is of the intellectual Gods. And the progression according to hebdomads in this order of Gods.
Who the three intellectual fathers are according to Plato. What the three undefiled monads are. And who the seventh deity is, that is co-arranged with the two triads.
How from the writings of Plato, the procession of the intellectual Gods into seven hebdomads may be collected by a reasoning process.

Who the mighty Saturn is, according to the theology in the Cratylus. And how he is in a certain respect intelligible, and in a certain respect intellectual. In which also, the dogmas are discussed concerning the union of intellect with the intelligible, and its separation from it.
What the kingdom of Saturn is. In what manner it is delivered by Plato in the Politicus. And of what it is the cause to the world, to the mundane Gods, and to partial souls.
What the Saturnian life of souls is. And what peculiarities of this circulation the Elean Guest delivers.
How souls are said to be nourished by intelligibles. And what the difference is of the nutriment derived from different intelligibles.
What the orders are which the mighty Saturn causes to preside over wholes. In which also, who the Saturnian intellect is that is delivered in the Gorgias is unfolded.
How this God [Saturn] is peculiarly called by theologists insenescible, or free from old age. And how Plato has delivered this peculiarity of him.
Who the vivific Goddess is. How she is the collector of the Saturnian and Jovian kingdoms. And what orders she possesses conjoined with both these kingdoms.
Who the third father in intellectuals is. How he proceeds from the causes prior to him. And that he is the demiurgus of the universe.
Demonstrations that the whole demiurgus of the universe, is the third father of the intellectual Gods.

An answer to those who say that there are three demiurgi according to Plato, demonstrating through many arguments that the demiurgic monad is arranged prior to the [demiurgic] triad, in the third order of intellectuals.
That Timæus especially delivers the peculiarity of the demiurgus, by calling him intellect. And that this pertains to the third of the intellectual fathers.

How according to another method it is requisite to discover the peculiarity of the demiurgus. And how the demiurgus is called in the Timæus effector and father. In which also, it is clearly shown, where the paternal, where the paternal and at the same time effective, where the effective and paternal, and where the effective only are, according to Plato. And in short, in what effector and father differ.
How following Timæus, according to a third method, we may purify our conceptions concerning the demiurgic monad.
A theological explanation of the speech of the demiurgus in the Timæus, distinctly evolving our conceptions about the demiurgic energy.
What the second speech of the demiurgus is to divisible souls. In what it differs from the former. And how in this all the measures of the life of souls are defined.
A summary of all that is said about the demiurgus, following the doctrine of Timæus.
Admonitions from what is said in the Cratylus, that Plato attributes fabrication to Jupiter.
Admonitions from what is said in the Cratylus of the fabrication of Jupiter. In which also the concord is demonstrated of the theology from names, with the arrangement of the demiurgus in the Timæus.
Admonitions of the fabrication of Jupiter from what is demonstrated in the Philebus. In which also it is shown, what the royal soul, and the royal intellect are.
Demonstrations of the same thing, from what is said in the Protagoras about the political science.
An argument shewing that Jupiter is the demiurgus and father of the universe according to Plato, from what is said in the Politicus concerning the twofold circulation [of the universe.]
How Jupiter subsists according to cause in animal itself, and how animal itself is in Jupiter.
How Timæus attributes to the demiurgus the unknown and ineffable.
Why Timæus thinks fit to denominate animal itself, and is of opinion that it may be known, but leaves the demiurgus unknown and ineffable.
Concerning the Crater in the Timæus, a theology teaching what the genera are that are mingled in it, and how it is the cause of the essence of souls.
That the Crater in the Timæus is fontal. And admonitions from the writings of Plato, concerning the principle and fountain of souls.
That the three vivific fountains co-arranged with the demiurgus, may be assumed from what is said in the Timæus, viz. the fountain of souls, the fountain of the virtues, and the fountain of natures.
Admonitions concerning the undefiled Gods; that there are such Gods according to Plato; and what the peculiarity is of their essence.
More manifest demonstrations of the hypostasis of the undefiled Gods, according to Plato.

Admonitions through many arguments how it is proper to denominate the undefiled Gods according to Plato. In which also, the union of them, what their separation, and what their peculiarity are, is delivered.
How from what is mystically asserted by Plato, auxiliaries may be obtained, concerning the seventh monad of intellectuals.
How Plato delivers in the Parmenides the summit of the intellectual Gods.
How Parmenides unfolds the middle order of the intellectual breadth, and through what signs.
How Parmenides defines the third order of intellectuals, and through what peculiarities.

That the ruling order of Gods is in continuity with the intellectual Gods. And that the division into fountains and principles may be assumed from the writings of Plato, through the theory about souls.
How the ruling Gods proceed. And that the supermundane peculiarity pertains to these Gods alone.

What the peculiarity is of the ruling Gods. That the assimilative is especially characteristic of them. And how the causes of assimilation are antecedently assumed in the demiurgus; and how in the intelligible paradigm.
What the powers are of the assimilative Gods. What their energies. And how many goods are imparted by them to the world, and to all mundane natures.
What the divisions are of the assimilative Gods. And that the greatest part of the discourse about them is concerning the middle orders in them.
Many demonstrations, that both according to Plato and other theologists, there is one demiurgus prior to the three demiurgi.
That Jupiter is twofold; one indeed, being prior to the three sons of Saturn, [but the other being one of them.] And how the three proceed from Saturn, and the one Jupiter.
That according to Plato also, the demiurgic monad subsists prior to the three sons of Saturn. Demonstrations of this from what is said in the Politicus, and in the Laws.
More manifest admonitions of the same things from what is said in the Gorgias, and in the Cratylus.
What the vivific triad is among the ruling Gods. And whence we may derive auxiliaries from the writings of Plato concerning the union and division of this triad.

What the convertive triad of the ruling Gods is; and what the monad which it contains. In which also, the union of Apollo with the sun is demonstrated; and it is shewn, how from what is said about Apollo we may be led to the theory of the solar orders.
What the undefiled order is of the ruling Gods. And how from the writings of Plato conceptions about it may be obtained.
How Parmenides forms his conclusions about the ruling Gods, in continuity with the demiurgic order. And that he characterizes the whole order of them, through similitude and dissimilitude.
What the supermundane and at the same time mundane genus of Gods is. And how through their own medium they preserve the continuity of the Gods that proceed from the demiurgus.
How the liberated Gods are characterized. And how from their liberated peculiarity they are exempt from the universe, and are co-arranged with the mundane Gods.
What the common powers, and what the common energies are of the liberated Gods, according with the essence that has been delivered of them.
Concerning the twelve leaders or rulers mentioned in the Phædrus, and that they have a liberated order.
Many and clearer demonstrations that the great leader Jupiter, and all the dodecad of leaders, are liberated.
An explanation from precedaneous causes whence the number of the dodecad in the liberated Gods is derived.
What the division of the liberated leaders is into two monads and one decad. And what the one division of them is.
The theology concerning each of the twelve Gods, unfolding the peculiarities of them from the subjects of their government.

Concerning the mother of the Fates mentioned in the Republic. Likewise concerning the triad of the Fates. What orders they have with reference to each other. What powers of them are delivered through divine symbols. What their energies are. And how Plato characterizes the liberated peculiarity.
How Parmenides forms his conclusions concerning the liberated Gods immediately after the assimilative Gods. And how he characterizes the order of them by touching and not touching.
